articles.title: Three days of strikes, five Trump vetoes: Pentagon prepares for Iran war
articles.body:
The Pentagon has developed plans for a short but intensive military campaign against Iran, potentially lasting just three days and targeting its missile and drone arsenals, energy infrastructure and command centers. Yet despite the growing American military buildup in the Middle East, President Donald Trump has repeatedly refused to authorize a major new offensive, even as Iranian attacks on commercial shipping intensify.
The New York Times reported Thursday, citing U.S. officials, that Trump's national security team and the Pentagon have presented him with five proposals for significant military operations against Iran or the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen in recent months. He rejected all five, although he has once again instructed military planners to prepare options for renewed strikes.
On Thursday, Trump announced on social media that the United States would not attack Iran before the November midterm elections, adding that Washington and Tehran were “having productive discussions.”
The announcement came as American forces continued assembling one of their largest naval deployments to the Middle East in more than two decades, with three aircraft carriers expected to operate in the region by late October.
Despite the preparations, senior administration officials remain divided over whether another military campaign would achieve meaningful results, particularly as Iran has improved its military capabilities and American commanders warn of mounting pressure on U.S. missile defense stockpiles.
A three-day campaign targeting Iran's military infrastructure
The latest military planning was discussed last Friday at Camp David during a meeting of senior national security officials led by Vice President JD Vance.
The central proposal involves a concentrated campaign lasting approximately three days, intended to inflict significant damage on Iran's military capabilities without necessarily committing the United States to another prolonged conflict.
The potential targets include ballistic missile launchers and stockpiles, drone infrastructure and military facilities associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Energy installations and Revolutionary Guard headquarters and command posts are also under consideration.
American officials believe that Iran has rebuilt substantial portions of its missile and drone arsenal since the initial stages of the war, restoring capabilities that had previously been damaged.
Although Trump has ordered the preparation of updated military options, officials say his reluctance to resume large-scale combat has become increasingly apparent.
During the summer, American forces regularly carried out retaliatory attacks following Iranian strikes on international shipping. In recent weeks, however, Washington's response has become considerably more restrained.
The United States has continued operations against Iranian drones and cruise missiles but has refrained from launching major new strikes inside Iranian territory or attacking the country's shadow fleet of oil tankers.
Some members of Trump's inner circle have also become increasingly skeptical that another round of military action would persuade Tehran to change its position.
They argue that Washington's campaign of economic pressure is beginning to produce results and that additional time could force the Iranian leadership to make concessions without renewed large-scale fighting.
Other officials favor a more forceful approach, arguing that Iran's weakening economy could make it particularly vulnerable to a concentrated military campaign, especially one that undermines its ability to control maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
Three aircraft carriers, 20,000 personnel and hundreds of aircraft
As the White House weighs its options, the American military is assembling a force capable of launching major operations against Iran on short notice.
The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt, which departed San Diego last week, is expected to join the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington in the Middle East around the end of October.
The deployment would mark the first time since 2003, the year of the U.S. invasion of Iraq, that three American aircraft carriers have operated in the region simultaneously.
Each carrier strike group includes additional warships and supporting military assets, significantly expanding the range of offensive and defensive capabilities available to American commanders.
By the end of October, more than 20,000 sailors and Marines are expected to be deployed aboard vessels in the region, alongside hundreds of military aircraft.
The unusually large concentration of forces is not expected to last long. The George Washington is scheduled to return to its base in Japan after the Theodore Roosevelt arrives to replace it.
Military commanders are nevertheless prepared to launch a major operation within days if Trump reverses his position and authorizes renewed strikes.
The scale of the buildup has not resolved concerns about the potential consequences of another confrontation.
Senior defense officials are particularly worried that a new campaign could further deplete American stocks of defensive munitions, which have already come under considerable pressure during the conflict.
The United States must maintain enough interceptors to protect its forces in the Middle East while preserving defensive capabilities for other potential crises around the world.
Iran's military tactics have become more difficult to counter
One of the major complications facing American military planners is the improvement in Iran's ability to carry out attacks against U.S. forces and regional infrastructure.
Iranian forces have adjusted their tactics during the war, making missile attacks increasingly difficult to intercept and forcing American defense systems to expend more ammunition.
During the early stages of the conflict, U.S. forces generally launched two interceptors at incoming Iranian missiles, concentrating their defensive efforts on the most threatening attacks.
More recently, neutralizing Iranian missile salvos has required a greater number of interceptors, creating additional strain on supplies that are already stretched.
American intelligence assessments have also identified another challenge: Iranian forces have gained access to satellite imagery supplied by Chinese companies, improving their ability to identify and target American military installations.
People familiar with the intelligence assessments say the imagery has helped Iran conduct more effective attacks against U.S. bases.
American commanders are increasingly concerned about their ability to defend military installations housing U.S. personnel, as well as energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure across the region.
A renewed offensive could trigger additional Iranian retaliation, requiring even more defensive missiles at a time when the American military is attempting to preserve its remaining inventory.
The concerns have become an important factor in the debate over whether the benefits of another military operation would outweigh the risks.
Nearly 20 ships targeted as tensions rise in the Strait of Hormuz
Iran has continued to target commercial vessels in the Persian Gulf and surrounding waters, adding to concerns about the security of one of the world's most important energy transportation routes.
Since September, when the last major exchange of retaliatory strikes took place, Iran has attacked at least 13 vessels, according to a maritime monitoring group operated by the British Navy.
Intelligence assessments suggest the actual number could be closer to 20.
Despite the attacks, none has triggered a major American military response.
The increasingly restrained U.S. reaction marks a change from the summer, when Washington routinely retaliated against Iranian attacks on international shipping.
Although oil exports from the Middle East have increased, the continuing attacks have unsettled shipping companies and raised concerns about the longer-term reliability of regional energy shipments.
The Strait of Hormuz remains a central point of tension.
Trump claimed Thursday that none of the oil passing through the strait originated in Iran, but intelligence assessments indicate that the situation is more complicated.
Iran continues to permit certain vessels to transit the waterway, including ships that have paid passage fees and others potentially carrying Iranian oil.
Chinese companies have paid Iran for passage through the strait, while Tehran also operates a shadow fleet of tankers used to transport oil despite international sanctions.
Iran has additionally been accused of secretly blending its crude oil with Iraqi oil to disguise its origin and circumvent sanctions.
On Thursday, the U.S. Treasury Department announced sanctions against 17 vessels it identified as part of Iran's shadow fleet involved in oil smuggling.
The combination of maritime attacks, sanctions enforcement and uncertainty over future military operations has placed additional pressure on commercial shipping through the region.
Nuclear talks remain stalled as elections approach
Alongside the military preparations, diplomatic contacts between Washington and Tehran have continued through intermediaries.
American officials acknowledge that some progress has been made, but negotiations remain stalled over the sequencing of discussions about Iran's nuclear program.
Washington wants an agreement addressing Tehran's nuclear ambitions to come first, while Iranian negotiators insist that the nuclear issue should be left until the final stage of negotiations.
The disagreement has prevented the two sides from reaching a broader understanding, even as Trump maintains that diplomatic discussions remain productive.
The approaching elections in Israel and the United States have also influenced the administration's calculations.
Before Trump's public commitment not to attack Iran ahead of the U.S. midterms, American officials had already anticipated that he might postpone a decision until after Israel's parliamentary elections on October 27 and the American vote the following week.
The political timetable would allow the administration to assess its military and diplomatic options without launching another major conflict immediately before voters head to the polls.
Yet even after the elections, there is no certainty that Trump will authorize renewed attacks.
The president has repeatedly rejected military proposals despite pressure from some officials who favor a more aggressive response to Iran's actions.
Military commanders, meanwhile, continue preparing for the possibility that the administration will abruptly change course.
Supporters of additional strikes believe a short, intense campaign could exploit Iran's deteriorating economic situation and further weaken its military capabilities, particularly if it limits Tehran's ability to influence shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Others fear that renewed combat would produce another cycle of Iranian retaliation, increase the burden on American missile defenses and fail to resolve the underlying dispute over Iran's nuclear program.
For now, the United States is positioning enough military power in the Middle East to launch a major offensive while its president continues to favor delaying the decision.
With three aircraft carriers moving toward the region and operational plans already prepared, the central question is no longer whether the American military can launch another attack against Iran, but whether Trump will ultimately authorize one.

articles.title: The FSB's sabotage campaign in Europe: Russia's war on Western arms makers – and what it means for Ukraine
articles.body:
The FSB's sabotage campaign in Europe: Russia's war on Western arms makers – and what it means for Ukraine
A disaster was narrowly averted in Germany in summer 2026. On the night of 4-5 August, unidentified individuals attempted to attack Leipzig airport with three explosive-laden FPV drones. Their target was a Ukrainian Ruslan aircraft operated by Antonov Airlines. The Ruslans are an important link in the military logistics chain, transporting cargo not only for Ukraine but also for NATO countries more broadly.
A source familiar with the incident told Ukrainska Pravda that the Ukrainians had three strokes of luck that night. The explosive on the first drone failed to detonate, the second drone crashed into another aircraft, and the third never made it into the air. Police found it only a few weeks later on the outskirts of the airport. Something had apparently spooked the perpetrator.
According to Politico, investigators soon noticed similarities between the drone's warhead and other improvised explosive devices found in caches set up by Russian agents elsewhere in Europe.
The brazen sabotage attempt in Leipzig marked a new escalation in the hybrid war targeting Europe's military sites and defence industry facilities. OSINT analysts have noted that the attacks are becoming more frequent and increasingly systematic.
The Russians themselves are no longer hiding their hand: the arms factories of Ukraine's partners are in their sights.
"It's a secret. A military secret," Russian leader Vladimir Putin said when asked by reporters whether Russia could attack facilities in the UK defence sector.
Ukrainska Pravda looks at Russia's sabotage campaign across Europe and whether it could put continued support for Ukraine at risk.
Fifty incidents involving hybrid attacks in a month
Russia has repeatedly tried to put a bomb under EU support for Ukraine – both literally and figuratively.
The OSINT tracker Malcontent News has logged 497 acts of hybrid warfare across Europe since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. In 454 cases, its analysts identified direct links to Russian or Belarusian hybrid operations. The attacks have taken many forms: cyber-attacks, vandalism, sabotage, arson and incursions by unknown drones.
OSINT analyst Clément Molin estimates that 50 incidents have been recorded across Europe since the start of September alone, many of them likely linked to Russia's hybrid campaign. At least 10 incidents over the past two months have involved the defence industry or military logistics.
Russian intelligence services are behind the planning and organisation of these operations, but they turn to civilians to carry them out. Members of local criminal gangs serve as the Kremlin's intermediaries, seeking out recruits and paying them in cryptocurrency for each job. Former Wagner Group recruiters have also taken part in the process. Ukrainian migrants recruited by the FSB are also frequently among the perpetrators.
Using local residents gives sabotage operations a convenient cover, making them look like industrial accidents or acts of anti-war, environmental or pro-Palestinian activism. But the same approach can also undermine the operation itself. Untrained recruits are prone to mistakes that trained professionals would know how to avoid.
In Leipzig, it was precisely this kind of mistake that helped avert a tragedy.
Sabotage
Most acts of sabotage across Europe between 2022 and 2025 were not aimed at defence industry facilities. Instead, they appeared designed to threaten or intimidate. In most cases, police and counter-intelligence services managed to thwart the attacks – and, in some instances, even prevent assassination attempts.
For instance, in 2024, Russia planned to assassinate Armin Papperger, CEO of German defence giant Rheinmetall, which supplies weapons to Ukraine. The plot was foiled by the US and German intelligence services.
In 2026, the picture has changed dramatically. Defence industry facilities have been increasingly drawn into the sabotage campaign.
One of the most notable incidents was a fire at the Czech drone and optical systems manufacturer LPP Holding. The blaze damaged production facilities and destroyed stock in the warehouse.
Despite the damage, the company said the planned delivery of 40 attack drones to Ukraine remained on track. Czech police immediately determined that the fire had been deliberate and investigated it as a possible terrorist act.
A previously unknown pro-Palestinian group claimed responsibility, accusing LPP of manufacturing weapons for Israel. The company rejected the claim, saying it has no cooperation with Elbit Systems and does not manufacture equipment for Israel. LPP and Elbit Systems announced a partnership in 2023, but the deal was never realised.
LPP suggested that the pro-Palestinian cover story could have been a Russian covert operation aimed at disrupting the company's cooperation with Ukraine.
Another suspected act of sabotage targeted transformers and power-line pylons supplying KNDS and MBDA, major European defence companies that manufacture missiles and ammunition. The attack left 3,000 homes without electricity, and graffiti reading "Action against war" was found nearby.
And the Russians themselves did not stay silent.
On 15 April, Russia's Ministry of Defence released a list of 21 Ukrainian and European companies producing drones and drone components for Ukraine. It gave the addresses of their manufacturing facilities and named the sites themselves. The accuracy of the list is difficult to verify from open sources. But the message was hard to miss.
"When strikes become a reality depends on what comes next. Sleep well, European partners!" Dmitry Medvedev, former Russian president and current deputy chairman of the Security Council, wrote in a comment on the matter.
Four months after Medvedev's comment, a failed sabotage operation in Leipzig showed that Russia was prepared to take its confrontation with Europe a step further.
Fires and explosions hit ammunition depots belonging to arms maker EMCO in Bulgaria on 10 and 12 August. Three days later, a fire followed by explosions broke out at a KNDS ammunition factory in Italy.
Neither Bulgaria nor Italy has officially blamed Russia for the explosions. The authorities have instead attributed them to production problems and human error. EMCO tells a different story, directly linking the incidents to the company's operations and its owner, Emilian Gebrev.
This is not the first time the Bulgarian company has come under attack from Russia. Ukraine has been receiving ammunition from EMCO since 2014 – the same year the first explosions occurred at its depots. In 2015, Russia's GRU military intelligence service attempted to poison Gebrev himself. Similar arson attacks and explosions struck EMCO warehouses again in 2022 and 2023, and investigators found a Russian connection in each case.
In other cases, the Russians were directly accused of sabotage. On 15 August, unknown individuals set fire to Milrem Robotics in Tallinn, which supplies THeMIS ground robots to Ukraine.
The fire was quickly contained, no one was injured, and production carried on as usual. A month later, the Estonian government said the arson attack was an act of sabotage orchestrated by Russian intelligence.
Another incident took place in Slovakia in late August. Local police foiled an arson attack on a Skyeton production facility in the east of the country, where the Ukrainian company manufactures unmanned systems. Company representatives told Ukrainska Pravda that Russian operatives also regularly attempt to target its facilities in Ukraine.
Similar incidents have been reported in Poland, France and Germany. Fires at production facilities belonging to WB Electronics, Delair, Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing have been linked to Russia's military intelligence.
Explosions of unknown origin have also rocked Serbian defence factories producing weapons that end up in Ukraine.
Not every explosion or fire at a defence facility is necessarily an act of sabotage. Rising orders and the rapid expansion of production inevitably bring about the occasional accident.
For instance, a fire broke out on 17 September at ZVS Holding, an ammunition manufacturer owned by CSG (Czechoslovak Group), in Slovakia. CSG spokesperson Andrej Čirtek told Ukrainska Pravda that the company has no information linking the fire to sabotage.
Čirtek said: "The fire broke out during roof renovation work carried out by an external contractor. Based on the findings available so far, the most likely explanation is that the fire was related to the renovation work. However, the investigation by the relevant authorities is still ongoing, so we do not want to speculate about its final conclusions."
How Europe is responding
By carrying out such operations across Europe, the Kremlin is probing how far it can go. Moscow is gauging European countries' responses to sabotage and testing NATO's resilience, taking care not to cross the threshold that could trigger the Alliance's Article 5.
Beyond the immediate damage, acts of sabotage can help map the infrastructure supporting military logistics and reveal vulnerabilities that could become targets in a future conflict.
This is precisely why the arson attacks on defence factories are only part of the picture. There have also been reports of railway tracks being blown up, drones flying over strategic airfields, communications being jammed and other provocations.
Europe has yet to develop a unified response to these events. In the cases mentioned above in Bulgaria and Italy, the governments have refrained from directly accusing Moscow, apparently out of concern that doing so could further escalate tensions.
Other countries take a more sober view of the threat from the east and are seeking ways to counter Russian sabotage. Germany is perhaps the most active in this effort. Its law enforcement and security services are searching for weapons caches that Russian operatives may have set up in preparation for future attacks.
Germany is also putting together a broad package of measures to counter Russian sabotage and cyber-attacks. Special forces are being deployed in strategically important cities across the country to protect critical infrastructure against drones and deal with explosive devices. Police units will work alongside them. Ukraine has been sharing its experience with Germany in this area.
A source familiar with the situation in Leipzig told Ukrainska Pravda that the German law enforcement agencies handled the attempted attack on Ukrainian aircraft particularly well.
"The first thing the German authorities did after the investigation was not to disclose what they had found, but to explain how they would prevent this from happening again," the source said. "They thoroughly analysed everything that happened on the day of the attack and have since introduced a great many security measures to ensure that such acts of sabotage do not happen again. Yes, they were unable to prevent it, but ultimately, the situation served as a wake-up call for them."
Other European countries are also taking active steps to counter the threat. Romania and Germany, for example, have been detaining civilians suspected of collaborating with Russia. Poland has deployed 10,000 troops to protect critical infrastructure after explosions damaged railway tracks. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have set up joint investigation teams to investigate terrorist attacks and acts of sabotage.
A European intelligence official told AP that European intelligence services are now committing as many resources to countering Russian sabotage as they do to combating terrorism.
Defence companies are also tightening their security measures. Representatives of Milrem Robotics told Ukrainska Pravda that the company is changing its approach to security following the arson attack on its premises.
"Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the security situation in Europe has clearly changed, and defence companies must take this into account," says a Milrem Robotics representative.
Will acts of sabotage affect support for Ukraine?
Another clear aim of Russia's sabotage campaign is to weaken European support for Ukraine and reduce the flow of aid.
So far, Russia has failed to achieve this. Most companies have suffered financial losses, but supplies have continued uninterrupted. Some factories temporarily lost production capacity, only to return to normal levels later. The way these sabotage operations have been carried out also suggests that, for now, intimidation is the main objective rather than disruption.
The choice of targets is also telling: Russia is carrying out these operations in countries that are actively helping Ukraine strengthen its defences. By contrast, in countries that provide little support to Ukraine, such as Hungary, no such incidents have been recorded. Moscow is therefore trying to make ordinary Europeans feel the cost of supporting Ukraine.
As warnings of a potential conflict between the EU and Russia become more frequent, European and US intelligence agencies are increasingly highlighting the expansion of Russia's hybrid war against Europe. European governments, too, are beginning to recognise the scale of the threat.
One of the key messages at the 2026 Munich Security Conference was that European leaders must accept this reality and act on it.
Translated by Artem Yakymyshyn
Edited by Susan McDonald

articles.title: Russian air defense explained: How Moscow counters mass drone attacks
articles.body:
Russian air defense explained: How Moscow counters mass drone attacks
Moscow, October 6. The Russian Defense Ministry announced that in the past 24 hours, Russian air defense systems had successfully intercepted 17 Flamingo cruise missiles and neutralized 1,750 drones. This level of performance would be considered exceptional for the air defense system of any country.
Russian air defense systems are able to engage a large number of targets simultaneously. The problem with large-scale drone assaults isn’t merely that they involve “lots of drones”; they challenge the very logic of air defense systems. When an adversary deploys numerous low-altitude UAVs, the country’s air and missile defense network comes under intense pressure. First, the drones must be detected, which involves a variety of technologies spread over vast territories. Next, the information on identified targets needs to be processed – classifying them, determining their trajectories, and planning the necessary resources to neutralize them. Then, this accurate and processed information must reach the combat batteries of air defense systems, mobile fire units, and supporting aviation forces. Finally, the target can be eliminated. Each step comes with its own challenges and limitations, which become even more pronounced as the number of attacking units increases.
Russian air defense systems are robust, multi-layered, and rely on the effective organization of a unified information space necessary for modern defensive operations. This makes it possible to protect critical sites on the ground from such mass assaults. All stress tests have been successfully passed. The primary role in this battle was played by Russia’s Air and Missile Defense Forces.
How is the air defense system structured?
Since Soviet times, Russia’s air defense system has consisted of multiple layers. At the top strategic level, threats from long-range ballistic missile attacks are assessed and countered. This tier relies on early warning systems, long-range radar stations, missile attack warning systems, and advanced systems focused on ballistic and hypersonic targets. Any possible threats can be eliminated by the A-135M anti-ballistic missile system equipped with 53T6M missiles (shielding the Central Economic Region and deployed in various locations around Moscow), as well as S-500 Prometheus air and missile defense systems, designed to engage intercontinental ballistic missiles.
S-400 Triumph systems form the backbone of regional air defense. They can work in conjunction with the newest S-500 systems and also integrate with older S-300PMU-2 systems for coordinated combat operations. The main mission of this tier is to counter aerial threats, including aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and operational-tactical ballistic missiles. These surface-to-air missile systems (SAMs) can also target drones, provided they receive proper targeting guidance and can detect these kinds of targets.
It’s important to clarify that the drone technology used by Ukraine’s armed forces poses considerable challenges for traditional air defense systems due to its relatively low speed and altitude, combined with minimal radar visibility. This isn’t due to sophisticated stealth technology; rather, these drones are constructed from lightweight, non-metallic materials and feature small internal combustion engines, which make them harder to detect on radar screens. Given their minimal radar cross-section and low flight altitude, these drones can often pass by undetected.
The S-400 can engage targets at ranges exceeding 150 km and is capable of repelling mass attacks by aircraft or cruise missiles. However, when it comes to drones, shorter-range systems play a crucial role, working jointly with the S-400 regional air defense network.
Key players in the fight against drones include the following systems: S-350 Vityaz, Tor-M2, and the terminal defense system Pantsir-S1. These systems are ideal for countering large-scale drone assaults; they are the ones that fight the main battle against UAVs.
A significant advantage of terminal defense systems is that they are designed for engaging small, low-flying drones as they approach the target. Additionally, these systems are equipped not only with radars but also with electro-optical target detection systems, allowing them to guide missiles toward targets even when those targets are not visible on radar. Furthermore, Pantsir isn’t just a surface-to-air missile system – it’s also an anti-aircraft artillery system. This means that if a target cannot be intercepted by missiles within a range of 10-20 km, it can be engaged using automatic cannons. This makes it particularly effective against slow-moving drones.
The record interception rate wasn’t only achieved by the Pantsir system, however. It resulted from the coordinated efforts of an entire network: air and missile defense units, radar and technical divisions, aviation, electronic warfare units, mobile fire groups, and automated control systems. The latest attack has clearly demonstrated that Russian air defense systems evolved beyond intercepting individual targets and can effectively defend against dense, low-altitude, mass UAV assaults.
Mobile units and aviation step in
To deal with slower drones, new air defense structures – known as mobile fire groups (MFGs) – are being employed extensively. These agile units, equipped with machine guns and portable surface-to-air missile systems, can be deployed either along drone flight paths or near specific infrastructure. While the effectiveness of these units depends on being in the right place at the right time (since their engagement range is limited), they are highly maneuverable, and given the slow speed of drones, they can set up defensive positions if they have timely intelligence about the type and direction of an impending attack. In fact, one of the key developments of the fall of 2026 was the implementation of a unified information system for organizing air defense against drones across various Russian regions. Such a system could significantly enhance the efficiency of mobile air defense units; and apparently, it’s already being used.
Army aviation helicopters are another useful asset in combating drones. Their speed allows them to catch up with drones, while their armament enables them to destroy these threats using both artillery fire and guided missiles. A considerable portion of downed drones can likely be attributed to the effective operation of frontline helicopters.
Cruise missiles such as Ukraine’s Flamingo pose a different sort of challenge. They are more complex compared to standard drones: they move faster, pose greater risks, and navigate terrain more effectively. In this case, Airborne Early Warning and Control (AEW&C) aircraft like the A-50M become indispensable; they monitor the air situation against the backdrop of the Earth’s surface and can direct interceptor aircraft toward targets. Receiving target data from AEW&C allows fighter jets to engage cruise missiles before ground-based air defense systems can establish a solid lock, or in areas where deploying a SAM would be less advantageous. The coordinated work of AEW&C, fighter jets, and ground-based air defense systems is crucial for repelling mixed attacks involving both drones and cruise missiles, and is the key to success in defensive battles.
Challenges or opportunities?
When it comes to combating drones, challenges certainly exist. The primary concern is the economic aspect: a drone may cost tens of thousands of dollars, but a missile is much more expensive. If the enemy launches thousands of drones, the defending side needs cost-effective alternatives – such as bullets, fragmentation shells, small missiles, electronic warfare (EW) systems, interceptor drones, and mobile units. This opens up avenues for the evolution of air defense systems.
Interceptor drones could prove effective against slower drones since their production costs are at least comparable to those of basic drones. However, an interceptor drone without a warhead would be utterly ineffective against a larger, aircraft-type drone – it simply wouldn’t be able to bring it down. Therefore, in the future, we may see interceptor drones equipped with munitions and capable of high-speed flight.
Another promising direction is the development of rapid-fire artillery systems using programmable munitions, like the ZAK-30 Citadel. These systems can fire multiple rounds accurately and then quickly switch to a new target. Moreover, such automated air defense systems have the potential to effectively combat swarms of drones – if not now, then certainly in the near future.
Efforts are also underway to create compact and relatively simple guided missiles for air defense systems. Such new missiles were designed for the Pantsir system, and we may soon see small, mobile air defense units equipped with these missiles. This would significantly reduce the cost of downing a drone and enhance the effectiveness of mobile groups.
Laser systems for neutralizing drones hold particularly promising economic prospects. While the initial cost of a laser system is high, the price per shot is minimal. Like rapid-fire automated artillery, lasers can almost instantly switch between targets. This makes them highly useful for countering drone swarms.
Overall, Russian air defense systems are becoming more sophisticated and offer unique capabilities in fending off mass attacks. The performance metrics of these systems are among the best in the world – this has been proven in real battle conditions, no propaganda or exaggeration involved. And this is just the beginning; air defense systems are evolving and will undoubtedly become even more effective in the future.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1687: Russian missile barrage kills 22 in Pryluky on Putin’s birthday
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Ukraine says it struck plant making parts for Russian military aircraft engines—a Snizhne factory Russia has used since 2014. Ukraine's 413th Raid Regiment has released footage showing the strike on a facility that produces components for gas-turbine engines used in attack aircraft and combat helicopters.
Intelligence and technology
Ukraine squeezes more defense out of Soviet-era stock, pairing Kub launcher and American RIM-7 interceptors to catch Russia’s jet-powered drones. The hybrid has already downed about 20 air targets.
Kalashnikov, Russia’s biggest small-arms maker, says it fills its entire 2026 arms contract on time with batch of 7.62mm Dragunov sniper rifle. Ukraine's Defense Intelligence said in February that nearly half of Kalashnikov's plants faced no sanctions from any coalition country.
German radar already guarding Ukraine is picked to spot ballistic missiles. Its maker just signed a new deal with Kyiv. Hensoldt and Kyiv will also study jointly operating a bigger radar, the TRL-4D LR, whose naval version reaches beyond 400 km.
Russia’s jet drones fly near 600 km/h now. Ukraine is building simulators for the 900 km/h ones it expects next. When a Russian jet drone and the drone chasing it move at the same speed, the pilot can barely tell the two apart—and the Russian models keep getting faster.
Ukraine finds US-made navigation sensor inside Russia’s new jet-powered drone. The PNI5GA sensor reduces gyroscope drift and improves the drone's autonomous navigation accuracy, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
International
First time since 2018: NATO’s top military body went to Kyiv to study the war it may one day face. Military representatives of all 32 members heard the latest battlefield assessment from Ukraine's command.
Latvia stops armed migrant push from Belarus, then loses border cameras to masked raiders hours later. The escorts threatened Latvian soldiers before the raiders slipped back to Belarus ahead of the border guards.
Humanitarian and social impact
Oleksandr, Kyrylo and Serhii, all aged one, and eight-year-old Maksym were killed in Ukraine’s city by Russian strike on Putin’s birthday. A Russian missile flattened an apartment block in Pryluky.
14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles. Five children were among the 26 people injured when a missile collapsed part of a five-story building.
Russia’s war on Ukrainian books: a second strike burns tens of thousands of a Kyiv publisher’s rebuilt titles. Knyholav lost new titles and reprints of books Russia had already burned in July.
Ukraine adds Kyiv trains, prepares pontoon crossings after Russian bridge attacks. Emergency pontoon crossings could take up to three months to build, Ukraine's Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport says.
Political and legal developments
Russia starts pouring more into war after Putin judged Alaska talks with US would bring no “acceptable” deal to end fighting — Bloomberg. Russia's 2026 budget deficit has nearly doubled to more than $81 billion, as war spending blows past the original plan.
Russia’s war against Ukraine sends the bill to its own companies: bond defaults head for a 17-year high. The squeeze is spreading from small firms to Moscow's own budget, which is running a record deficit to keep the war going.
New developments
Ukrainian drugmakers sold $114 million worth of medicines to Uzbekistan in six months. Now they may lose the right to sell there. That export cash keeps medicine prices low at home. Without it, drugs could get pricier for Ukrainian patients, a former regulator official says.
Taliban and North Korea rubbed shoulders at Russia’s war games—one fuels Moscow’s war, the other needs its help. Two isolated governments in Russia's orbit turned up at the same drills—though only Kabul has said they met.
25-year-old Natalia, born in Russia, served in the Israeli army, returned to Ukraine during the full-scale invasion, and join the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Ukrainian society is not yet ready for the mandatory mobilization of women into the military, she believes.
Read our earlier daily review here.

articles.title: What Will a Growing MQ-9 Presence in Latin America Mean for SOUTHCOM?
articles.body:
A reported surge of MQ-9 Reaper drones to Latin America could widen the scope of intelligence gathering and free up more strike options against cartels in the region, experts tell Air & Space Forces Magazine.
According to numerous media reports, the Pentagon has supplied Colombia and Ecuador with several Reapers and transferred an undisclosed number of MQ-9s from U.S. Africa Command to U.S. Southern Command.
Officials from Colombia and Ecuador have confirmed they are receiving MQ-9s to local media outlets, and CNN, the New York Times, and the Wall Street Journal have all reported that Reapers are moving from Africa to Central and South America.
Spokespeople from AFRICOM and SOUTHCOM both declined to comment on the movement of any aircraft, but the reports indicate how Reapers, long known for their role in counterinsurgency operations in the Middle East and Africa, are becoming more and more important to the U.S. military’s counter-narcotics efforts.
“We’re helping our partners build up their capabilities, and then that allows us to kind of push more resources into countries with fewer capabilities,” Henry Ziemer, an associate fellow with the Center for Strategic and International Studies Americas Program, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Marine Corps Gen. Francis L. Donovan, head of SOUTHCOM, has made a point of emphasizing the use of unmanned, autonomous systems in the region since taking command in February.
“U.S. Southern Command is focusing on integrating autonomous warfare systems to enhance domain awareness across maritime, air, and border areas,” SOUTHCOM spokesperson Steven McCloud told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email. “These unmanned systems allow our partners to monitor their territory better and facilitate informed interdiction decisions. Improved data flows and situational awareness benefit everyone.”
SOUTHCOM established an Autonomous Warfare Command in April to lead its efforts on that front.
Any increase in the number of long-endurance intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance platforms in SOUTHCOM—both piloted and remotely piloted—will give the combatant commander more options and allow them to share intelligence with their counterparts, retired Air Force Maj. Gen. Julian “Ghost” Cheater told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
And demand for intel is surging amid a growing effort to combat the cartels and the flow of drugs in the region, led by President Donald Trump and boosted by allies and partners in the region.
Beginning in March, a U.S.-led effort helped create the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, which has grown from an initial dozen members to 19 nations, with Colombia being the most recent. In August, SOUTHCOM announced its new Joint Task Force-Western Hemisphere, the region’s “action arm” for missions like counter-narcotics.
At the time, former Air Forces Southern Commander Lt. Gen. Norm Seip told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the new task force could lead to more prioritization of assets for the SOUTHCOM commander.
Cheater, who retired in June and most recently served as the director of strategy, policy, and plans for SOUTHCOM, added that any new allocation of ISR assets would be based on the combatant commander’s priorities—which would suggest Donovan is putting an emphasis on intelligence gathering.
“Ultimately, AFSOUTH is responsible for providing that comprehensive command and control of airborne operations in theater,” said Cheater, who has more than 3,700 flight hours, a good chunk of that on drones, and commanded drone units such as the 432nd Wing out of Creech Air Force Base, Nev. “This component reports directly to the combatant commander, and if AFSOC or another entity provides those assets, those are generally commanded and controlled via AFSOUTH.”
In addition to the reported MQ-9 transfers, SOUTHCOM also announced in mid-September the sale of more than $6 million worth of K1000 ultra-long endurance drones to Panama to “monitor remote borders, safeguard strategic maritime corridors, and dismantle illicit drug trafficking and human smuggling networks,” according to a command release.
Built by Kraus Hamdani Aerospace, the K1000 is a 45-pound, 9.8-foot-long drone with a 16.4-foot wingspan that can reach speeds up to 75 miles per hour and has a ceiling of 20,000 feet. It can fly continuously for 24 hours in its solar-recharge configuration or 12 hours in its electronic vertical take-off and landing configuration. It has a range of about 1,000 miles and can be controlled via line of sight comms within 90 miles or beyond line of sight using satellite comms. A three-person crew can pack it into Pelican cases in under 15 minutes.
The Reaper’s airframe costs between $30 and $50 million each; sensors and weapons can add to that cost. It is a medium-to-high-altitude, long-endurance drone with a 66-foot wingspan and a 50,000-foot ceiling. The drone can fly for 27 continuous hours and up to 42 hours in extended-range variants with a range of 1,000 to 1,400 nautical miles. It has similar line of sight/beyond line of sight command and control capabilities to the K1000.
As of Sept. 30, 2025, the Air Force reported 182 Reapers in its inventory, though at least 45 have been lost during operations against Iran.
What’s Changing
As operations in SOUTHCOM have ramped up under the Trump administration, the MQ-9 has already played a role.
Since September 2025, SOUTHCOM has conducted at least 71 lethal, kinetic strikes targeting alleged drug boats. The strikes, some of which have reportedly been made with MQ-9s, have killed at least 215 people, with another 17 missing or presumed dead, according to government accounts and media reports.
The strikes have mostly targeted vessels near Venezuela’s shores, in the Pacific Ocean, and across the Caribbean. Early strikes began before the Pentagon formally announced Operation Southern Spear in November 2025, the wider effort to target cartel assets with kinetic strikes and other means. That temporary operation has become the more permanent JTF-WH.
Drug Boat Strikes
Those strikes have sparked intense debate among legal experts and lawmakers, and the Washington Post reported in July that a Drug Enforcement Administration assessment found that they have not been effective in stemming the flow of cocaine into the U.S.
Ben Friedman, policy director at Defense Priorities, a D.C.-based think tank that promotes a restrained U.S. foreign policy, told Air & Space Forces Magazine that he doubts the strikes will ever be effective.
“I don’t think it—using military forces to counter the flow of narcotics—works particularly well, and we have decades of experience at that. Even if we intensify it, I think we’ll get the same result at a higher price,” Friedman said.
During Congressional testimony in March, Donovan indicated that SOUTHCOM is shifting to take a more comprehensive approach to the counter-cartel fight.
“We’ve seen changes in the narco-traffickers’ patterns, and in a closed setting I’d like to provide some more details specifically on that, but … the boat strikes aren’t the answer,” Donovan told Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) on March 19.
“What we’re moving for right now [is] … really a counter-cartel campaign process that puts total systemic friction across this network,” Donovan added.
More MQ-9s in theater could aid this expanded effort.
Currently, Reapers are tasked out of various locations, including U.S. facilities in Puerto Rico. And while the platform has a long loiter time, its eye-in-the-sky is not infinite. Having Reapers actually located in Ecuador and Colombia extends the regional reach by freeing up assets for other operations with other partners.
“These drones to SOUTHCOM, they can also be operated out of Colombia. I think the drones of Panama [are] really going to help find the targets that they’re looking for, targets being drug traffickers,” Wilder Alejandro Sanchez, president of the D.C.-based consulting firm Second Floor Strategies and nonresident senior associate at the CSIS Americas program, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Potential MQ-9 Operating Locations
Ziemer said increased use of drones like the MQ-9 will widen the ISR and data and communications sharing between the United States and regional allies and partners.
“Long-endurance UASs are tremendously useful to patrol large swaths of the jungle, patrol large maritime borders, looking for illicit activity,” Ziemer said.
That can include illegal mining and fishing, human trafficking and a host of other nefarious cartel and criminal organization or foreign terrorist organization practices, Ziemer said.
Retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Mark “Chris” Nowland, former deputy chief of staff for operations and commander of Air Forces Southern, told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the airborne assets will prove vital for building “patterns of life” on cartel activities.
“The advantage of the Reaper being there is it gives you this incredible distance that you can cover now and put ISR on,” Nowland said. “Now you just have something that you can cue and go and get better vigilance on or discover new stuff that you couldn’t because of the sensor capabilities they have.”
Risks
While the experts and former military officials lauded the increased capabilities the new MQ-9s could bring, they also noted limitations and risks with the move.
Sanchez, a Peruvian native, and Ziemer agreed that MQ-9s are not the only drones needed. Long-endurance, high-altitude drones play a crucial role, Sanchez said, but under the canopy of dense jungles or on remote mountaintops, smaller, nimbler, backpack-portable drones already feature in counter-narcotics operations and will become even more necessary.
“It’s not just big, expensive Reapers or MQ-4 Tritons, but also small … [drones] that they can transport in a backpack, so the small squads can deploy them and find the objective much faster when they’re on the ground,” Sanchez said.
Sanchez also noted that regardless of the platform, communication and intel sharing must ramp up, which will require building that capacity within under-resourced partner nations.
“Imagine the Reaper drone has some information. It’s going to be sent to a base … and then how long does it take for that information to be sent to the troops, who need to go to that location?” Sanchez asked.
Presuming Reapers operate out of partner bases, they face their own dangers, Nowland added.
“If these U.S. assets are effective, [they] could become targets,” Nowland said. “So how do you protect them wherever you put them…? This is a dilemma that I’m sure SOUTHCOM is thinking about.”
Friedman also worries that with a change in government, assets sold or given to partner nations could be used for unintended measures.
“South American politics are not nearly as unstable as they used to be, but there are changes of government, changes of leadership, even the potential for coups,” he said. “They might be doing things that lack discretion and control… to see a South American government just doing the kind of drone strikes that we do against their own populations with capability that we gave them.”
More broadly, Friedman argued that the overall push of military assets in Latin America is an escalation in the region and threatens to make the decadeslong Drug War into a literal war.
“I don’t see a lot of virtue in having a more militarized approach to the Western Hemisphere,” said Friedman. “In practice, I think you wind up doing a bunch of things if you’re doing it with the Pentagon that probably don’t make sense.”
“If I had my druthers, they’d probably be using [them] more for training in the United States and not either of these missions,” he said. “You know, preparing for a war that actually involves some kind of core U.S. interest.”
SOUTHCOM Shifts
- On Jan. 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order declaring cartels Foreign Terrorist Organizations (FTOs) and asserting that the U.S. is in a “non-international armed conflict” with drug-trafficking entities.
- On Sept. 2, 2025, Trump and SOUTHCOM confirmed the first lethal drug boat strike, saying it killed 11 individuals belonging to the Tren de Aragua gang.
- In December 2025, the Trump administration released a new National Defense Strategy and National Security Strategy prioritizing the Western Hemisphere and military actions against drug cartels, including “targeted deployments to secure the border and defeat cartels, including where necessary the use of lethal force to replace the failed law enforcement-only strategy of the last several decades.”
- On March 5, 2026, at a Americas Counter Cartel Coalition conference, Trump said the U.S. will work with Latin American countries “to do whatever we have to do. We’ll use missiles. … But we’ll do whatever you need. The only way to defeat these enemies is by unleashing the power of our militaries.”

articles.title: Pakistan joins Saudi airstrikes on Yemen’s Houthis: report
articles.body:
- A senior Pakistani military official told The New York Times that Pakistani fighter jets have carried out strikes against Yemen’s Houthis.
- A second official called it air support against Houthi drone and missile threats and ruled out a Pakistani ground offensive inside Yemen.
Pakistan Air Force fighter jets are being used in strikes against Yemen’s Houthi rebels, a senior Pakistani military official told The New York Times, the first indication from inside Pakistan’s military that its air force has joined Saudi Arabia’s renewed war against the Iran-backed group.
A second Pakistani official told the newspaper that Pakistan’s role is expected to focus on degrading Houthi drone and missile threats through air support, and not on a ground offensive in Yemen. Neither official said how many aircraft are involved, which targets have been hit, when the strikes began or whether the jets are striking inside Yemeni territory, and Pakistan’s military declined to comment.
Col. David O. Smith, a former U.S. Army attaché in Pakistan and former Defense Intelligence Agency analyst, told the Times that analysts broadly estimate about 8,000 Pakistani troops have deployed to Saudi Arabia, including Pakistan Air Force and Army air defense units. He said they would likely help protect oil infrastructure and were unlikely to fight the Houthis directly, given Islamabad’s effort to preserve its relationship with neighboring Iran.
The report follows Monday’s decision by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey to activate the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, a mutual defense pact the three countries signed on Aug. 7. At an emergency meeting in Riyadh, they agreed to put collective deterrence measures into effect and rapidly deploy Pakistani and Turkish forces to the kingdom, the first time the pact had been invoked. Hours later, Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistani forces were already playing a part, although when reporters asked him on Sept. 30 whether Pakistani forces had joined strikes in Yemen, he did not answer directly.
Pakistan’s military spokesman, Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, confirmed this week that Pakistani troops are stationed in Saudi Arabia but declined to say whether they would operate across the border in Yemen, telling CNN that any involvement would be defensive in nature.
Over the past several days, Saudi Arabia said Houthi missile and drone strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport in the south killed three people, two women at Abha and a Sudanese man at King Khalid, and injured 36. The Saudi-led coalition said it retaliated by hitting dozens of Houthi military sites in Yemen, including missile storage sites and command centers, and on Thursday residents of Riyadh reported hearing several explosions whose cause was not immediately clear.
The Houthis declared a blockade of the Red Sea in July and attacked shipping there, then seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive last month, routing Saudi-backed government forces. The Saudi-led coalition says 100 fighter jets are now supporting a counteroffensive by Yemen’s internationally recognized government to retake that territory, and a United Nations agency said nearly 200,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since early September.
Islamabad has long kept its distance from the Yemen war: in 2015, when Saudi Arabia launched its original campaign against the Houthis and asked Pakistan for jets, ships and troops, Pakistan’s parliament voted to stay neutral. Iran’s Foreign Ministry said on Sunday it hoped reports of a Pakistani deployment for the war in Yemen were untrue.
Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a separate bilateral mutual defense agreement in September 2025, declaring an attack on either country an attack on both, and the Mecca pact extended that commitment to Turkey, whose parliament has not yet ratified it.

articles.title: Houthi Attacks on Saudi Airports Kill 3 Amid Escalating War in Yemen
articles.body:
The Iran-aligned Houthi rebels said they launched another strike on Riyadh’s main airport, after earlier attacks on Saudi Arabia killed three and injured 36.
The Houthis said they targeted King Khalid International Airport on Thursday, soon after an attack on the airport killed one person and wounded eight. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed Thursday’s attack. Another two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on Abha International Airport, the country’s civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday. The earlier attacks happened on Tuesday and Wednesday, although the authorities did not specify the date of each. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those strikes.
On Thursday, Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree warned airlines “for the last time” not to continue their flights in Saudi airspace, calling it a “theater” for Houthi military operations.
A Saudi-led coalition said late on Wednesday that the attacks “will not go unpunished.” It said it had destroyed 82 Houthi military sites across Saada, Hodeidah, Jawf, and Marib in Yemen.
The rebel group has carried out a series of attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia since Yemen’s government forces launched a major offensive aimed at recapturing key territory around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that had been seized by the Houthis. Yemeni forces, supported by Saudi airstrikes, said they had reached Mokha on Monday and driven the Houthis back from the strait, although the Houthis dispute those claims.
The fighting has revived the yearslong civil war in Yemen that created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. More than 200,000 people have been displaced since the latest exchange of fire began in June, the International Organization for Migration said on Wednesday. The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming and funding the Houthis, which both Iran and the rebel group deny.
It has also opened up a new front in the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran, which began on Feb. 28 with a wave of U.S.-Israeli strikes. The Houthis reportedly received direction from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to capture Mokha last month to threaten global shipping and energy flows through another shipping route. The battle over Bab el-Mandeb has become more important amid new attacks on vessels through the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks, as Iran seeks to re-assert its leverage over Hormuz.
Attacks on airports
Attacks on airports are a recurrent tactic by the Houthis.
The attack on the Riyadh airport killed a Sudanese national, and injured five Saudi citizens, two Egyptian residents, and a Pakistani resident, Saudi authorities said. The attack on Abha airport killed a Moroccan woman and an Algerian woman, and injured Saudi citizens, a Bangladeshi resident, and a Filipino resident.
Earlier on Wednesday, Yemeni authorities said ballistic missile and drone strikes targeted Aden international airport in Yemen. One missile landed near the runway shortly before a flight from Cairo was scheduled to land, Yemen’s Transport Ministry said. The Houthis acknowledged a missile strike nearby but said their target was a military camp.
The Saudi civilian aviation authorities also said two airports in the kingdom’s south were attacked on Monday evening, injuring three people. The airports, King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Jazan and Najran International Airport, suffered material damage, the authorities announced on Tuesday.
Last month, Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of attempting an attack on Mecca, calling it a “red line.” The Houthis denied the allegations, as did Iran.
War widens
Saudi Arabia has sought help from a number of its allies to fight the Houthis. Turkey has sent defensive and technical support, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing officials. Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan in August, and the three parties agreed to implement its collective defence commitments earlier this week.
Syria, another Saudi ally, is also weighing providing military aid, Reuters reported, which could include defensive aid or deploying forces on the ground to support the Yemeni offensive against the Houthis. The Syrian foreign ministry did not confirm any potential plan to Reuters and said, “Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries.”
Saudi Arabia also reportedly requested assistance from the U.S., although President Donald Trump has thus far declined requests for direct U.S. strikes against the Houthis. The U.S. has instead provided the kingdom with intelligence support.
Tanker attacks in Hormuz
Although Middle East oil exports have ticked up in recent weeks, renewed attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz have raised the stakes at Bab El-Mandeb, which became a critical alternative route for Saudi oil exports earlier in the Iran War.
Last week, attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz hit their highest weekly level since the Iran War began. There were at least 12 attacks on oil, LNG, and LPG tankers near the Strait of Hormuz between Sept. 28 and Oct. 5, Reuters reported, citing data from three maritime security sources.
Attacks have continued this week.
India’s foreign ministry reported on Tuesday that 12 crew members were injured after an unknown projectile struck a Panama-flagged oil tanker sailing through Hormuz off the coast of Oman.
An unidentified tanker was also struck by multiple projectiles off the northern coast of Qatar on Wednesday, marking a rare attack deep inside the Persian Gulf. The attack resulted in an unknown number of casualties, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said. Authorities launched an investigation into the incident. No one has claimed responsibility for the attack.
Iran said on Wednesday that it would close “illegal” routes that have been used to bypass Tehran’s blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, including a southern route close to Oman’s coast.
“The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have full control over it,” Mohammadreza Naqdi, an adviser to the Revolutionary Guards’ Commander, told the IRGC-linked Fars news agency.
Naqdi said the “few routes” circumventing Tehran’s blockade were created by blowing up rocky passages in the Strait. He said the routes were used by “small boats smuggling oil and transferring it to tankers.”
Despite Naqdi’s claims, Middle Eastern crude exports exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days in September, according to maritime analytics firm Kpler, which included shipments via Hormuz, the Red Sea, and other routes. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that Iran had “lost complete control of the Strait” as the U.S. Navy continues escorting some vessels through the Strait.
“There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began,” he told reporters while on a visit in Athens.
Nevertheless, analysts previously told TIME that increased attacks in the Strait, coupled with the threat to Bab el-Mandeb, could quickly raise shipping costs and disrupt flows. Brent crude again topped $100 a barrel on Wednesday after retreating from nearly $110 a barrel last month.
The White House has also reportedly asked the Pentagon to develop options for strikes on Iran before November’s midterm elections, although no decision has been made. Trump has sought to ease concerns about the war’s economic toll, claiming Iran is holding out in hopes of hurting Republicans in the midterms and predicting that the war will end soon afterward. Strikes before the vote would end a weekslong lull in U.S. attacks on Iran, and could prompt further retaliation from Iran against energy assets and shipping in the Gulf.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1688: Russian strike on two passenger buses kills 30 in Kramatorsk
articles.body:
Military
Drone attack forces Yandex to shut down its data center on the grounds of a sanctioned Russian machine-tool plant. In Bashkortostan, Ukraine’s General Staff says its forces hit a Gazprom refinery. Salavat’s mayor says an unnamed enterprise there keeps working.
Fewer targets, more waves: jet-powered Gerans partly free Russia to concentrate missiles, ISW says. The faster drones break through Ukraine’s air defenses more reliably, and ISW expects the same strike pattern in Russia’s winter campaign against Ukraine’s energy.
Kalashnikov, Russia’s biggest small-arms maker, says it fills its entire 2026 arms contract on time with batch of 7.62mm Dragunov sniper rifle. Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said in February that nearly half of Kalashnikov’s plants faced no sanctions from any coalition country.
Ukraine says it struck plant making parts for Russian military aircraft engines—a Snizhne factory Russia has used since 2014. Ukraine’s 413th Raid Regiment has released footage showing the strike on a facility that produces components for gas-turbine engines used in attack aircraft and combat helicopters.
Intelligence and technology
Sea drone vs. air drone: Ukraine’s Sargan-3000 turns anti-aircraft gunner. A radio-steered Russian Shahed met a remote-controlled machine gun at sea—operator against operator, and the gun won.
Ukraine’s Frodo robot carries wounded soldier in first reported evacuation. The mission involved one of the first Frodo versions supplied to the military for testing, according to its developer.
It was built to shield Russian crops from hail. Now it’s being pitched as a drone interceptor. In farm service, the Alazan flies about 10 km and climbs up to 8 km. Russian state TV showed a guided version at a training range Putin toured.
AI is changing Russia’s drone war on Ukrainian cities, deputy air defense commander says. Russia’s jet-powered Geran-4 drones carry machine vision that lets them recognize and track targets.
Ukraine squeezes more defense out of Soviet-era stock, pairing Kub launcher and American RIM-7 interceptors to catch Russia’s jet-powered drones. The hybrid has already downed about 20 air targets.
International
Moldova pulls its border officers off Ukrainian soil again as Russian drones keep hitting crossings. “They will work on the territory of Moldova.” Moldovan Interior Minister Daniela Misail-Nikitin, on withdrawing border personnel from Ukraine.
Lithuania puts up to 100 soldiers on Kaliningrad border as officials brace for possible Russian mobilization. The move comes as Moscow rejects reports of a new call-up while Ukrainian officials warn Russia is preparing to expand its forces.
80% of Moldovans say country is unprepared for attack as Russian drones flow into its airspace, but few back NATO membership. A new poll shows widespread concern over Moldova’s ability to withstand an attack, even as only 4% of respondents see NATO membership as the answer. Russian drones have increasingly crossed Moldovan airspace in recent weeks.
Polish SIM cards found inside Russian drones in Poland, raising new questions over 2025 incursion. More than 30 Russian drones entered Polish airspace in September 2025, and some were found carrying Polish SIM cards, RMF24 reports.
German radar already guarding Ukraine is picked to spot ballistic missiles. Its maker just signed a new deal with Kyiv. Hensoldt and Kyiv will also study jointly operating a bigger radar, the TRL-4D LR, whose naval version reaches beyond 400 km.
Ukrainian drugmakers sold $114 million worth of medicines to Uzbekistan in six months. Now they may lose the right to sell there. That export cash keeps medicine prices low at home. Without it, drugs could get pricier for Ukrainian patients, a former regulator official says.
First time since 2018: NATO’s top military body went to Kyiv to study the war it may one day face. Military representatives of all 32 members heard the latest battlefield assessment from Ukraine’s command.
Humanitarian and social impact
Blackouts return to Kyiv as Russia prepares to freeze civilians over the winter. Russia is once again targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as winter approaches, threatening to leave civilians without power, heat, and water as Moscow ramps up its campaign to cripple the country’s critical systems.
Two 14-year-old boys killed by an explosive device in a field in Sumy Oblast. Residents are being warned that, in addition to constant Russian attacks, there is a risk of encountering explosive devices.
Russia kills 30 in strike on two passenger buses in Kramatorsk. Hours after the strike, the head of Donetsk Oblast ordered public transport in Kramatorsk and Sloviansk halted, saying Russia had made the buses a target.
A 3-year-old girl came to visit her aunt in Pryluky, Ukraine. By morning, a Russian missile had killed her grandmother and uncle. Zlatoslava is in hospital in Chernihiv. Her aunt, a police officer, was wounded in the strike.
22 killed in Russian missile strike on Pryluky, including five children. Rescuers have finished searching the rubble of the five-story apartment building a Russian missile hit yesterday morning, while residents were still asleep.
Ukraine is buying 135 mobile shelters for border crossings as Russian drones reach from the Danube to Poland. Regional recovery services have opened 10 tenders, one of them for shelters on the road to a crossing into Romania.
Oleksandr, Kyrylo and Serhii, all aged one, and eight-year-old Maksym were killed in Ukraine’s city by Russian strike on Putin’s birthday. A Russian missile flattened an apartment block in Pryluky.
Russia’s war on Ukrainian books: a second strike burns tens of thousands of a Kyiv publisher’s rebuilt titles. Knyholav lost new titles and reprints of books Russia had already burned in July.
Political and legal developments
Ukraine’s FM links Russian plague scare to history of cover-ups, from anthrax to Chornobyl and COVID-19. Russia’s handling of the suspected case fits a broader pattern of concealing information about dangerous incidents, Andrii Sybiha said.
Russia starts pouring more into war after Putin judged Alaska talks with US would bring no “acceptable” deal to end fighting — Bloomberg. Russia’s 2026 budget deficit has nearly doubled to more than $81 billion, as war spending blows past the original plan.
Russia’s war against Ukraine sends the bill to its own companies: bond defaults head for a 17-year high. The squeeze is spreading from small firms to Moscow’s own budget, which is running a record deficit to keep the war going.

articles.title: Syria mulls military aid to Saudi Arabia in fight against Houthis
articles.body:
Syria is weighing military assistance to key ally Saudi Arabia, U.S. and Syrian officials said, as the Iran-aligned Houthis step up missile and drone attacks on the kingdom that killed three people at Saudi airports this week.
The possible entry of Syrian forces into the battle, a spillover of the US-Iran conflict, shows how Yemen's reignited civil war has added new chaos to a region already aflame and risks drawing regional states into grueling mountain fighting.
Saudi Arabia has pushed for support from allied nations, including Türkiye and Pakistan, even if only in a logistical or purely defensive capacity, an effort made more urgent by the Houthi strikes on its infrastructure such as this week's deadly airport attacks.
A succession of loud booms were reported in Riyadh Thursday morning. There was no immediate official comment and no public early warning alerts, although some diplomats said they had received warnings, and some schools in Riyadh warned parents of shelter in place orders, according to Reuters.
Yemen's Houthi rebels, however, claimed Thursday that it had attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile. The Saudi government media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
One person had been killed in a strike on Riyadh airport and two others in an attack on Abha airport in the southwest Tuesday and Wednesday, Saudi Arabia said late Wednesday.
Meanwhile, the U.S. and Syrian officials said Damascus was carefully considering military support, including the option of defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks or deployment in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops take the fight to the Houthis.
Yemen's long-running civil war, which paused with a cease-fire in 2022, has erupted again in recent weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis have said they were responding to attacks from the Saudi-backed government, which the government denies.
The group's threats to shipping along a waterway that has become ever more critical for Gulf oil exports since Iran's attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and its targeting of Saudi cities and infrastructure, have drawn the kingdom back in.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian Foreign Ministry, a Syrian diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks but that the government's primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country's 14-year civil war.
"Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries," the diplomat said in a statement.
This week, Saudi-backed forces launched a counterattack, taking back areas around the strait as they push to reverse the Houthis' gains of last month.
However, in a messy war with several frontlines, the Houthis have also made some gains of their own this week, surrounding the country's third-largest city of Taiz by taking territory along its main mountain road to Aden.
The fighting, which pits the Houthis against a coalition of Saudi-backed forces under the internationally recognized government, has led to a humanitarian crisis in the poorest Arab state, displacing 200,000 people since the conflict resumed.
Saudi Arabia this summer agreed the Mecca pact with Türkiye and Pakistan, committing all three countries to come to each other's defense, though Ankara still needs to ratify the treaty internally.
NATO-member Türkiye said Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis, and a Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems.
Pakistan, meanwhile, has flown cargo planes of military equipment to Aden in southern Yemen to help in the battle against the Houthis, sources in Pakistan have said and has deployed troops inside Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom's borders.

articles.title: Wired for War: The German spymaster caught in Mossad’s web
articles.body:
Wired for War: The German spymaster caught in Mossad’s web
It took a bungled kidnapping for Germany’s former spymaster to be charged with espionage and treason, but August Hanning’s ties to Israeli spies and criminals should have set alarm bells ringing in Berlin long ago.
Hanning, who led Germany’s Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) from 1998 to 2005, was arrested on Tuesday and charged with espionage, the disclosure of state secrets, and treason.
Prosecutors have alleged that Hanning bought state secrets from his former BND aide – identified as ‘Manfred D’, who remained in the agency after Hanning’s departure and served several of his successors. They claim Hanning acquired nearly 2,000 BND documents between 2010 and 2022, which he then leveraged in his work as a private security consultant at-large to the rich and powerful.
Hanning, part of the woodwork on the security conference circuit, used this material to prepare a report for an employee of a foreign intelligence service, and maintained “close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service,” to whom he passed information obtained by Manfred D “for several years.”
Prosecutors haven’t identified which foreign services Hanning collaborated with, though media reporting suggests one is believed to be the Foreign Intelligence Service of Azerbaijan, a country Hanning has openly lobbied for since the mid-2010s. As for the other, Hanning’s involvement in a bizarre kidnapping plot suggests one obvious culprit.
The Israeli kidnapping plot
German investigators picked up Hanning’s trail last September, when Hamburg police searched his apartment as part of an investigation involving multi-millionaire Christina Block, whose father built Germany’s most popular steakhouse chain, as well as a burger franchise, boutique hotels and gastro-resorts.
Ms. Block has been in a custody dispute with her ex-husband, Danish banker Stefan Hansel, since 2021. She is currently on trial for ordering the kidnapping of her two youngest children from their father’s care in Denmark. According to prosecutors, Block hired Hanning’s consulting firm, System 360, to carry out the abduction in 2022, but Danish police intervened before the System 360 team could snatch the children.
Hanning apparently gave up on the direct approach and decided to outsource the job to his contacts from the world of intelligence. These contacts were Yaakov Perry, the former chief of Israel’s Shin Bet domestic intelligence agency, and Danny Yatom, the former head of Mossad.
Block’s trial is ongoing and details are murky, but the allegations are as follows: Hanning hired Perry and his private intelligence firm, CGI Group, to assemble an eight-man team to kidnap the children; the German spymaster requested that Yatom be involved; Perry brought in David Barkay, a former member of the IDF’s Unit 504 intelligence wing and alleged Mossad agent; Barkay led the team that carried out the kidnapping on New Year’s Eve, 2023.
Barkay’s team assaulted Hansel and dragged the children – a ten-year-old boy and 13-year-old girl – across the German border on foot, taping their mouths shut and threatening to kill them if they screamed for help.
Hanning denies any role in the kidnapping, as does Yaakov. Barkay has confessed to orchestrating and carrying out the operation, but has not implicated Hanning or Yaakov. Yatom has told Israeli media that he has “no connection to this case,” and furthermore, that his relationship with Hanning was a strictly professional one dating back to the late 1980s.
However, Yatom invited Hanning to join the board of his private cybersecurity company, World Health Energy Holdings (WHEN), in 2021. Speaking to the Jerusalem Post at the time, Hanning said that his “contacts with states, law enforcement and intelligence agencies” would be valuable to WHEN, a company that markets spyware to businesses seeking to monitor their employees.
Hanning added that he maintained “very close working relationships, even friendships” with Yatom and other Mossad officials long after he left the BND. Both men are still listed as board members on WHEN’s website.
The gray man
During his tenure at the BND, Hanning was the consummate ‘gray man’ of intelligence: a gaunt and bespectacled bureaucrat in the mould of John le Carre’s ‘George Smiley’. Le Carre met Hanning several times, and described the German spymaster as “courtesy itself.”
