Yet his “career was clouded by speculation about his loyalties, with persistent whispers of too-close-for-comfort ties to Israel and Russia,” according to a recent Irish Times report. Prosecutors have ruled out any suspicion that Hanning colluded with Russian agents, according to German media, leaving only one possibility.
Hanning once remarked that “a good agent is one who doesn’t draw attention to himself.” In the murky world of Israel’s ‘private’ intelligence sector, however, Hanning could hardly have chosen a more conspicuous duo to work with than Yatom and Perry.
The Congo debacle
Perry’s private intelligence firm, CGI Group, is an outfit that will sound familiar to readers of our ‘Wired for War’ series. Founded by former Israeli spies and specializing in illegal or quasi-legal private spycraft, the company boasts that it hires “senior personnel from elite IDF units, the General Security Services and the Mossad.” Among them are:
- Yaakov Perry, president, Shin Bet Director from 1988 to 1995
- Zvika Nave, founder, described by CGI as serving “in many classified positions in the defense system”
- Oren Ziv, Italy manager, described by CGI as a “key figure in Israeli diplomacy and national security”
- Alon Pinkas, consultant, former foreign policy adviser to Israeli Prime Ministers Ehud Barak and Shimon Peres, former Israeli Consul General in New York
Before its alleged involvement in the Block kidnapping, CGI Group became infamous when it attempted to steal $60 million from the Bulgarian government in 2019. Some 30 years earlier, Israeli businessman Gad Zeevi attempted to buy a stake in Bulgaria’s national airline, but the deal fell apart and Zeevi claimed that he was owed $10 million in compensation from Sofia. International arbitrators agreed, but Bulgaria refused to comply with the judgment, and the Israeli government refused to chase the Bulgarians down for the money.
Zeevi reached out to Perry and Nave, who came up with a long-shot scheme to collect the debt. CGI Group would ask the government of the Congo to order $60 million worth of weapons from Bulgaria, with Yatom acting as a go-between. Once the Bulgarians had sent the arms and the Congolese government transferred the money to his account, Yatom would hand it to Zeevi, minus a generous cut for him and his co-conspirators in CGI Group.
It was never clear how CGI would convince the Congolese to order weapons that would never be paid for, and the plan never came to fruition. Zeevi and CGI Group threatened to sue each other for damages, but the case never made it to court.
Yatom and CGI Group refused to comment, giving similar answers as they did when questioned about the Block kidnapping. “I don’t want to talk about my business activities,” Yatom told Israel’s Globes news outlet in 2022. “We don’t talk to the media,” Nave said.
Red flags ignored
Despite the fact that Yatom and the CGI spies colluded to defraud a NATO and EU member state in 2019, German investigators didn’t ask questions when Hanning joined Yatom’s company two years later. No investigation was opened when he spoke to the Israeli media of his “close friendship” with the former Mossad chief behind the swindle. Hanning’s ties to the Israeli intelligence underworld, apparently the subject of “persistent whispers” in the corridors of the BND, were evidently brushed aside or ignored.
None of this is to say that Shin Bet or Mossad is, without a doubt, the “foreign intelligence service” that Hanning passed secrets to. However, his contacts with Perry and Yatom certainly point that way, as does his work to advance Israeli foreign policy goals.
Hanning aided Israeli efforts to push the US into war with Iraq in late 2002, when he told then-CIA Director George Tenet that the BND had “plausible and convincing” evidence that Saddam Hussein was developing chemical and biological weapons. Hanning’s source, an Iraqi defector codenamed ‘Curveball’, later admitted to fabricating the claims.
Hanning now sits on the board of ‘United Against Nuclear Iran’, a Washington-based think tank funded by pro-Israel megadonors Miriam Adelson and Thomas Kaplan, which has explicitly advocated for military strikes on Iran since 2008. Adelson and Kaplan supply around three quarters of the group’s funding, with the remainder coming from smaller Jewish organizations and individual donors.
Europe’s wilful ignorance
Anyone following our ‘Wired for War’ series will recognize the pattern here. Over and over again, the actions of private Israeli spy firms are ignored by European governments, even when the Israeli state itself is involved in the skulduggery. The British government has refused to investigate Israeli meddling in Scottish elections, in order to “avoid giving offense” to the perpetrators. The EU has stayed silent on Israeli interference in elections in Cyprus and Slovenia, and on the proliferation of Israeli spyware throughout the union.
Meanwhile, governments at the EU and national level continue to sound the alarm about Russia’s invisible and unprovable “hybrid war” against the West. Fires, false drone sightings, and even natural disasters are all presented as examples of this shadow war, while the most blatant malfeasance from other foreign powers is ignored.
One day before Hanning’s arrest, his successor at the helm of the BND, Martin Jaeger, warned German MPs that Russia is “waging a shadow war,” and that “no other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany.” Had he looked at the company August Hanning kept, he might have reassessed his position.

articles.title: Sam Altman says AI will make ‘bad things’ happen. Exhibit A: needless death | Moustafa Bayoumi
articles.body:
Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, has some words for you about his company and the future of artificial intelligence.
“One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use it],” Altman told Politico’s new technology podcast and newsletter Decoded.
Yikes. This statement – and the approach it represents – is, well, problematic, to say the least. It’s also emblematic of precisely the kind of world-building and world-destroying that is happening with today’s technology in front of all our eyes, with precious little input from the rest of us.
Altman’s mention of the “bad things” that AI might bring makes it sound like AI’s failures mistakenly create innocent, minor problems or even silly little episodes, such as the time when Google’s “AI Overviews” told users to put non-toxic glue on pizza so the cheese will be less likely to slide off. Good advice is helpful. Bad advice? Chalk it up to being a bad thing.
But culinary adventurism is hardly the only realm that AI operates in and the damage AI is inflicting has already and repeatedly proven itself to be dangerous and even potentially deadly to humans.
OpenAI is embroiled in a lawsuit after the tragic suicide of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old student who initially began using OpenAI’s ChatGPT for homework help. The family’s lawsuit alleges that the teenager took his own life with the chatbot’s encouragement. (OpenAI has claimed Raine misused the platform.)
And Raine’s action is hardly the only one. OpenAI is facing multiple lawsuits filed by different families of victims of suicide and self-harm.
Nor is suicide the only “bad thing” to emerge in the AI universe. In February of this year, on the first day of the war in Iran, two Tomahawk missiles struck the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in the city of Minab, killing at least 120 children. (A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the US was probably responsible for the strike.)
In a recent investigation into the attack, Bloomberg News reported that an AI-linked system was used to target the school. In this case, the system is called Maven, and it is made by Palantir.
Unnamed defense officials told Bloomberg that “inside Centcom, which conducted the US attack, some personnel relied too much on the artificial intelligence embedded in Maven Smart System”. The report also adds that “in the past year, the Defense Department has rapidly made Maven a cornerstone of the US military apparatus”.
AI is helping to produce these tragic and needless deaths, but bad things happen, I guess.
Or there’s the little detail that the US may have come within a hair’s breadth of starting a major war against a superpower, all due to an AI error.
In September, CNN reported that an unidentified AI chatbot used by the US military decided that a Chinese ship in Middle Eastern waters was carrying components of a nuclear weapons program. According to CNN, US planes took off on an interception mission and US military personnel were preparing to board the ship.
Only then did the military look more closely at the report they were basing the mission on and realize the chatbot’s mistakes.
Also found in CNN’s frightening story is that the analyst who used the chatbot to come up with the shoddy analysis then used AI again to write the report, which set the whole thing in motion. A twofer of bad things, I suppose.
Why does it seem that these technologies, which, in the words of Trump’s White House, are “empowering Americans to achieve what was previously impossible across science, medicine, and nearly every other domain of human endeavor”, get such serious stuff so wrong and so often?
And isn’t it true that the more we rely on AI, the more dangerous these little mistakes become? And why were we never consulted about any of this in the first place?
Could it be that what’s behind the artificial intelligence revolution may be less about the utopian or dystopian future (take your pick) that’s just around the corner and more about the enormous amount of money that is being poured into these companies in the present?
AI may be the only thing keeping Trump’s economy afloat right now. And it’s paying dividends. According to the New Yorker, OpenAI “is reportedly preparing for an initial public offering at a potential valuation of a trillion dollars” and Sam Altman “may become one of the wealthiest and most powerful people on the planet”.
Those bad things? They only happen to other people.
Meanwhile, we are being warned almost every day that AI systems are getting so smart that they’ll end humanity.
But maybe the real worry here is not that the machines are taking over.
It’s that the humans are giving up, ceding control and responsibility in the name of hyping up a product that has shown itself as being really good at taking jobs away from people, stealing the intellectual property of others, writing some piss-poor undergraduate essays, spying on you and your license plates and bringing us to the brink of world war three because God forbid humans should actually question the output from machines. Or the makers of those machines.
What we need is real, tangible and enforceable government oversight over these technologies, which are quickly becoming a dominating force in all our lives. We must collectively have the right to decide how AI should be used. And despite what you may hear, China already regulates its AI companies quite aggressively.
Instead, Donald Trump, Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta and Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia believe that the AI companies should simply regulate themselves, so they have come up with something called the AI Accords.
Signed by leaders of Meta, Nvidia, Google, Anthropic, xAI and OpenAI, the accords ask tech companies to “implement robust internal controls and monitor the capabilities and alignment of its models”, among other things. “Over time,” the agreement states, “it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.”
I’m not holding my breath.
Trump, who has ordered the term artificial intelligence be discarded for “super intelligence”, posted the accord on social media on 29 September. The document, titled The White House Accord on Super Intelligence, can still be seen on his account and the White House’s official account. It’s signed by all six tech leaders and Trump, who in the document is labeled “President of the Unites States.”
Super intelligence, indeed.
In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org
- Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel to Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnist

articles.title: Fewer targets, more waves: jet-powered Gerans partly free Russia to concentrate missiles, ISW says
articles.body:
Russia is concentrating missiles on a smaller, more specific set of targets, and its jet-powered attack drones are part of the reason, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed. Its combined attack overnight on 7 October killed 22 people in Pryluky, the State Emergency Service (SES) said as of the morning of 8 October. Russian milbloggers noted the shift the same day.
Russia often uses concentrated drone and missile strikes to overwhelm localized Ukrainian air defenses and destroy urban centers, ISW noted. Pryluky, where the strike killed children, was one of the areas a Russian channel says drew a significant share of the Kh-101s that night. With winter close, ISW expects the same pattern against Ukraine's energy grid, with jet drones partly letting Russia keep its missiles for priority targets without firing many more.
Missile waves on a few areas, Russian channels claim
Russia launched 48 Kh-101, Iskander-K, and Kalibr cruise missiles overnight on 7 October, Ukraine's Air Force reported. It also fired ballistic missiles, Zircon and Oniks anti-ship missiles, and 130 strike and decoy drones, 46 of them jet-powered Shahed-type models.
Russian milbloggers claimed the same day that Moscow had grouped a large part of its missile salvo into repeated waves on a few areas, while other weapons kept stretching Ukraine's air defenses elsewhere. The pro-war Russian Telegram channel Dva Mayora described the change as a switch from striking with splayed fingers to a series of hits with missile "fists." Defenders must then absorb a sharply rising load around one chosen site as one wave follows another, the channel claimed.
Citing Ukrainian monitoring channels, it claimed that roughly 30 or more Kh-101 cruise missiles flew toward Pryluky, Kremenchuk, Svitlovodsk, and Oleksandriia in Chernihiv, Poltava, and Kirovohrad oblasts. It put the Kremenchuk group at up to 15 missiles, Kh-101s and Kalibrs among them, aimed at the area of Kremenchuk and its hydroelectric plant.
Jet drones take some of the load off Russia's missiles
ISW said the jet-powered versions penetrate Ukrainian air defenses deeper and more reliably than propeller models. In ISW's assessment, that partly lets Russia concentrate cruise and ballistic missiles on priority targets without significantly raising missile use. Russia builds about 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet drones a month, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) told Militarnyi in August.
Ukraine spent three years learning to catch Russian drones—so Russia made them fly faster
ISW expects Russia to apply the pattern in a likely brutal winter campaign against energy infrastructure. Russia likely intends to make city life untenable and force Ukraine to capitulate to its demands, ISW assessed. Such tactics have not worked before and are unlikely to work now, analysts added.
They called cheap countermeasures to jet drones and small cruise missiles vital, alongside Western air defense aid such as US-made Patriots, which can stop ballistic missiles. Ukraine has already paired a Soviet-era Kub launcher with American RIM-7 interceptors to catch jet drones.

articles.title: Syria considers help in Yemen war after Saudi airports come under Houthi fire
articles.body:
Plane damaged at Riyadh airport as Houthis escalate attacks, sources say
RIYADH/DUBAI, Oct 8 - Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis escalated their campaign of strikes against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, trying to shut down the kingdom's airspace and oil facilities with missile fire that has killed three people this week and left a plane badly damaged.
The group said it had struck Riyadh airport and warned workers to stay away from energy plants, which would be targeted.
Shrapnel from an interception or another projectile hit had left the commercial plane belonging to Saudi state carrier Saudia Airlines heavily damaged after catching fire while parked at an airport terminal on Thursday, three people briefed on the matter said.
They said no passengers were believed to have been on the plane at the time but they could not rule out any injuries as a result of the incident. A thick black column of smoke and flames were shown rising from Riyadh airport in video verified by Reuters.
Saudi Arabia's government media office, its civil aviation authority and Saudia Airlines did not respond to emailed requests for comment.
Lufthansa and Air India said they were suspending flights to Riyadh after Houthi attacks.
Separately, Saudi officials said debris from an intercepted missile had hit a kindergarten and medical complex in Riyadh.
The Houthis say they are targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in Yemen's reignited civil war. Saudi Arabia says it is backing an offensive by Yemen's UN-recognised government to take back territory from the Houthis.
The conflict, now an overspill of the US-Iran war, has added new chaos to a region already aflame, and threatens to draw other states into gruelling mountain fighting, with Syria now considering deploying troops to assist Saudi Arabia.
The kingdom has pushed for support from allied nations, including Turkey and Pakistan, even if only in a logistical or defensive capacity, as it tries to reverse Houthi gains in southwest Yemen, by the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
Those requests have taken on more urgency since Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people had been killed this week in strikes on Riyadh airport and Abha airport in the southwest.
DELAYS AND CANCELLATIONS
The Houthis have made Saudi airports a focus of their strikes, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said it had destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the group towards Riyadh and another towards Khamis Mushayt, home to a major airbase.
According to data compiled by aviation analytics company Cirium, almost half of departures from Riyadh airport had been cancelled by 1500 GMT, with 31 more cancellations expected for Friday in all Saudi airports.
Flight tracker FlightRadar24 indicated numerous delayed arrivals and departures at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Thursday. The airport advised travellers to contact airlines to check the status of flights before trying to travel.
Riyadh is due to host a major meeting of energy policy makers, the WPC Energy Congress, this week.
Several multinational firms based in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) told staff to work from home after loud booms were heard on Thursday morning, five people familiar with the matter said, including some affected staff.
The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment, and KAFD was not immediately available for comment.
Some diplomats said they had received warnings, and some schools in Riyadh told parents there were orders to shelter in place, though authorities did not issue a public alert. Reuters could not identify the source of the booms.
CIVIL WAR REIGNITED BY CONFLICT IN IRAN
Yemen's long-running civil war, which paused with a ceasefire in 2022, has erupted again in recent weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Their threats to shipping and attacks on Saudi cities and infrastructure have drawn the kingdom back in. This week, Saudi-backed forces launched a counterattack, taking back some areas around the strait.
However, in a war with several front lines, the Houthis have made gains of their own, surrounding Yemen's third-largest city, Taiz, by taking territory along its main mountain road to Aden.
The fighting, which pits the Houthis against a coalition of Saudi-backed forces under the internationally recognised government, has led to a humanitarian crisis in the poorest Arab state, displacing 200,000 people since the conflict resumed.
One US and one Syrian defence official said Syria was carefully considering options for military support, including defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks, or an offensive deployment to help take the fight to the Houthis.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia but that its focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from its own civil war.
NATO-member Turkey said on Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis. A Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems. REUTERS

articles.title: Zelensky Visits Pryluky With UK’s Miliband, Thanks EU for €1.2B Tranche for Drones
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky traveled to Pryluky with UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to honor the victims after a Russian barrage – coinciding with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s 74th birthday – left 22 civilians dead, including five children.
In a series of statements issued on Thursday, Oct. 8, Zelensky condemned Wednesday’s strikes and confirmed that the strike on the apartment building left 54 people injured. During the visit, the two leaders met with residents who survived the attack and were briefed on the scale of the destruction.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We must support our people,” Zelensky said, pointing to a veteran who lived in the apartment building destroyed by Russia.
“When partners are literally standing alongside Ukrainians, it truly matters,” he continued, thanking Miliband for standing beside him in Pryluky and alluding to Western partners who continue supplying Kyiv with funding and air defense it needs to protect itself against Russia’s aggression.
A city left without homes and shelters
The damage extends far beyond the destroyed building. According to Zelensky, more than 100 residential buildings across Pryluky were damaged, along with schools, kindergartens, shops, businesses and other critical infrastructure the city depends on.
Residents who spoke with the president described a shortage of both shelters and housing. In response, Zelensky ordered the head of the Chernihiv Regional Military Administration to quickly help those who have nowhere to live, adding that temporary assistance should eventually be followed by permanent solutions.
Trump Envoys in Talks With Putin’s Money Man Over Russian Gas, Reports Say
“It is also important that the victims ultimately receive new housing,” he said.
Those whose homes were in the destroyed building should be allowed back into their apartments once the security situation permits, Zelensky said, placing the head of the State Emergency Service (SES) in charge of the process.
Human cost of Russia’s war
Ukrainian authorities consistently remind their partners that the war is not a distant fact on paper, but a reality measured in human lives and relentless terror.
This became particularly visible in the last few weeks, as Russia increased its strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure following the departure of senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner from Moscow.
The two visited Moscow on Sept. 5 to hold talks with Russian diplomats and Putin himself, aiming to broker an end to the war. For the first time ever during their tenure, the envoys also visited Kyiv just a day after.
Despite all three sides describing the negotiations as positive and productive, Russian barrage amplified.
The latest attack on Pryluky left 17 civilians hospitalized, including a five-year-old girl. It also highlighted gaps in the city’s protection.
After the health minister briefed him on efforts to build shelters in medical facilities, Zelensky ordered officials to speed up the work and secure additional funding. The hospital’s own shelter must be repaired as a priority, he said, while a new, modern one is built in its place.
Together with city authorities, the health minister and the head of the Chernihiv Regional Military Administration will be responsible for the project, Zelensky said.
He also tasked the interior ministers with inspecting every shelter in the city.
Deadliest strike in a wave of attacks
The Pryluky attack was the deadliest in a broader Russian assault launched on Wednesday, Oct. 7.
A Kh-101 cruise missile was used to strike the five-story apartment block as Russia targeted cities across Ukraine with ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as Shahed drones, before continuing with aerial bombs during the day.
As rescuers continued recovering bodies, the toll from Russia’s latest attacks kept rising. By Thursday, Zelensky said strikes on Pryluky, Kramatorsk, Kyiv and other cities had killed 78 people and injured 215 in recent days alone.
He described the attacks as a severe escalation and “terror directed against people and life,” warning that world leaders must not ignore what is happening.
EU and US support to continue
The same concerns were raised during a telephone call with European Council President António Costa later on Thursday.
Zelensky also thanked Costa for the €1.2 billion (l $1.4 billion) tranche that arrived in Ukraine on Wednesday, saying the money would go toward defense, primarily drones.
“This will provide tremendous support,” Zelensky said.
Beyond immediate military needs, the two leaders discussed the timeline for opening the next clusters in Ukraine’s EU accession talks, a winter energy package and further financial assistance. The call came ahead of the EC summit in Brussels, scheduled for Oct. 15-16.
Between Zelensky and Costa, an agreement was reached to meet in a trilateral format with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Zelensky also briefed the EC President on meetings with US officials planned for the coming days, particularly Oct. 9-10, noting that a Ukrainian delegation is already on its way.
You can also highlight the text and press Ctrl + Enter

articles.title: Russian attack on bus kills at least 30 people near Ukraine frontline
articles.body:
A Russian missile strike on a bus in the eastern city of Kramatorsk has killed at least 30 people, officials have said, in one of the worst attacks by Moscow on Ukrainian civilians this year.
The regional prosecutor’s office in the Donetsk region said on Thursday the vehicle had been hit at 10am by an aerial bomb. “As of now, the death toll from this morning’s attack has risen to 30. Eighteen people were wounded,” it said, adding that all local public transport had been suspended.
Images posted by police showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris, as well as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus. A second bus had also caught fire, officials said. The strike targeted an area next to a dental clinic on the city’s Yuvileina Street.
Three people had also been killed by shelling in the village of Bilenke, outside Kramatorsk, they added. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Kremlin had deliberately targeted an “ordinary public transport stop”.
Some of those killed could not be identified because of the severity of their injuries, Ukraine’s president added. He said the number of victims could “sadly rise”, as doctors fought to save the lives of those wounded.
He said: “This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and a response from the world is a must. A forceful response – exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have brought. May all those killed rest in peace.”
The bombing follows a gruesome Russian strike on Wednesday on a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The building collapsed, entombing those inside. At least 22 people were killed, including five children, aged between one and eight.
Visiting the scene with Ed Miliband, the British foreign secretary, Zelenskyy urged the US to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage so that Ukraine could hit targets inside Russia such as launch sites. So far, Donald Trump and Elon Musk have refused Kyiv’s request.
Miliband said there was “no clearer sign of Putin’s evil, evil intent and strategy in this conflict” than this week’s murderous attacks. He said: “Putin once said that he was going to win on the battlefield. He is trying to win by terrorising civilians.”
Writing earlier on social media, Zelenskyy called on western allies to take “concrete steps” to boost Ukraine’s depleted air defences, amid a round-the-clock Russian onslaught in recent weeks featuring ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
“Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft, and investments in interceptors – all of this is directly helping save lives every day. Important talks with our partners will take place today and tomorrow,” Zelenskyy said.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk form part of a “fortress belt”. They are the last two big cities in northern Donetsk under full Ukrainian military control. Russia has been trying to capture them for more than a decade, after a brief period in which Russian forces occupied Sloviansk in 2014.
The cities are home to thousands of civilians, as well as Ukrainian soldiers. In recent months, roads have been festooned with nets to protect traffic from marauding enemy drones. These defences offer little protection, however, against aerial bombs.
“These are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army,” the Donetsk regional governor, Vadym Filashkin, said on Telegram after Thursday’s strike. “Russia comes to Ukrainian land with death.”
He added: “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.
“Russia deliberately flouts every conceivable rule of warfare and the norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians.”
There was criticism of the White House’s policy of engaging with Vladimir Putin, whom Donald Trump has invited to December’s G20 summit in Miami, Florida. The Kremlin has yet to say if Russia’s leader will take part.
The former US ambassador to Moscow Michael McFaul said on social media that Russia was guilty of terrorism. “There is no other word for it. Putin is running a terrorist state. That officials from my country call this terrorist a nice guy is deeply embarrassing for me.”
Putin has demanded Ukraine cede the rest of the eastern Donbas region still under its control. Kyiv refuses to hand over its territory, believing Russia will take any concessions and carry on fighting.

articles.title: UK Announces $71M Winter Aid, New Sanctions on Russia
articles.body:
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband pledged £54 million ($71 million) to Ukraine ahead of winter and unveiled fresh sanctions against Russia on Thursday, Oct. 8, during his first visit to the country since taking office.
Miliband announced the measures alongside President Volodymyr Zelensky and Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, with whom he toured the site of a deadly Russian missile strike in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Five winters on, the people of Ukraine are still living under constant threat of Russian strikes, energy blackouts and death,” Miliband said, according to the UK governmental website.
“My message to [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is clear – You cannot wait us out,” he continued, reaffirming UK’s support for Ukraine despite ongoing hybrid warfare threats from Russia, which have significantly intensified in recent months.
The UK pledged another £6 million (approximately $8 million) to Ukraine specifically for the “pursuit of justice” for Russia’s war crimes. As of Oct. 2, Ukraine had opened nearly 244,000 criminal cases over crimes committed by Russian forces and their accomplices on the country’s territory, including almost 227,000 war-crime investigations.
Strike on Pryluky left 22 people dead
The strike on an apartment building in Pryluky coincided with Russian Putin’s 74th birthday, and it left at least 22 civilians dead, including five children.
Zelensky Visits Pryluky With UK’s Miliband, Thanks EU for €1.2B Tranche for Drones
According to Zelensky, 54 people were injured just in that strike alone, while the overall number of Russian attacks left 78 people dead and 215 injured nationwide in recent days. He described the attacks as a severe escalation and “terror directed against people and life,” warning that world leaders must not ignore what is happening.
During their visit earlier on Thursday, the three leaders spoke with survivors of the attack and with emergency workers who had taken part in the rescue effort.
“Russia could end this war tomorrow,” Miliband said. “Instead, we’ve seen escalating attacks, including on key infrastructure and Ukrainian cultural landmarks.”
According to him, the UK’s support for Ukraine is rooted not only in European and NATO security, but also in a wider global effort to defend justice and the rule of law.
How the funding will be allocated
The new funding comes as Ukraine continues to appeal to its Western allies for air defense and financial support ahead of the upcoming winter, when Russia is expected to intensify its campaign against critical infrastructure, including the power grid and water-supply systems.
Of the total pledged, £20 million (about $26 million) will go toward Ukraine’s energy security; to support crews carrying out emergency repairs to the power grid after Russian strikes, provide backup generators and solar power for use during blackouts, as well as to fund technologies to help Ukraine diversify its energy sources.
The remaining £34 million (roughly $45 million) will be allocated for heating and water systems. According to the UK’s government, the amount also includes direct cash assistance.
Aid will be delivered together with the Ukrainian government and partners including UNICEF, the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and the Ukrainian Red Cross.
Fresh sanctions on Russia
Beyond financial support, Miliband announced fresh sanctions on around 40 individuals and entities in Russia’s financial, oil, and technology sectors.
With the latest package, more than 90% of Russia’s total oil production capacity is now covered by UK sanctions, according to the government.
So far, Britain has sanctioned more than 600 vessels and over 3,500 targets in total under its Russia sanctions regime.
On Oct.1, the UK has announced a new package of 31 sanctions, focusing on global disinformation networks and individuals responsible for the torture of Ukrainian civilians and the forced deportation of children.
Late September, when the EU compromised on the extension of the sanctions on about 3,000 individuals and entities in exchange for the delistment of two Russian oligarchs closely connected to Putin, the UK pledged to keep its own sanctions in place.
The measures are intended to send a message to Russian diplomats and those who support Russia’s war to step back from escalation and move toward a ceasefire.
According to Sybiha’s statement on X, the meeting coincided with the sixth anniversary of the Agreement on Political Cooperation, Free Trade and Strategic Partnership, which Ukraine and the UK signed in London.
Since then, he said, relations between the two countries have reached a new level, strengthened by the historic 100 Year Partnership Agreement that their leaders signed in Kyiv last year.
“We also launched the second meeting of the Political Pillar of the Ukraine-UK Strategic Partnership Dialogue and agreed to continue expert-level discussions in Kyiv,” Sybiha said, expressing gratitude to the UK for its “comprehensive support” – which currently equates to £25 billion (about $33 billion), including £16 billion (roughly $21 billion) in military support.
