articles.title: Ukraine hit a data center operated by the Russian tech giant Yandex. How vulnerable is Russia’s internet to further drone attacks?
articles.body:
Ukraine hit a data center operated by the Russian tech giant Yandex. How vulnerable is Russia’s internet to further drone attacks?
What happened?
Overnight on October 8, Ukrainian forces struck Yandex’s data center in Sasovo, in Russia’s Ryazan region, with drones, causing a fire. No one was injured, but the data center temporarily shut down completely. This disrupted some of Yandex’s own services, as well as those of companies that used the tech giant’s infrastructure in Sasovo.
In the morning, users complained of problems accessing Yandex Disk and Yandex Documents. Disruptions then spread to Yandex Mail, the Yandex-owned Cian, Avito, IVI, MegaFon, Russian Railways, T-Bank, and several property developers and media outlets. The cascading disruptions across the Russian internet throughout the day may have been linked to an attempt to redistribute server capacity after the fire in Sasovo.
The data center occupies part of the former Sasta machine tool factory and houses two of Yandex’s three supercomputers, Lyapunov and Chervonenkis, which are used to train neural networks.
Whether these systems were damaged is not yet known. The overall extent of the damage is also unclear. Yandex shares have already fallen by more than 3% following the attack, according to Moscow Exchange data.
So it got hit. They’ll fix it, right?
We don’t know. Much depends on how badly the fire damaged the equipment. Even if restoring the data center is technically possible, it might simply not make sense, partly because of the threat of further attacks. After a series of successful Ukrainian strikes on large Wildberries warehouses, for example, the online retailer’s management decided to spread its inventory across smaller facilities. Yandex may take the same approach.
Some of the data stored at the Ryazan data center, however, may be recoverable. If Yandex customers uploaded their data to the cloud, those files were stored simultaneously at different company data centers — more precisely, in four “availability zones.” Yandex said in 2019:
All of this data is replicated: When an object is edited, created, or deleted, every copy is updated.
Things are a little more complicated for other companies’ virtual machines hosted there. Customers are responsible for backing up that data themselves. They could have used the separate paid service Yandex Cloud Backup, which would also have stored their data at several data centers. Or they could have chosen another solution — or made no backups at all.
Why do services stop working when data centers are hit?
Because these facilities store user data and house the servers that companies and organizations rent to run their websites or internal infrastructure.
Data centers can withstand a temporary power outage thanks to their own diesel generators, the loss of an individual communications link thanks to connections to multiple telecom providers, and even a small fire thanks to automatic fire suppression systems. But, like online retailers’ warehouses, they have proved defenseless against drone strikes. Unless, of course, they are housed in former Cold War shelters — Europe has several such data centers.
Should we expect more attacks like these — as with oil refineries, Wildberries, and Ozon?
Nothing can be predicted with certainty during a war. But the context matters.
The strike on Yandex’s data center looks like a logical Ukrainian response to systematic Russian military attacks on Ukrainian digital hubs, including Cosmonova and Datagroup facilities. Since late September, Russian forces have damaged or destroyed the data centers of at least eight companies.
Russia’s Defense Ministry officially called these strikes a “forced digital detox.” Today, a few hours after the attack on Yandex’s data center, Andriy Kovalenko, the former head of the Center for Countering Disinformation at Ukraine’s National Security and Defense Council, wrote:
Two can play that game.
Which other data centers in Russia could be targeted? And could strikes on them bring down the entire Russian internet?
Any technology hub could be at risk, but a nationwide digital blackout is unlikely.
Sarkis Darbinyan, a lawyer specializing in digital rights and an expert with RKS.global, told Meduza that a single strike on a regional data center cannot take down a major service entirely. Modern IT companies have infrastructure spread across the country, so when equipment fails, user traffic is automatically rerouted to backup systems. Russia’s main data centers are concentrated in Moscow and the surrounding region and are very well protected. Disabling them all would be an extremely ambitious undertaking, Darbinyan said. Russia has close to 200 data centers in total.
Darbinyan believes further targeted attacks on regional facilities belonging to Rostelecom, Sber, VK, or Selectel are possible in theory:
They could cause local disruptions, but would affect local residents more than the country as a whole: Regional government systems, online school gradebooks, medical customer relationship management systems, and internet-connected cash registers would temporarily stop working. These services could be down for anywhere from a few hours to a day while administrators reconfigure the systems.
Another potential target for Ukrainian forces is MSK-IX, Russia’s largest internet exchange point. It has become a “symbol of the centralization of the Russian internet,” Darbinyan said. If MSK-IX is hit, he told Meduza, internet access across the country could slow dramatically, alternative communications links could become overloaded, and the websites of small companies and local providers could temporarily become inaccessible. Even then, however, the internet would not shut down entirely, Darbinyan said:
This is a fundamental feature of the network, built into it back in the days of ARPANET so that it could withstand even a nuclear strike. So attacks like these only impair services temporarily, for a few hours — they certainly don’t cause a complete digital collapse.
Are these strikes legal? And why attack internet infrastructure at all? After all, it’s civilians, not the military, who suffer the most…
Indeed, if we accept that this is primarily civilian infrastructure, neither army’s strikes on data centers appear justified. The Geneva Conventions explicitly state that a facility is a military objective if it makes an “effective contribution to military action” and its neutralization “offers a definite military advantage” to the attacking side. In cases of doubt, it is presumed to be civilian — meaning this infrastructure cannot be attacked without clear evidence.
Unfortunately, when it comes to data centers, Russian forces — and, following their lead, Ukrainian forces — are clearly ignoring the question of legality. For example, Russia’s Defense Ministry justified its strikes on Ukrainian data centers by saying that the grounds of one facility “were used by units of Ukraine’s Defense Ministry and other security agencies to store dual-use goods.” Another data center allegedly handled “the processing and transmission of intelligence for the Ukrainian armed forces.” The ministry provided no evidence for these claims.
As for the military rationale, at least some data centers meet the criteria for targets in long-range strike campaigns. Meduza’s Explainers desk previously set out these criteria:
- The facilities are poorly protected and can be destroyed with just a few drones carrying small warheads
- Their coordinates are well known
- They contain large quantities of valuable goods
- Systematically destroying these businesses can damage the enemy’s economy
- Disrupting internet infrastructure can also make civilians feel just how much the war is costing their country and, in theory, fuel public discontent with the government’s actions.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Journalists analyse intercepted Russian plan to destroy Ukraine's energy infrastructure
articles.body:
Journalists analyse intercepted Russian plan to destroy Ukraine's energy infrastructure
Journalists from Skhemy, an investigative project by Radio Liberty, have examined a Russian plan to pressure Ukraine, which identifies as priority targets for strikes "nodes" near Ukraine's western border through which electricity is imported, major hydroelectric power plants and even nuclear power plants.
Source: Radio Liberty
Details: The journalists obtained a copy of the Russian plan from sources in Ukrainian forces and studied it in detail.
The plan intercepted by Ukraine concerns Russia's strategy to cut electricity and heat supplies to Ukraine's major cities by up to 90%.
"One of the largest attacks took place on the night of 29-30 September, when hundreds of Russian strike drones and ballistic missiles were launched against the energy infrastructure of the capital and Kyiv Oblast," Radio Liberty recalls.
At least three of the facilities attacked that night – two combined heat and power plants in Kyiv and one thermal power plant in Kyiv Oblast – were identified by Skhemy journalists as being included in the Russian plan.
The plan, apparently prepared by the Russian side and provided by Ukrainian intelligence, was presented to Ukraine's partners in Paris on 17 September by Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal at the energy meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group (also known as the Ramstein format), Radio Liberty notes.
The copy of the plan contains an analysis of Ukraine's energy capacity and calculations of the number of missiles, drones and bombs Russia would need to cut major cities such as Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa off from electricity, heat and water.
The list of facilities "to be hit" includes nuclear power plants alongside small boiler houses.
However, the plan assesses them solely in terms of Ukrainians' electricity consumption in gigawatts, without any mention of the potential nuclear threat, the analysts note.
The plan identifies four priority targets: power generation and electricity supply, water supply, sewage and heating.
The first priority is to disable "nodes" near the western border through which electricity is imported from Europe.
These include cross-border power lines, high-voltage substations near the border and interconnectors – systems linking the power grids of Ukraine and EU countries, receiving European electricity and transforming it before transmitting it further into the country.
The plan also refers to major hydroelectric power plants, located mainly on the Dnipro and Dniester rivers, and the shutdown of three nuclear power plants – South Ukraine, Rivne and Khmelnytskyi. The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant has been under Russian occupation since March 2022.
The plan lists a total of 60 key targets, including the aforementioned hydroelectric and nuclear power plants and interconnectors, as well as thermal power plants, combined heat and power plants, substations, boiler houses, wastewater treatment facilities, pumping stations and other state and municipal facilities on which electricity, water, sewage and heating depend.
The plan says that such attacks would require basic types of weapons: up to 770 Molniya and Geran UAVs and Dan-T/Banderol drone-launched cruise missiles, as well as 170 FABs (here and throughout the article, a modification of a high-explosive aerial bomb equipped with a universal planning and guidance module) and 75 Kinzhal aeroballistic and Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
The plan contains a detailed calculation for each facility, specifying how many weapons and of what type would be needed to disable it, Skhemy reported.
So, two Iskander missiles are envisaged for the destruction of a nuclear power plant (the plan refers to an "outdoor switchyard" – a high-voltage installation located outdoors that receives and transmits electricity). Accordingly, six missiles are required to destroy the equipment at three nuclear power plants.
As for hydroelectric power plants, up to 25 Molniyas, Gerans or Dan-T/Banderols, or three Kinzhal missiles, are allocated for each.
"In other words, for the destruction of 10 major Ukrainian hydroelectric power plants, depending on the distance to the launch site or line of contact, the document calculates a total of up to 30 Molniyas (for facilities located up to 60 km from the line of contact) and around 240 Gerans and Dan-T/Banderols, which can be replaced by Kinzhal ballistic missiles (probably up to 30)," Radio Liberty says.
For combined heat and power plants (five transformers), the calculation is likewise 25 Gerans and so on, or three Kinzhal missiles per facility. The plan also says that each combined heat and power plant could require around 25 FAB-500 bombs and five Iskander-M missiles.
For a substation (three transformers) or an interconnector, the calculation is 15 Molniyas and so on, or three Kinzhal missiles per facility. For housing and utilities infrastructure, it is 25 FABs or five Iskanders per facility, while a boiler house would require 20 Gerans.
Moreover, next to the section on boiler houses, the authors of the plan explicitly note that "due to their proximity to residential areas, the use of other types of weapons could result in civilian casualties".
The Russian plan specifies the types of weapons to be used "depending on the target and distance".
For example, it lists Molniyas and FAB-500s for distances of up to 40-60 km; Geran-4, Dan-T/Banderol and Iskander-M for 60-500 km; and Kinzhal, Kalibr, Oreshnik and Zircon for more than 500 km.
The capital's facilities occupy a special place in the plan, with Kyiv's energy system analysed and presented in detail.
The authors of the plan note that the capital's energy system is fairly extensive but identify five substations in the "Kyiv ring" serving different parts of the city as its "bottleneck", or more precisely, its weak point.
"Overall, according to the document, hitting 12 key substations in the three cities mentioned above should halt up to 90% of electricity supplies. For this, the authors of the document specify 40-50 Molniya drones and 130-140 Geran-4 or Dan-T/Banderol drone-launched missiles," Radio Liberty says.
Experts interviewed by the journalists say the plan is not a final operational plan but rather a set of calculations.
They also say this is not a new tactic, as Russia has systematically attacked Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, turning cold and darkness into a weapon.
Subscribe on Patreon to back our journalism long-term.

articles.title: It was built to shield Russian crops from hail. Now it’s being pitched as a drone interceptor
articles.body:
Russia has shown a drone interceptor built on the Alazan, a civilian anti-hail rocket, Militarnyi reported. The sample went on display at a weapons exhibition that Russian dictator Vladimir Putin toured at the Chebarkul training range in the Urals on 2 October.
Ukraine now sends drones at Russia by the hundreds, by Moscow's own count. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses intercepted nearly 900 overnight into 6 October. Russia's missile-based air defense was built to repel aircraft raids and a few cruise missiles, not swarms of low-flying drones.
In May, Ukrainian intelligence said Russia was adding four regiments, 24 battalions, and 162 batteries to counter Ukrainian strike drones. The converted Alazan, which Militarnyi calls an anti-drone system, is one more piece of that search. Meanwhile, the commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert Brovdi, said his forces struck 300 Russian air-defense assets between January and 19 September.
From hail reagent to shrapnel
Based on the size of the sample on display, the interceptor builds on the Alazan-2M or Alazan-6 series, Militarnyi assessed. The outlet put the stated cost at up to $12,000 per unit but did not say who named the figure. In civilian service, the rocket flies about 10 km, climbs up to 8 km, and carries about 0.5 kg of reagent. For air defense, the developers plan to replace that reagent with a fragmentation warhead.
Militarnyi's analysis of the published photos describes the front end as a steering assembly: four cruciform deflector fins, probably paired with a seeker or a fuze. At the rear sit folding stabilizers and the open nozzle of a solid-fuel motor, held in a metal cradle.
One sample among 300 exhibits
The Kremlin's account of the visit lists more than 300 weapons on display, including interceptor drones, but does not mention the rocket. Propaganda channel Russia 1 aired the interceptor in its report from the visit, and the Kremlin pool of state news agency RIA posted photos.
Read also
- Ukraine squeezes more defense out of Soviet-era stock, pairing Kub launcher and American RIM-7 interceptors to catch Russia’s jet-powered drones
- Ukrainian units hit record number of Russian air defense systems and radars in September, one of them 552 kilometers away
- Ukraine’s answer to Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds: a small new missile named Nika, heading into testing

articles.title: Russia's winter campaign against energy infrastructure has begun. Will Kyiv be left without electricity, heating and water?
articles.body:
Russia's winter campaign against energy infrastructure has begun. Will Kyiv be left without electricity, heating and water?
On the night of 29-30 September – ten days earlier than last year – Russia's winter campaign against Ukraine's energy infrastructure officially began. Ekonomichna Pravda (EP) sources say Russian ballistic missiles and drones have been primarily targeting energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding region. Their targets include thermal power plants, combined heat and power plants, hydroelectric power plants and electricity transmission infrastructure.
Last winter demonstrated the problems that massive strikes on critical infrastructure can cause in people's everyday lives. This year Ukraine is heading into the heating season better prepared. Power generation has been restored, backup power sources secured, security measures strengthened, equipment stocked up, and repair crews replenished.
But as everyone knows, no level of protection can fully shield the power grid from Russian attacks, meaning that Ukraine is highly unlikely to get through the winter without some disruptions to electricity, heating and water supplies.
Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin has no desire, and certainly no plans, to agree to an energy truce any time soon, given that he sees further strikes as a means of exerting pressure on the Ukrainian authorities and influencing Kyiv's position ahead of possible negotiations.
Moscow is likely to focus its attacks on Kyiv, Ukraine's most densely populated city, in an attempt to influence the public mood in the capital – something the Ukrainian authorities cannot afford to ignore.
The Kremlin's overall objective is to bring about a humanitarian catastrophe and render the Ukrainian capital uninhabitable. Read on to find out how Kyiv is preparing for the heating season, what challenges lie ahead, and what its residents should expect.
Resilience Plans
In early March, Ukraine's National Security and Defence Council approved Comprehensive Resilience Plans for regions and major cities. The plans set out step-by-step roadmaps to prepare critical infrastructure for the next heating season.
EP has looked at what the plans involve, how much they are expected to cost to implement, and whether they can all feasibly be put into practice before the cold weather arrives. The plans cover four key areas, some of which may overlap.
- The first area concerns protection for critical infrastructure. It covers air defence measures and the completion of Level 2 protective shelters at facilities belonging to Ukrenergo (Ukraine's state-owned electricity transmission operator), Naftogaz (the largest national oil and gas company), the Gas Transmission System Operator of Ukraine, and regional electricity distribution companies.
- The second area involves building 1.5 GW of distributed generation capacity, primarily in the city of Kyiv and Dnipropetrovsk, Odesa, Poltava and Kyiv oblasts. Distributed generation refers to smaller power generation facilities located closer to consumers, rather than centralised in a small number of large plants.
- The third and fourth areas are about ensuring uninterrupted heating and water supplies.
At the heart of the plans is a simulation of a total blackout, designed to answer a crucial question: how would the city keep its heating and water systems running if that were to happen? "The concept has been dubbed 'Dark, but warm.' In other words, the lights might go out after a bombardment, but there must always be water and heating," Oleksandr Kharchenko, director of the Centre for Energy Research, told EP.
Immediately after the government adopted the Resilience Plans, energy sector sources told EP they were overly ambitious and optimistic and said they doubted that all the measures could be implemented before winter.
Three years would be a more realistic timescale for completion of the work, the sources said. What has been achieved so far, and how is Kyiv preparing to go into the heating season?
What will happen to the electricity supply?
Before Russia began to attack its power grid, Ukraine had a significant electricity surplus. Generation comfortably exceeded domestic demand.
Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal says Ukraine currently has over 15 GW of generating capacity available during the evening, when demand is at its highest. And that's with only six of Ukraine's nine nuclear reactors in operation (the other three are undergoing maintenance). The plan is to increase available generation capacity to 19.6 GW by 1 November and 21.4 GW by the end of the year.
Meanwhile, electricity consumption last week ranged from 6,800 MW at its lowest to 10,200 MW at its peak. The sharp drop in consumption across the country is linked to Russia's constant attacks on major metals companies, which have been forced to halt production.
Electricity consumption will obviously go up in winter, but if all the planned repairs are completed, power generation should be sufficient to keep the system balanced in normal winter temperatures, a source at an energy company told EP.
"However, we have to factor in that the energy sector will come under attack," the source noted. "We had enough generation capacity on paper at the end of last September too, but after several waves of attacks, we ended up with a shortfall of 5,000-6,000 MW."
So the main risk this winter is not a shortage of generation capacity at the outset, but how quickly that capacity could be lost due to further Russian attacks.
For Kyiv, this is particularly important. Russian attacks have already destroyed a significant portion of the capital's power generation capacity. Some of that capacity is slated to be restored, but once brought back online, the facilities will become priority targets again.
The second major area of preparation is therefore to ensure a reliable electricity supply for the capital. The Kyiv energy ring is built around four 330 kV substations, supported by dozens of smaller 110 kV substations.
The Resilience Plan envisages providing Level 2 protection for these sites. According to sources who spoke to EP, some of the work is already complete and the remainder is due to be finished by the end of the year, despite government statements about a freeze on capital expenditure. Level 2 protection is designed to withstand drone attacks, but not ballistic strikes.
Another part of Kyiv's Resilience Plan is establishing backup power sources. A document seen by EP puts the capital's peak winter load at 2 GW. Critical infrastructure accounts for around 280 MW, and a reserve of generators and cogeneration units is to be set up specifically to keep those facilities supplied.
EP sources say around 150 MW of the planned 200 MW of distributed generation capacity has already been commissioned. According to an energy market source, the city could have 180-185 MW available by the end of the year. Privately owned facilities with a combined capacity of 55-60 MW could also come online before winter; around half of them are ready to start operating.
The main function of distributed generation is to keep critical infrastructure running if the main generation sources or the grid are damaged.
In other words, if there is an electricity shortage, priority will be given to water supply systems, boilerhouses, hospitals, communications, transport and other essential services. For ordinary consumers, emergency or hourly power outage schedules will be in place, as they were last year. What will this mean for the public?
A senior manager at a state-owned energy company told EP: "If temperatures fall below -10°C and some generation capacity can't be brought back online in time, we could be looking at around eight to ten hours of power cuts per day. That's assuming there are no further attacks.
Then there's the pessimistic scenario – heavy strikes and widespread destruction. In that case there might be only four hours of electricity a day, leaving Kyiv without power for up to 20 hours," the source added. Even so, EP sources say Russia will not be able to plunge Kyiv into a total blackout.
In other words, the worst-case scenario for the capital is prolonged power cuts for most consumers, but critical infrastructure kept powered up.
The source concludes: "No one can give an accurate forecast right now. The situation depends on many factors. It will depend on where and how the attacks happen, which power plants are still working, and how quickly they can be brought back online."
What are the risks to Kyiv's heating supply?
Heating is a more complex issue. Kyiv's heat supply system has historically been highly centralised: around 70% of the city is heated by three large combined heat and power (CHP) plants.
That is why backup heat sources are one of the key priorities of the Resilience Plan: modernising old boilerhouses, building new ones, installing cogeneration units, and creating connections between different sections of the heating network.
The idea is that if a major CHP plant goes down, individual districts will be able to receive heat from alternative sources. The problem is that Kyiv's huge CHP plants cannot be fully replicated in just a few months.
"Kyiv's CHP plants have a capacity equal to that of several regional capitals. They were built over decades, when the Soviet Union had virtually unlimited resources," a source in the Kyiv city administration told EP.
For that reason, Kyiv will not be able to fully protect its heating supply system from losing heat this year. An EP source close to the government said that between 2,500 and 3,000 apartment blocks may be left without a backup heat supply this winter. Another source believes the number could be even higher. There are 12,000 apartment blocks in Kyiv.
"It's hard to say exactly which apartment blocks might be left without heating, but potentially the areas at risk are parts of the Solomianskyi, Holosiivskyi and Pecherskyi districts, Teremky, Berezniaky, parts of the Dniprovskyi district, part of Troieshchyna, and even the Obolonskyi district," Kharchenko says.
As with the power supply, what happens next will depend on the scale of the attacks.
The optimistic scenario assumes that the main heat sources will be partly operational and any damage would be repaired quickly, in which case Kyiv should get through the winter without widespread heating disruptions. Backup boilerhouses and bypasses should help localise any problems.
But if the Russians launch massive strikes on thermal power stations and large boilerhouses, heating problems are inevitable. "There are three major plants in Kyiv that have already been attacked. You don't need a crystal ball to know that they're going to be attacked again," says an EP source at an energy company. On 30 September, Russian forces launched relentless strikes on one of the capital's CHP plants.
If this happens, the city will switch to emergency mode. Backup boilerhouses, generators, emergency response teams and mobile equipment will be deployed wherever possible. Critical infrastructure will be prioritised above all else.
But some residential buildings will have no backup heat supply. In the worst-case scenario, the city will have to rely on electricity to make up for the shortfall in heating.
"As a last resort, if some areas have no heating, they should be exempt from rolling blackouts, or at least the power cuts there should be shorter than in the rest of the city. And people will rely on electric heaters to keep warm, just as they did last year," the source explains.
"There are no guarantees that Kyiv will have heating," the source in the city administration told EP. "Ballistic strikes mean there can be no guarantees in principle. A lot will depend on how intense the attacks are."
But one thing is different from last winter. According to Kharchenko, Kyiv will be more resilient to attacks even in the most challenging scenario, as backup boilerhouses, generators, hospitals, staff and invincibility centres are now better prepared. [An invincibility centre is a heated premises stocked with food and power banks to assist residents facing hardships due to power cuts – ed.]
Kyiv will not be left without water, but there are some caveats
Water is another critical part of the picture, as Russia could target the capital's water supply in an attempt to trigger a humanitarian disaster.
Kyiv's Resilience Plan focuses on keeping the water utility running even if the power goes out. To achieve this, pumping stations and other key water supply and drainage facilities must be equipped with backup power sources.
According to EP sources, almost half of the planned 40 MW of backup power has now been commissioned. The rest is due to be completed by the end of the year.
The good news is that most of Kyiv's water infrastructure is underground, so it is more resilient to attacks. However, the water supply system cannot be fully protected from the effects of massive strikes.
"Most of the infrastructure is underground," an EP source in the government notes. "Even at water intakes and large water treatment plants, a significant part of the infrastructure is underground. But concentrated ballistic strikes could still cause serious damage."
According to the source, even major damage to the system would not automatically leave the entire city without water. In the worst-case scenario, the problem would be water quality and the supply to some districts.
Another EP source did not rule out the possibility that in certain circumstances, some areas of the city could be without water for a week or longer. Residents are therefore advised to ensure they have stocks of drinking water at home.
* * *
To sum up, Kyiv is heading into this winter objectively better prepared than it was a year ago. The city has more backup generation capacity, better-protected facilities, alternative heat sources, generators, and well-rehearsed plans for dealing with large-scale attacks.
But that doesn't mean the winter will be easy. None of these measures offers a cast-iron guarantee, because the scale of future attacks and the damage they will cause cannot be predicted in advance.
So the main question is not whether there will be problems – there will be. The question is how quickly the city can bring damaged facilities back online and whether its backup capacity and reserves will be enough to prevent local problems from turning into a city-wide crisis.
For Kyiv, as for the country as a whole, the biggest unknown is something that can't be predicted or controlled: the scale and intensity of future Russian attacks.
Mykola Topalov
Translated by Artem Yakymyshyn
Edited by Teresa Pearce

articles.title: Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile Will Integrate onto B-52
articles.body:
The Air Force’s B-52 bomber may soon be able to carry up to 20 stealthy long-range anti-ship missiles to strike moving targets at sea, a key capability in a potential fight with China.
An Oct. 7 notice from Naval Air Systems Command states that the command plans to award a contract to Lockheed Martin to integrate its Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile on the B-52.
The anticipated award “is for efforts associated with LRASM integration on the B-52 aircraft platform, to include missile software updates, associated testing, test asset repair, and failure review boards,” the notice states.
The B-52 can already carry up to 20 Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles, on which the LRASM is based. The two missiles share similar dimensions.
Naval News first reported on the possibility of integrating the LRASM onto the B-52 in 2019, though the idea languished for several years. But the ability to put LRASMs on the B-52 would have massive implications in a large-scale conflict, retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger, a former B-52 pilot, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“A handful of B-52s will be able to deliver more weapons on maritime targets and do so over much longer ranges than the Navy’s carrier-based aircraft per day,” said Gunzinger, now as the director of future concepts and capability assessments for the Mitchell Institute of Aerospace Studies.
Spokespeople for NAVAIR and Air Force Life Cycle Management Center did not immediately responded to a request for comment. Lockheed spokesperson Scott Swofford declined to provide any further details about the effort, deferring to the Pentagon, but did tout LRASM’s capabilities.
“As a precise, stealthy and survivable cruise missile, LRASM provides multiservice, multiplatform, and multimission capabilities for offensive anti-surface warfare,” Swofford said. “By leveraging Lockheed Martin’s expertise in successful cruise missile productions, LRASM brings low-risk and long-term, flexible capabilities to the warfighters’ anti-surface warfare environment that no other inventory weapon provides.”
A Necessary Tool
The Oct. 7 notice continues a push to integrate LRASM onto the bomber fleet—the Air Force revealed in June that a B-2A Spirit employed a LRASM to strike a decommissioned amphibious transport vessel during a Pacific exercise, the first time the U.S. military has acknowledged the B-2’s use of that missile.
Such a pairing is important, Gunzinger said.
“The Air Force’s bomber force will be our military’s predominant maritime strike force, considering the number of anti-ship cruise missiles they can carry per sortie and deliver over intercontinental ranges, if necessary,” Gunzinger said. “And LRASMs will give our bomber force the ability to strike moving targets at sea with unprecedented accuracy.”
The move will expand commanders’ options to strike maritime targets while launching from airbases in lower threat density areas, he said, without putting aircraft carriers at risk.
LRASM Development
- 2009: DARPA and the U.S. Navy initiate the program to develop advanced anti-ship strike capabilities.
- 2012: DARPA cancels the supersonic LRASM-B variant to focus exclusively on the subsonic, stealthy LRASM-A based on the JASSM-ER.
- 2013: Lockheed Martin completes the first successful air-launch flight test of the missile from a USAF B-1B bomber.
- 2015: The Pentagon officially designates the stealthy anti-ship missile as the AGM-158C.
- 2017: Lockheed Martin receives the first low-rate initial production contract
- 2018: The U.S. Air Force achieves Early Operational Capability with the AGM-158C on the B-1B Lancer.
- 2019: The U.S. Navy achieves Early Operational Capability integrating the missile onto F/A-18E/F Super Hornets.
- 2024: The U.S. Navy completes four-missile salvo testing and begins flight testing the round on the F-35C
- 2025: Initial flight testing expands to the F-35B short-takeoff/vertical-landing variant.
- 2026: Lockheed Martin expands factory capacity and contract modifications to boost annual production.
Sources: Lockheed Martin, Air & Space Forces Magazine, USNI
LRASM and JASSM
Lockheed produces both the the AGM-158 JASSM and the AGM-158C LRASM. There is also the AGM-158-JASSM Extended Range variant, which can hit targets out to 500 miles.
Currently, the B-1B Lancer, B-2A Spirit, B-52H Stratofortress, F-15 variants, F-16 variants, and C-130 Hercules can carry the JASSM.
The Air Force is also integrating the JASSM onto the F-35A Lightning II and the B-21 Raider.
The LRASM’s range hovers close to the baseline JASSM variant, just beyond 200 miles.
Air & Space Forces Magazine recently reported on JASSM and LRASM production progress based on Pentagon acquisition reports released in July.
The reports noted that, as of April, the Navy and Air Force were expanding their production plans for the shared munition. Lockheed had delivered a total of 5,348 JASSMs to both services. The company’s current production capacity is 600 JASSMs a year, with short-term plans to boost that to 860 missiles annually.
That’s key, as a recent Center for a New American Security report estimates that the Air Force has ripped through a quarter of its JASSM inventory during Operation Epic Fury.
Lockheed announced a new AGM-158 JASSM-FLEX variant in September at the AFA Air, Space & Cyber conference. The new variant lets users swap out the nose and launch options for various payloads and other configuration needs, which might include an LRASM option.
“The AGM-158 FLEX airframe concept was driven by a strategic need to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats, insert emerging technologies quickly, manage obsolescence, and provide, at scale, a cost-effective missile family that can be repurposed for a wide range of missions while delivering timely, relevant capability to the warfighter,” a Lockheed Martin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine via email.
The Air Force spent $200 million in fiscal 2025 for a second-source engine for the LRASM and JASSM-ER. Lockheed plans to spend between $8 and $9 million through 2030 to boost production on existing lines.

articles.title: Leaked Russian Blueprint Counts 1,000 Weapons to Freeze Ukraine
articles.body:
An alleged Russian document calculates that three Kinzhal missiles could be used against each combined heat and power plant and 20 attack drones against each single boiler facility as part of a wider campaign to deprive Ukrainian cities of electricity, heating and water.
The Ukrainian investigative project Schemes, run by RFE/RL, said on Thursday, Oct. 8, that it obtained a copy of the document from sources in Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The file outlines approximately 60 critical targets and calculates that Russia would need roughly 1,000 weapons to disable them: up to 770 drones and drone-missiles, 170 guided aerial bombs and 75 Kinzhal and Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
The document does not constitute a confirmed order for attacks. Experts consulted by Schemes described it as an analytical estimate that could be used to justify weapons production and establish how many munitions would be required for a future operation.
Russia calculates weapons for each target
The document is titled “Analytical Brief: Analysis of Ukraine’s Energy Generation and Utilities” and is dated August 2026.
Its authors are not identified, its metadata has been altered and some pages are missing. It also does not specify which Russian officials received the presentation before Ukrainian intelligence allegedly intercepted it.
Schemes said the file relies partly on publicly available information from OpenStreetMap, Worldometers and the websites of Ukrenergo, Ukrhydroenergo, Kyivteploenergo, the Energy Ministry and DTEK. Other assessments are attributed only to unnamed Russian military experts or a “working group.”
Poland Ends Russian Drone Probe After Failing to Identify Perpetrator
The document names four priority sectors: electricity generation and distribution, water supplies, sewage systems and heating.
Its list of 60 targets includes hydroelectric and thermal power plants, combined heat and power facilities, electricity substations, cross-border interconnectors, boiler houses, water-treatment facilities and pumping stations.
According to the calculations:
- Equipment connecting each of Ukraine’s three operating nuclear power plants to the grid would require two Iskander missiles to disable.
- Each major hydroelectric power plant could require up to 25 Molniya, Geran or Dan-T/Banderol drones, or three Kinzhal missiles.
- Each combined heat and power facility could require 25 drones or three Kinzhals. The document also considers approximately 25 FAB-500 guided bombs and five Iskander-M missiles for each facility.
- A substation or electricity interconnector could require 15 drones or three Kinzhals.
- A boiler house could require 20 Geran or Dan-T/Banderol weapons.
The authors acknowledge that boiler houses are close to residential areas and state that using other weapons against them could cause civilian casualties.
Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa are principal targets
The document identifies Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa as the main target cities. It also lists Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Kherson, Poltava, Chernihiv, Kryvyi Rih, Cherkasy, Kropyvnytskyi, Lviv, Vinnytsia and Ivano-Frankivsk as priorities.
Kyiv’s energy system receives particular attention. Although the capital has an extensive network, the authors identify five substations forming part of the “Kyiv ring” as potential weak points.
According to the calculation, disabling 12 key substations serving Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa could halt as much as 90 percent of their electricity supply. The document estimates that this would require 40-50 Molniya drones and 130-140 Geran-4 or Dan-T/Banderol weapons.
The same material was previously examined by The New York Times, which reported that Moscow’s apparent objective was to cause a humanitarian emergency by cutting large cities off from electricity, heating and water.
The proposed campaign reportedly begins with attacks on interconnectors through which Ukraine imports electricity from Europe, followed by attacks against 10 major hydroelectric plants and equipment connecting the South Ukraine, Rivne and Khmelnytskyi nuclear power plants to the national grid.
Not a final attack order
Energy Research Center Director Oleksandr Kharchenko cautioned that the document should not be interpreted as a direct combat order.
“This is not a combat directive,” he told Schemes, describing it as a presentation intended to demonstrate the concept to senior Russian officials.
A Ukrainian defense-industry representative who had seen the material before being contacted by journalists offered a similar assessment. The source said the calculations could support requests for manufacturers to produce certain quantities of weapons.
An actual operational plan would be a separate document specifying how weapons would be distributed and when attacks would take place, the source said.
Schemes could not independently establish who prepared the file. The defense-industry representative assessed that it probably originated in the Russian Defense Ministry or one of its subordinate bodies.
Ukraine’s military intelligence, Foreign Intelligence Service and Security Service had not formally authenticated the document by the time the investigation was published.
“Cold terrorist calculation”
Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal presented Russia’s alleged preparations to European partners during a G7+ energy meeting in Paris on Sept. 17.
Shmyhal described the material as a “cold terrorist calculation,” saying it contained tables specifying the weapons considered necessary to destroy individual facilities.
Since the full-scale invasion began, Ukrainian prosecutors have opened investigations into 3,374 Russian attacks affecting 1,177 energy facilities, according to figures provided to Schemes.
At least three facilities attacked during Russia’s large-scale barrage on Sept. 30 – two combined heat and power plants in Kyiv and a thermal power plant in the Kyiv region – also appeared in the document.
On Oct. 7, Russia launched 70 missiles and dozens of attack drones across Ukraine, hitting energy infrastructure and residential buildings. The nationwide death toll later rose to at least 32, including five children.

articles.title: Drone attack forces Yandex to shut down its data center on the grounds of a sanctioned Russian machine-tool plant
articles.body:
A drone attack overnight on 8 October caused a fire that hit part of Yandex's data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, about 580 km from Ukraine, and the site is fully stopped, the Russian tech company told Russian media. The data center sits on the grounds of Sasta, a sanctioned machine-tool plant, Russian outlet Astra said, citing Wikimapia data. Astra's OSINT analyst found from eyewitness footage that the fire hit the plant.
Since late September, Russia has been striking data centers in Kyiv that keep Ukraine's internet and online services running. Now a drone attack has stopped one of the data centers that Russia's largest tech company relies on.
Yandex counts the damage
Yandex warned that some services may be unavailable, while its core services kept running and no one was hurt. Ryazan Oblast Governor Pavel Malkov claimed two drones were downed, a roof caught fire at an enterprise in the Sasovo district, and windows were blown out in several homes.
The power failure took down a wide range of Yandex Cloud infrastructure, including computing capacity, networks, data storage, databases, Kubernetes, cloud services, AI, and security and monitoring systems, Ukrainian outlet ZN.ua reported, citing Exilenova+.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported that the plant was hit, without naming an attacker. The channel said Sasta, which claims a place on Russia's register of defense-industry companies, makes computer-controlled machine tools, including five-axis machining centers, and previously supplied the Tactical Missiles Corporation (KTRV) and Roscosmos. The plant's value to the arms industry lies in machines that cut precision parts, not in finished weapons, the channel said.
Citing Exilenova+, Militarnyi reported that Ukraine's Defense Forces hit the plant. It also linked Sasta to Iskander missile supply chains. No source has said whether the plant or the data center was the target, and no Ukrainian official has claimed the Sasovo strike. Sasta has been under US sanctions since November 2023, UK sanctions since February 2024, and Ukrainian sanctions since April 2025, a sanctions database shows.
Salavat: Kyiv reports a hit
Ukrainian forces hit the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat complex in Bashkortostan, about 1,380 km from the front line, causing a fire, Ukraine's General Staff said. It said the complex processes up to 10 million metric tons of hydrocarbons a year and serves Russia's armed forces. Its key unit, the ELOU-AVT-6 primary oil refining unit launched in 2012, can process 6 million metric tons a year, Militarnyi reported. Astra's analyst placed the fire a few kilometers outside Salavat, possibly near the refinery.
Salavat Mayor Marat Zagidullin claimed that debris from several drones fell in the industrial zone that morning and started a fire.
"The enterprise continues to work," he said.
Astra noted earlier hits on the complex on 24 September 2025, on 14 July 2026, when refining fully stopped, and on 13 August 2026.
Russia's strikes on Ukraine's data centers
Russia has repeatedly hit data centers in Kyiv since 23 September. Strikes hit the COSMONOVA data center twice, the second time knocking it out, and the Parkovyi data center stopped working completely on 1 October after a series of strikes. In early October, Russia destroyed the dline.ua data center in Kyiv.

- Ukraine says its strikes have knocked out more than 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity
- Drones hit Russia’s Volgograd and Samara overnight—fires near a Lukoil refinery, a chemical plant, and likely Europe’s largest oil tank farm in Samara

articles.title: Kremlin-linked Matryoshka bots accuse France’s Macron of militarism and Germany’s Merz of profiting from aid to Ukraine
articles.body:
The Kremlin-linked Matryoshka bot network has launched a new wave of disinformation targeting European leaders, this time focusing on French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The campaign is highlighted by contradicting false claims that Macron is both overly militaristic and dangerously weak, along with false accusations that Merz has personally profited from aid intended for Ukraine. The posts were collected by AntiBot4Navalny, a project that monitors bot activity on social media.
Macron’s “toxic masculinity”
One of the main themes promoted by the Matryoshka network was France’s test of a new ballistic missile, which was indeed launched from a nuclear-powered submarine on Oct. 6 with Macron looking on. In a post on X, the French president wrote:
“Very few nations possess such expertise…To be free, one must be feared. And to be feared, one must be powerful.”
In videos circulated by the bot network, Macron is accused of “toxic masculinity.” The claim is falsely attributed to Kimberly Kagan, president of the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), an organization whose brand, logo, and personnel are frequently used by the Matryoshka network to lend credence to its false claims. Kagan is also made to appear to say that such weapons would be incapable of standing up to Russia.
Another video, falsely presented as coming from French broadcaster RFI, says Macron is bluffing and claims France’s military sector is “catastrophically” behind “the rest of the world,” leaving him with nothing to do but “wave around cardboard missiles that cannot even get out of the water.”
Another video, falsely attributed to the media monitoring company NewsGuard, claims the footage of the missile test itself was generated using artificial intelligence.
Some of the posts also link the missile test to protests by high school students that spread across France over the past week. The bot network claims the students are protesting the country’s militarization; however, the demonstrations were actually driven by problems in the education system, including concerns over teacher shortages, substandard facilities, and the overall quality of instruction.
The videos also claim that some French politicians fled the country because of the protests, withdrawing from the presidential race. Speaking in the name of a supposed French analyst, Matryoshka claims that the demonstrations “showed the true face of French politicians” and that Macron himself is “a worthless person.”
Merz’s ratings and alleged corruption schemes
Matryoshka also targeted neighboring Germany. According to the bot network’s claims, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is at the center of a corruption scandal. Videos falsely presented as coming from outlets including Bellingcat allege that Merz pockets at least 25% of every aid tranche sent to Ukraine.
Earlier this week, Merz announced a new major aid package for Kyiv worth 1 billion euros. In one Matryoshka video, Bellingcat founder Eliot Higgins is falsely depicted as saying Merz would personally receive at least 250 million euros from the tranche, while Ukrainian officials would allegedly divide most of the remainder among themselves. The fake Bellingcat content claims similar schemes operate in other countries and says Macron’s income has “tripled” thanks to a similar arrangement.
Following the real news about the 1 billion-euro aid package, other Matryoshka fake posts focused on an alleged drop in Merz’s approval rating, claiming it had fallen 23%. The bots also claim that the protests in France will soon spread to Germany, citing the country’s large migrant population as the supposed trigger while predicting an escalation in clashes with police within the next six months.
AntiBot4Navalny said such posts may offer clues about issues currently concerning the Kremlin, as bot networks can serve as an indicator of what topics the Kremlin is interested in amplifying.
What is Matryoshka?
Antibot4Navalny’s researchers coined the name Matryoshka to describe a Russian operation that produces and spreads fake stories through a coordinated infrastructure of bots, trolls, and anonymous platforms. Its aim is to create artificial information “noise” and manipulate perceptions of events both inside Russia and abroad. The Antibot4Navalny project named the operation after the eponymous Russian nesting doll — the bots hide behind one another, and disinformation is spread in layers across different platforms, making the source harder to identify.
The mechanism works in two ways. First, it creates large numbers of fake profiles posing as ordinary people, independent media outlets, or think tanks. These accounts generate dozens of posts a day, imitating local styles of speech. Second, identical content is launched simultaneously across multiple social media platforms at the same time. In order to appear convincing, the bots use the logos of well-known Western media outlets and human rights groups.

articles.title: Syria weighs deploying thousands of troops to Yemen – Axios
articles.body:
Syria weighs deploying thousands of troops to Yemen – Axios
Syria could join a Saudi-backed military offensive against the Houthis in Yemen by deploying thousands of troops, Axios has reported, citing US officials.
Yemen’s internationally recognized government forces have launched a major counteroffensive to recapture territory seized by the Iranian-backed Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, including areas around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Saudi-led coalition has backed the operation with extensive airstrikes against Houthi positions.
According to an Axios report, Riyadh and Damascus are discussing the deployment of up to 20,000 Syrian troops. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who previously led the Islamist group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), is reportedly considering the proposal but has yet to make a decision.
The issue came up during al-Sharaa’s meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh on Tuesday, the sources said. Saudi Arabia is seeking to reinforce Yemeni government forces, which US officials described as less well-trained than the Houthis.
Washington does not oppose the proposal in principle and sees it as a way to bolster the offensive without deeper American involvement, according to Axios. US Central Command has also been consulted on how Syrian troops could be deployed.
The Syrian units under consideration reportedly include thousands of Islamist foreign fighters who fought against former President Bashar Assad under the HTS umbrella before his overthrow in December 2024. Their involvement could deepen sectarian divisions, as the fighters include Sunni Islamists, while the Houthis follow Zaydi Shiite Islam.
Reuters separately reported that Damascus was considering military assistance, including defensive support for Saudi Arabia or participation in operations inside Yemen. However, Syrian presidential adviser Ahmad Zaidan denied that Riyadh had requested troops, describing the reports as baseless.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa is in Riyadh for talks with MBS. https://t.co/LWZajNI04M
— Open Source Intel (@Osint613) October 6, 2026
The renewed fighting follows Houthi territorial gains along the Red Sea coast in September, threatening shipping through Bab el-Mandeb, a vital trade route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The waterway has gained particular importance following disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran. The Houthis also claimed to have effectively encircled Taiz, a major city linking northern and southern Yemen with the Red Sea coast, after cutting a vital supply route to the southern port city of Aden.
The Saudi-led coalition said on Monday that 100 fighter jets had participated in the offensive and claimed to have destroyed 324 Houthi targets. The Houthis have retaliated with missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory, including strikes on airports in Riyadh and Abha that killed several people, according to the Saudi authorities.
Riyadh has also secured military support from Türkiye and Pakistan under a collective defense agreement dubbed the ‘Muslim NATO’ that was signed in August.
The Yemen conflict escalated after the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year. Fighting largely subsided following a 2022 truce, before flaring up again this year.

articles.title: Russia, Belarus warned as NATO’s Ukraine-related steps risk nuclear conflict
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Moscow and Minsk are concerned about NATO’s actions concerning the Ukraine conflict, which could lead to a nuclear conflict, the parties to the Treaty on the Establishment of the Union State of Russia and Belarus said in a joint statement published on the Russian Foreign Ministry’s website.
"We express special concern over the activities of NATO and its member states, aimed at creating challenges and threats to the security and interests of Russia and Belarus," the statement reads.
In particular, Moscow and Minsk regard as the most destabilizing NATO countries’ actions triggering serious risks, "primarily ongoing hostile steps regarding the Ukraine crisis, which risk leading to a direct armed conflict between nuclear powers, as well as plans and practical steps to deploy US and other Western medium-and shorter-range ground-launched missiles in Europe."
In addition, Russia and Belarus pointed to "efforts to build missile defense capabilities that define and fuel the European segment of the United States’ global missile defense system, deploy military infrastructure and major combat forces, as well as step up military activities by the alliance’s member states along the borders of the Union State of Russia and Belarus, develop schemes and capacities of the so-called joint NATO nuclear missions based on the US nuclear weapons deployed in Europe."

articles.title: 22 killed in Russian missile strike on Pryluky, including five children
articles.body:
The death toll from Russia's 7 October missile strike on Pryluky, a city in Chernihiv Oblast in northern Ukraine, has risen to 22, including five children, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said on 8 October. Another 54 people were injured, and 15 were rescued from the rubble.
Pryluky suffered the heaviest losses in Russia's 7 October attack, which struck cities across Ukraine. The attack involved about 70 missiles, many of them ballistic, as well as Shahed drones.
Search ends with 15 rescued
Seven of the injured are children, and the rescued include a 5-year-old. The search-and-rescue operation, which involved more than 500 emergency workers, has ended, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles
A five-story building hit early in the morning
Russia attacked Pryluky with cruise missiles and directly hit a five-story apartment building, Chernihiv Oblast head Viacheslav Chaus said. The strike came in the morning, when people were still asleep.
The strike hit the apartment building, a children's and youth creativity center, and a business, according to the National Police.
The death toll rose through 7 October and overnight. On the morning of 7 October, the National Police reported five dead and 26 injured. By the afternoon, the State Emergency Service put the figure at 14, including four children. By the morning of 8 October, it had reached 22, Chaus said. Four of the children died at the scene, and one died in hospital.
Russian strikes in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia
Russia attacked Kyiv and 12 oblasts overnight on 7 October, Zelenskyy said. Two people were killed in each of Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia.
Air defense downed or suppressed five ballistic missiles, 39 cruise missiles, and 117 drones, while missiles and drones hit 18 locations, according to the Air Force.

articles.title: Houthis strike Saudi airports after ‘final warning’ (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Houthis strike Saudi airports after ‘final warning’ (VIDEOS)
Yemen’s Houthi forces have reportedly struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with missiles for the second time in a day, hours after issuing a “final warning” to airlines against operating in Saudi airspace.
The Houthis hit the airport with two cruise missiles on Thursday evening, the group’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree announced in a statement. Houthi forces also hit Abha Airport and King Khalid Air Base with ballistic missiles, Saree added.
“The strikes were precise and direct, resulting in the disruption of air traffic at the two airports and causing damage to them and the air base,” Saree said. The Saudi government has not acknowledged the strikes. The head of the Saudi military coalition against the Houthis in Yemen, Turki al-Maliki, has claimed that two missiles were intercepted before they reached Riyadh, and one was intercepted before it reached King Khalid Air Base.
Earlier on Thursday, Houthi forces hit King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile, which Saree said “struck its target with precision and caused the disruption of airport operations.”
Video footage shared by the Houthis showed a thick plume of smoke rising from the apron of the airport, while footage shared on social media suggested that the missile landed directly on a parked aircraft belonging to the Saudia airline.
After the first strike, Saree issued what he called a “final warning to all global airlines,” warning them to stay out of Saudi airspace, “which has become a theater for our military operations.”
Around 40% of flights in and out of Riyadh were canceled on Thursday. Almost two dozen carriers have canceled or suspended service to the Saudi capital amid the Kingdom’s escalating conflict with the Houthis. Air India and Lufthansa both announced on Thursday that they would not fly into Riyadh until next week.
Saudi Arabia has been waging war against the Houthis since 2015, although the fighting was paused by a ceasefire in 2022. Fighting resumed this July after Saudi-backed forces struck the runway at Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis responded with strikes on Saudi targets, while Saudi jets resumed large-scale airstrikes on Yemen.
The conflict escalated further in September, when the Houthis made their largest territorial gains in years, taking Mocha and key positions along the Red Sea coast and around Bab el-Mandeb.

articles.title: Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko advises residents with friends or family outside the city to consider leaving temporarily amid escalating Russian attacks
articles.body:
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko advises residents with friends or family outside the city to consider leaving temporarily amid escalating Russian attacks
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko has suggested that residents with friends or relatives outside the Ukrainian capital consider leaving the city temporarily, he told AFP in an interview.
“Every day brings new reports of destroyed buildings, of people injured and killed, as the shelling of our city intensifies,” the mayor said. “Today the issue is survival,” he added.
He stressed that he would never call for a full evacuation of the city.
“That’s Putin’s goal… the best scenario for Putin is that we all leave and hand over our empty cities and our country to him,” Klitschko said.
Klitschko also said Kyiv is preparing backup heating systems for winter and stockpiling fuel, food, and drinking water. But he said even proper preparations might not be enough if air defenses cannot repel the attacks.
Russia began stepping up its attacks on Kyiv in September. Daily attacks from September 22 to 28 alone killed 13 Kyiv residents and injured more than 160. In early October, Russian forces also began striking some of Kyiv’s most important transport links — the bridges across the Dnipro River, which had not previously come under attack. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered Russian military commanders to disregard the rules of warfare when carrying out airstrikes on Ukraine.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Zelensky has a message for Washington: Don’t call peace impossible while refusing to put more pressure on Putin
articles.body:
Zelensky has a message for Washington: Don’t call peace impossible while refusing to put more pressure on Putin
Meduza presents statements about the war in Ukraine by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in an October 8 interview with the Greek newspaper Kathimerini, as well as the response from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Marco Rubio
Well, unfortunately, [Russia’s invasion of Ukraine] seems to be going into its fifth year, which was never the original plan. I don’t think that was Putin’s plan for this war, so it hasn’t gone the way he planned it. And I think what it is now, unfortunately, is a strategic stalemate, which is a dangerous thing. Strategic stalemates are only broken in one of two ways: (a) through a negotiated settlement, or (b) through escalation by one side or both that ends up spreading beyond the confines of the original conflict.
Right now, there don’t seem to be prospects of a negotiated settlement. We are prepared to play whatever role we can in making that happen. And we have tried in the past, but so far it’s been elusive. The Russians have defined victory as the totality of Donetsk; they’ve repeatedly stated that as their goal, and they continue to state that as their goal. And that’s a condition that, for Ukraine, is simply unacceptable. And so, a diplomatic solution has eluded us, but we are prepared, if we can play a constructive role, to make it happen.
In the meantime, we watch with great concern as escalation could happen. Just yesterday, some ships were attacked in the Black Sea through a coordinated drone attack. We’re worried about a sabotage operation in a neighboring country that can spiral out of control. And, obviously, I think there are clear indications that Russia will use the upcoming winter as something they want to use to destroy what remains of the electric grid in Ukraine and force them into capitulation.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has grown more effective in its ability to conduct long-range strikes deep into Russia. So, we share the same concern. The whole world is going about this thing like something that could escalate and perhaps become a broader conflict. So, we stand prepared to facilitate and continue to explore any opportunity for a negotiated settlement. We think it would be good for Russia and Ukraine, but so far, it’s proving elusive.
Volodymyr Zelensky
We’ve heard all sorts of things during this war. So many dead ends, difficult situations, and so on. We — ordinary people, leaders, politicians — back ourselves into corners. Even on the first day of the war, we weren’t cornered, because one man tried to back an entire nation into a dead end, and the people rose up and defended their country. We didn’t let the Russians do that. We had high hopes that we would receive support. And that support began to arrive.
But after that, you can’t, you see, on the one hand make deals with the Russians about some future economic projects and, on the other, say that we’re in some kind of political situation, a diplomatic dead end, or whatever. We’re not at a diplomatic dead end. Cut off his economy entirely. Sew Russia’s mouth shut. Stop feeding them with your sales. Just impose sanctions on their weapons.
Make Starlink available to us, to Ukraine. You made it available when you were responding to Iran, and everything worked there. Israel had complete control of the skies. Complete control of the skies over Iran. So when you need it, it works that way.
Right now, we’re talking to various colleagues in Europe and America, and I tell them frankly: China is developing an alternative to Starlink. And they’re getting close. And they’ll give it to Russia. Russia could gain that kind of dominance. We’re talking to Europeans who are also developing several technologies along these lines. They’d be happy to help us, but they’re still not as close to achieving the result we need.
And simply controlling the skies so we can defend ourselves — we’re talking about defense here. The United States has that capability. It does. It would cost them nothing, absolutely nothing, to help Ukraine. And I’ve said frankly: Give us that. Help us defend our airspace and dominate it. Then Putin will come to the negotiating table. Why? Because he’ll lose everything. He’ll lose everything. Three months, two months — he’ll lose everything.
But instead, we’re waiting for the Chinese to develop their equivalent and hand it over to the Russians. So where’s the truth in that? Where’s the honesty? Where is any of it? What dead end? What dead end? This isn’t a dead end. It’s called unwillingness. It’s not a dead end.
