articles.title: Greece agrees up to $4 billion US arms deal, sources say
articles.body:
Greece agrees up to $4 billion US arms deal, sources say
ATHENS, Oct 8 - Greece has agreed to spend up to $4 billion upgrading more of its F-16 fighter jets and buying advanced missiles from the US, two senior sources told Reuters on Thursday, a day after a visit by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Greece had already planned to spend about €28 billion by 2036 to buy US made F-35 fighter jets and helicopters, and to build the "Achilles Shield" a multi-layer anti-ballistic and anti-aircraft system with Israeli-made weapons.
"The agreement includes new advanced missiles and bombs for the F-16 Viper the F-35 fighter jets, and the Black Hawk helicopters. Also the upgrade of old F-16 fighter jets to Viper version," a senior defence Ministry official told Reuters.
The official added that most of the procurements have been included in the government's multi year defence plan and will not put additional pressure to the country's financials.
A senior foreign ministry official confirmed the above, adding that the cost will be spread over several years.
Rubio said on Wednesday in Athens that the two NATO allies had agreed on a joint security plan for counterterrorism information sharing between their law enforcement agencies.
Greece agreed to buy 20 Lockheed Martin F-35 fighter jets and 35 Sikorsky UH-60M Black Hawk helicopters in 2024. Is upgrading about 82 F-16s to Viper version and wants to upgrade 37 more Block 50s to Vipers at a cost of about $1 billion.
The move is part of Greece's bid to modernise its armed forces as it emerges from the 2009-18 debt crisis that led to years of austerity.
Greece spends nearly 3.5% of its gross domestic product on defence, a higher proportion than many other NATO countries, due to its long-standing dispute with Turkey. REUTERS

articles.title: The GRU’s dud drone: How Russian intelligence botched a sabotage plot at Leipzig airport
articles.body:
Following the failed sabotage operation at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August, many media outlets, citing sources in law enforcement, named some of the perpetrators and reported on the likely involvement of Russia’s military intelligence agency (GRU). However, they were unable to provide concrete evidence. The Insider not only managed to find direct proof that the sabotage operation was organized by the GRU, but also identified additional operatives in the Leipzig plot who had previously been linked to sabotage operations in Poland.
A joint investigation with Der Spiegel.
On the evening of Aug. 4, a drone carrying explosives crashed into the wing of a Ukrainian An-124 cargo plane parked at Leipzig/Halle Airport in the German state of Saxony. The device failed to detonate, and the drone fell to the ground, where it was discovered several hours later by a bus driver. At the time, the aircraft was empty, but shortly before the incident, it had transported ammunition from France via Leipzig. One can only speculate as to the level of destruction that might have resulted had the act of sabotage succeeded in causing the explosion of an aircraft loaded with ammunition.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the police investigation and intelligence data pointed to Russian responsibility for the attempted attack. Media reports, citing sources familiar with the investigation, identified the suspects as Oleg L. and Andrei K. both of whom were said to be linked to the GRU. One of the suspects was reported to hold Latvian citizenship, a detail confirmed by Latvian intelligence authorities, but no further details or supporting evidence were presented at the time.
Now, however, The Insider has managed not only to identify the perpetrators but also to prove the GRU’s involvement in organizing the sabotage operation.
How the GRU organized (and failed) the sabotage operation in Leipzig
On a cold morning in January 2026, GRU Colonel Denis Smolyaninov (on the right in the photo below) was walking through Moscow in interesting company — with knife-throwing coach (who also happens to be a deacon of the Orthodox Church) Vladimir Trofimov (left) and arms dealer Andrei Usachev (center). It is unclear what the group discussed that day, but Usachev appears to have had information to share with military intelligence officer Smolyaninov.
Andrei Usachev, 54, began his military career in Russia’s Airborne Forces. In 2000, he was sentenced to nine years for an armed robbery that took place at a currency exchange office, and after his release, he went into the business of manufacturing and trading weapons. Usachev’s company, “Oruzheynaya Palata,” initially thrived after becoming a supplier to the Russian National Guard. However, in 2023, reports revealed that their “Vyzhigatel” system turned out to be nothing more than a cheap Chinese drone — the SkyfendHunter SHH100 — which had been imported into Russia illegally. Usachev left the company, but his expertise in military drones was still in high demand — which is why he drew the attention of Russia’s military intelligence agency.
Usachev’s interest in drones was not merely theoretical. His billing records, obtained and reviewed by The Insider, show that on July 13, 2026, Usachev called Oleg Levushkin, an acquaintance from the city of Pskov. In everyday life, Levushkin was known as a biker and a small-time businessman who ran a small company importing tea, coffee, and spices. However, for the GRU, Levushkin had a more important asset: Latvian citizenship, which meant he could freely enter the EU.
Levushkin did not act alone. His accomplices were the ones who actually carried out the failed sabotage operation — and they turned out to be familiar to The Insider from a separate sabotage operation that took place two years ago.
Belarusian criminals and the arson at Leroy Merlin
According to the investigation, Levushkin’s accomplice was the direct perpetrator of the failed Leipzig sabotage operation: Andrei Karshakov, a citizen of the Republic of Belarus residing in Russia (the same “Andrei K.” whom the investigation referred to publicly). Reporting by German media has indicated that traces of Karshakov’s DNA were found on an antenna that, according to investigators, was used to amplify the drone’s signal while the operator directed it to its target.
This was not Karshakov's first act of sabotage. As it turns out, he had taken part in an arson attack in the Polish city of Łódź two years earlier. On July 25, 2024, a shelf containing plant protection products and insecticides ignited at the Leroy Merlin hypermarket. Firefighters extinguished the blaze within an hour, estimating the damage at 200,000 zlotys (approximately 45,000 euros). The probable cause was cited as a violation of storage regulations. At the time, the Polish media did not pay much attention to the incident.
However, law enforcement took notice of two suspicious individuals who had been in Łódź at the time. The Insider identified them thanks to videos in which they were caught on camera withdrawing money from a local ATM. One of them turned out to be the aforementioned Karshakov, and the other was another Belarusian, Maksim Lapunov (he officially changed his last name but somehow managed to continue using his old passport under the name Maksim Kolosov).
Flight records indicate that Lapunov was involved in the Leipzig sabotage. On July 19, 2026, two weeks before the drone was discovered at the German airport, Lapunov flew from St. Petersburg to Ankara and then to Belgrade, all in the same day. According to sources within the law enforcement agencies of a European country that spoke to The Insider, Lapunov likely made his way from Serbia to Germany.
It cannot be ruled out that there were other participants in the Leipzig sabotage. Border crossing data indicates that Karshakov often traveled with his accomplices, also Belarusians living in Russia: Vyacheslav Aysin, former police officer Denis Shulgan, and Roman Kovalevsky (who has a rap sheet in Russia that includes theft and robbery). The role of Karshakov’s accomplices in the Leipzig sabotage remains unclear, though it is interesting to note that Aysin regularly visited Germany — including the city of Leipzig.
Criminals in service of the GRU
GRU Colonel Smolyaninov was born in 1976 in Chelyabinsk, where he graduated from the Chelyabinsk Higher Military Aviation School for Navigators. He then served in Smolensk before receiving further training at the GRU Academy on Narodnogo Opolcheniya Street in Moscow. He eventually moved to St. Petersburg, where he began working at the GRU’s 172nd Command and Reconnaissance Center, where his work focused primarily on Ukraine.
Smolyaninov was involved in recruiting criminals to carry out missions abroad. As early as 2023, the independent Russian investigative outlet Dossier Center reported on how he had recruited neo-Nazis previously convicted of murder to work as agents in Ukraine.
Among the criminals recruited by Smolyaninov were some true stars of the Russian underworld. For example, former GRU officer Vladimir Borisov, nicknamed “Praporshchik,” had founded the organized crime group Falcon-95 in St. Petersburg in the 1990s and employed several methods he picked up at the intelligence agency, including advanced wiretapping techniques and professional makeup for hitmen that was prepared by specialists from the Lenfilm film studio. Despite numerous murders, kidnappings, and hostile takeovers of multiple businesses, the gang’s leader managed to avoid serious charges in court, receiving only a suspended sentence.
In 2014, Borisov tried to establish his own private military company (PMC). That effort apparently laid the groundwork for his alliance with Smolyaninov, as the GRU was actively helping create PMCs at the time to provide cover for its operations. However, unlike the late Yevgeny Prigozhin (another St. Petersburg ex-con), Borisov did not achieve much success. In 2017, he even found himself wanted in connection with the hostile takeover of the state-owned Institute of Architectural and Construction Design. He went into hiding in Bulgaria before being extradited to Russia in 2021.
Borisov was believed to be serving a prison sentence in Russia. However,The Insider has confirmed that he was released soon after his initial incarceration and issued a new passport, which he has since used for his extensive travels abroad.

articles.title: Russia wants Europe used to not reacting, Helsing warns
articles.body:
Russia is not just testing Europe’s reaction, it is training Europe not to react at all, Helsing’s UK boss told #ApexEurope.
Russian testing of European defences is meant to wear down the continent’s willingness to respond at all, the UK managing director of the military artificial intelligence company Helsing told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Ned Baker was speaking on the European Industrial Leadership Panel, chaired by Lieutenant General (Retired) Stuart Skeates, the chairman of Apex Europe, and he took up an argument made in the session immediately before his.
He said: “They’re not just testing us to see our reaction, they’re actually testing us to get us used to not reacting, and that’s the worst possible thing that we can do, is settle into a kind of slightly European malaise. The time for delivery, the time for action, is now.”
Helsing describes itself as an Anglo-German company, and Mr Baker set out the thinking behind its founding. “We were founded in 2021, based on the belief that Europe needed new technologies, new capabilities to defend itself, but also that amongst those technologies, military AI was going to become the defining characteristic of defence in the future, and I think we have seen that play out to a certain extent in Ukraine,” he said. “I think there is a lot more for NATO to do to adopt those technologies.”
“We’ve been very fortunate to raise a little bit over 2.5 billion pounds in capital over Helsing’s life, and it’s our responsibility, obviously, to deploy that capital wisely to build these technologies,” he said. “But the fact that we’ve managed to raise that capital is also a kind of a once-in-a-generation opportunity. If the threat is a once-in-a-generation risk, then the capital that is available to us now is a once-in-a-generation opportunity, and it is here in Europe, and we should take advantage of it.”
What the company does with it includes strike drones supplied into Ukraine over several years, work he described himself as very proud of, and what he called Europe’s first fully autonomous fighter jet.
Asked how companies operationalise the rapid iteration seen in Ukraine, he began with a form of information older than any of the technology. “The first one is such an important one, but it’s a piece of data that’s existed for centuries, millennia, is just user feedback, just basic user feedback, getting hands-on with operators, and as much as we can blurring the lines between technologists and tacticians, so that we can learn what works, what they need, and getting close to the end-user problems,” he said.
Helsing can do that, he said, because it uses its own money to develop products to a level of maturity where they can go out on exercise with the British Army or the German Army and be tried in front of soldiers, with the results fed back into development. On Ukraine he was blunt about what the shortened cycle means for everybody else. “If you do not have that kind of 24-7 service of tell me what’s working, oh, you found something, let’s go and fix it, then that is not peculiar to Ukraine,” he said. “That is just the new normal, and it will become the new way of functioning for the new style of warfare we will have to fight.”
Collecting real-world data to train models is expensive, slow and hard to do at the volume modern systems need, which is the problem behind the company’s most striking claim of the session. Helsing has built internal tooling, not sold as a product, to generate synthetic training data.
He said: “We pump lots of money and lots of brains into it to build synthetic AI data, so we can basically simulate environments. These environments can be changed at the touch of a parameter. Make it night. Make it day. Make it snowy. Make it rainy. Show me a T-72. Show me this. And you get then a synthetic AI data pack that you can train your models on.”
He went on: “That has been revolutionary for us. That has changed those model training cycles from months and potentially years down to hours, and that’s not just training strike drones. That is how we are going to do reinforcement learning for fully autonomous fighter jets, for fully autonomous unmanned surface vessels.”

articles.title: Zelensky Says Ukraine Is Aware of US-Russia Economic Discussions
articles.body:
Ukraine is aware of the content of various discussions between US and Russian authorities, but has no intentions of making the details public yet, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Zelensky made the remarks while speaking to reporters on Thursday, Oct. 8, in response to a question about which economic agreements Washington and Moscow are discussing.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We know a lot… about various dialogues, but I am simply not ready to talk about them publicly and in detail,” Zelensky said, according to Ukrinform.
Although the President did not specify which discussions he was referring to, his comments came hours after Reuters reported – citing five anonymous sources familiar with the matter, including a White House official – that US and Russia had discussed bringing an American investor into the Nord Stream gas pipelines.
Nord Stream reportedly discussed
According to Reuters, the talks involved senior US special envoy Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and Kirill Dmitriev, a close adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Kushner reportedly sees business deals as key to securing a possible settlement.
Earlier in September, the two envoys visited both Moscow and Kyiv in an effort to broker an end to Russia’s war, which reached a deadlock over irreconcilable differences between Ukraine’s and Russia’s demands, including Moscow’s proposals that Kyiv cedes its sovereignty as part of a peace settlement.
Zelensky Visits Pryluky With UK’s Miliband, Thanks EU for €1.2B Tranche for Drones
Although all three sides – the US, Ukraine and Russia – described the negotiations as productive and positive, the Kremlin consistently rejects proposals for a ceasefire and has increased its strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure since.
Dmitriev, Russia’s envoy who heads the Russian Direct Investment Fund and has long pushed for Russian gas exports to Germany to resume, has emerged as one of Moscow’s main points of contact with the Trump administration.
Late September, he headed to New York to meet with the Trump administration, with the agenda previously agreed upon with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Diplomacy remains stalled
Earlier on Thursday, during a visit to Pryluky, where a Russian missile strike killed 22 people the previous day, Zelensky questioned how Washington and Moscow could discuss future economic projects while efforts to end the war remain stalled.
He also announced that a Ukrainian delegation would travel to the US for talks on Friday and Saturday, Oct. 9-10, and called on Trump to increase pressure on Russia.
Ukrainian authorities have repeatedly argued that Moscow shows no real willingness towards ending the war, pointing to the repeated strikes on Ukrainian cities.
During the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York held late September, 51 countries signed a joint statement urging Russia to accept an immediate, unconditional ceasefire.
However, the Kremlin has rejected and mocked every such proposal so far.
During the same summit in New York, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov reiterated that Moscow would not pause its “special military operation” – a term Russia uses to downplay the war in Ukraine, currently in its fifth year – even during negotiations.
He also claimed that Ukraine would have kept its 1991 borders if the European nations had not “engaged in their shenanigans.”
The comment came just a month after Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day.

articles.title: Meet the Nobel Peace Prize Contenders Who Could Beat Trump This Year
articles.body:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday revisited his argument that he deserves to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize this year, telling reporters in the Oval Office that he has done “far more” than any other U.S. President.
“I don't know what their decision is going to be. They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me,” Trump said, insisting that it would be a “great discredit” to the Norwegian Nobel Committee if they do not announce him as the recipient Friday morning.
“I've stopped maybe the total obliteration of the world, because Iran will never have a nuclear weapon, and that's a positive thing,” he claimed, listing the reasons why he believes he is deserving of the prestigious prize.
Trump said he was “very honored to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more” than him. The 2025 winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, notably gave her medal to Trump in January as she pressed the U.S. to support democracy in Venezuela, days after the U.S. capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores.
Following the regifting of the medal, the Norwegian Nobel Committee emphasized that “the prize itself—the honor and recognition—remains inseparably linked to the person or organization designated as the laureate by the Norwegian Nobel Committee.”
Trump has long said he is deserving of the prize. The leaders of Israel, Cambodia, and Pakistan have all previously said they nominated Trump. However, all nominations remain private and the Norwegian Nobel Institute doesn’t release a shortlist of contenders. Still, each year, names are circulated in public discourse and bets are made as to who might come out on top.
The Norwegian Nobel Institute has registered a total of 287 candidates for this year’s prize, of which 208 are individuals and 79 are organizations.
As Trump’s war with Iran stretches into its eighth month, polls have tipped him as an unlikely contender to walk away with this year’s award. Amid mounting speculation over who may be the chosen recipient, here’s a look at some of the contenders.
Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms
The start of Sudan’s current civil war in April 2023 escalated an already desperate humanitarian crisis. Fighting between the government and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in late 2025 pushed civilians further toward risk of famine, with even more people displaced and killed.
Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms have provided desperately needed relief. The collapse of the state and increasingly difficult access for humanitarian groups over the past three years has led to a rise of 700 ERRs across all of Sudan’s 18 states, mobilizing over 26,000 volunteers, according to Alsanosi Adam, a journalist and ERR volunteer himself.
The community-led initiative provides healthcare, food assistance, education, civilian protection, and psychosocial support. According to Right Livelihood, volunteers have been detained and tortured while offering assistance.
The charity is a lead contender to win the Nobel Peace Prize, with Polymarket citing a 17% chance.
Mark Carney
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in Office last April amid an emerging trade rift with Trump and threats from Washington to annex Canada and make it the 51st state.
The tariff threats escalated and, following the collapse of negotiations in August, the U.S. and Canada are now engaged in a trade war.
Carney has opened up new trading and diplomatic relations with China and Europe in an effort to move away from U.S. reliance. He delivered a defiant speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, denouncing “American hegemony” and insisting there has been a “rupture in the world order.”
Carney’s efforts to unite Canada in the face of Trump’s threats have seemingly helped his popularity at home, with his approval rating back up to 66%, according to new data from Liaison Strategies.
When it comes to the Nobel Peace Prize, he’s more an outsider, with a 1% chance of receiving the honor.
Pope Leo
Pope Leo XIV, the first American pope, has made strident global outreach efforts since his ascension to the head of the Catholic Church in April 2025.
His repeated calls for peace, including his spotlight on Gaza, have made an impact, and even earned him criticism from Trump.
“Today, sadly, war has returned, even to Europe: a new senseless slaughter, claiming countless civilian lives every day,” Leo told European leaders in September, referencing the Russia-Ukraine war. “We must ask whether we are truly making creative efforts to advance world peace, or whether we are simply seeking to stem the tide of war and better prepare ourselves for wars that we assume are still to come.”
In the aftermath of the first U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, Leo said “stability and peace are not achieved through mutual threats, nor through the use of weapons, which sow destruction, suffering, and death, but only through reasonable, sincere, and responsible dialogue.” 
Trump responded by falsely claiming that Leo would “be fine with Iran having a nuclear weapon”—Leo rejected the claim and urged critics to speak “truthfully.”
Pope Leo stands with a 1% chance of being awarded the prize.
Mykola Kuleba
Mykola Kuleba co-founded Save Ukraine in 2014 during the early days of the conflict in Eastern Ukraine. The organization’s work has become increasingly important since Russia’s full-scale invasion of its neighbor in 2022.
Missing Ukrainian children have become a focal point of humanitarian efforts amid the war, with Moscow contending that it relocated children in an effort to protect them. Save Ukraine has so far helped reunite 1,763 children with their parents, but the organization has said thousands more need to be brought home.
“[Kuleba’s] work combines direct humanitarian action with strong advocacy for children’s rights, making him a compelling candidate for international recognition,” said Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO), as he detailed his list of suggested candidates for the 2026 prize.
Kuleba is currently listed as having a 9% chance.
Yulia Navalnaya
Yulia Navalnaya, widow of Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, has become an activist in her own right, challenging President Vladimir Putin’s regime and fighting for democracy.
Alexei died in an Arctic penal colony in February 2024. A few weeks later, Yulia vowed to take up his cause in an interview with TIME, where she expressed hope that Russia might one day be a “normal, democratic country”—the future Alexei “dreamed about.”
Navalnaya is listed as having a 5% chance of winning the Nobel Peace Prize.

articles.title: Polish man suspected of helping Russian plot to assassinate Zelensky sentenced to 5.5 years
articles.body:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland.
The sentence was handed down by the court of appeal in Lublin on Thursday, increasing by two years a jail term issued by a lower court earlier this year. The ruling is now final and binding.
Sąd zaostrzył karę dla Pawła K. Chodzi o współpracę z rosyjskim wywiadem #lublin #szpieg #rosja #wywiad #wyrok https://t.co/Vg2zTx35l4
— Fakt (@Fakt_pl) October 8, 2026
The 51-year-old former Polish soldier, who has been named only as Paweł K. under privacy law, was detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) in April 2024.
Investigators found that the suspect had declared his willingness to collaborate with Russian intelligence and, between December 2022 and March 2024, had established contact via email and instant messaging with Russians involved in military operations against Ukraine, including army officers.
Prosecutors determined that Paweł K. had been assigned tasks including gathering and transmitting information regarding security at Rzeszów airport, which is the main hub for goods and people being transported in and out of Ukraine.
“These activities could have been used by Russian intelligence services, including in the context of planning a possible assassination attempt on the head of a foreign state, that is, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky,” wrote Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office earlier this year.
Poland and Ukraine have revealed further details of a foiled plan to assassinate @ZelenskyyUa at Poland's Rzeszów airport.
A Polish man was last month indicted in relation to the incident, which he is accused of seeking to carry out on behalf of Russia https://t.co/Lrp99vH4s2
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 23, 2025
Last year, the head of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said that Paweł K. had been “recruited decades ago and firmly believed in the Soviet cause”. Polish prosecutors have not commented on that claim.
However, they did find that the suspect had declared his willingness to join Russian “sabotage structures”, including the Wagner mercenary group and Unit 29155 of the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency, which is tasked with carrying out destabilisation activities.
Paweł G. denied the accusations against him and claimed that he had actually been trying to help capture Russian war criminals by deceiving them into trusting him, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).
His defence attorney argued that the information Paweł G. had transmitted regarding Rzeszów airport was “trivial and publicly available”, according to news website Onet.
In January this year, Paweł K. was found guilty of espionage and illegal possession of ammunition by the district court in the city of Zamość, which sentenced him to three and a half years in prison.
However, prosecutors appealed against that ruling, arguing that the suspect deserved a longer jail term of seven and a half years. In a judgement issued on Thursday, the Lublin appeals court agreed that Paweł G’s initial sentence had been “grossly lenient” and increased it by two years, reports PAP.
“Submitting an offer to work for…the intelligence service of a country that is at war with a country directly neighboring Poland, a country that is making quite extensive unfriendly gestures towards Poland, cannot be treated leniently,” said judge Artur Achrymowicz.
Poland has charged three of its own citizens with working on behalf of Russian intelligence.
They are accused of spreading disinformation, conducting reconnaissance of NATO troops, and undergoing firearms training in preparation for acts of sabotage https://t.co/maYd0kb9HW
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 20, 2026
Poland has become a primary target for acts of espionage, sabotage and disinformation conducted by operatives working on behalf of Russia.
In many cases, they are so-called “disposable agents”: individuals already on the ground, often amateurs hired and paid through messaging apps such as Telegram, rather than professional spies or soldiers.
The AWB last year launched 48 investigations related to espionage, more than twice as many as in 2024. Over those two years, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined
A report published earlier this year by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe.
Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism.
Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026
In January, Polish prosecutors indicted five people – four Ukrainian citizens and one Russian – accused of carrying out a plot on behalf of Russia to plant explosives in packages that were then dispatched by courier services across Europe.
In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops.
In July this year, a Russian married couple who had been studying in Poland were jailed for spying on behalf of Moscow and involvement in a plot to send a parcel bomb.

articles.title: Putin just turned 74. Russia’s State Duma isn’t getting any younger either. Here’s how the country’s parliament has aged over the past three decades.
articles.body:
Putin just turned 74. Russia’s State Duma isn’t getting any younger either. Here’s how the country’s parliament has aged over the past three decades.
In late September 2026, after reviewing the results of elections to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, Russia’s Central Election Commission chief Ella Pamfilova said:
The Duma has gotten a little younger. It wasn’t old to begin with, but it’s gotten younger.
To support her claim, Pamfilova cited the lawmakers’ average age at the end of the previous session and the start of the new Duma: 57 and 53, respectively.
That comparison is incorrect, however. The newly elected lawmakers are indeed younger on average than those who served during the spring sitting of the eighth, outgoing session.
Comparing lawmakers’ ages at the start of each session shows the State Duma has been steadily aging, according to Meduza’s calculations. BBC Russia reached the same conclusion.
The State Duma’s first session was elected in December 1993, and lawmakers convened for their first meeting in January 1994, when their average age was 45.8. By the second session, the average age had risen to 47.2.
In the fifth session, which began work in 2007, the average age exceeded 50 for the first time.
Since then, the average age has continued to rise, reaching 54.3 in the ninth session. The difference from the first session is 8.5 years.
How we calculated this
Meduza compared lawmakers’ ages as of the date of each session’s first meeting. Vacant seats were not counted, which is why some previous Dumas had fewer than 450 members. The fourth session, for example, began work with 447 lawmakers after the “against all” option won in three electoral districts, leaving those seats vacant until repeat votes were held several months later.
Meduza calculated lawmakers’ average and median ages using their dates of birth, rounding the results to the nearest tenth of a year. The lists of lawmakers and their dates of birth were compiled from Central Election Commission documents, State Duma records, and other published biographies.
Age is calculated as of the day of each session’s first meeting, and party affiliation is based on faction membership on that same date.
Each successive session is older than the last
Nearly one in three lawmakers in the new Duma has already turned 60. United Russia has the most lawmakers in that group: 109, out of 349 seats the party won overall.
United Russia’s lawmakers age 60 and older alone outnumber all lawmakers from every other party combined: only 101 lawmakers in total were elected to the rest of the Duma, including members of Russia’s Communist Party (KPRF), New People, the LDPR, A Just Russia, and Rodina, along with four independent candidates.
Almost a quarter of the Duma’s lawmakers — 106 of 450 — have already reached retirement age (currently 64 for men and 59 for women); 81 of them were elected from United Russia.
How we calculated retirement age
Russia carried out a pension reform in 2019, so Meduza used the retirement age in effect for each given year when calculating the number of retirees in the Duma. Women born between 1964 and 1968 and men born between 1959 and 1963 follow a transitional retirement schedule. The thresholds are listed on the Social Fund’s website.
Northern work experience and other benefits were not factored in.
Lawmakers’ average age depends directly on the Duma’s oldest members: the older they are, the higher the overall figure. To rule out the possibility that a few outliers are driving the increase, Meduza also calculated the median age.
In the first session, the median age was 45.3: half the lawmakers were younger, half older. In the current session, it is 54.2, a difference of almost nine years.
This means aging has affected every age segment of the Duma, though the trend has not been uniform: in 2011, for example, the median age dipped slightly.
The change is visible even without averages. In 1994, 127 lawmakers under 40 were elected to the Duma’s first session, almost a third of the original lineup that convened for its first meeting. In the new Duma, only 51 lawmakers are under 40, or one in nine.
There are now almost as many lawmakers age 70 and older: 49. Just 10 years ago, at the start of the seventh session, there were only 19, and in the Duma’s first session there were none at all.
The record for age at the start of a session had previously belonged to KPRF member Vladimir Dolgikh, who was 87 when the sixth Duma began work in December 2011. In the ninth session, United Russia’s Vladimir Resin broke that record; he turned 90 in February.
Before being elected to the State Duma, Resin spent many years heading Moscow’s construction sector and served as first deputy mayor of Moscow under Yuri Luzhkov. LDPR leader Leonid Slutsky likely owes his career to Resin: in private conversations, he calls Resin “Dad.”
The Duma’s oldest lawmaker has a special duty: under the Constitution, he is the one who opens the first meeting of a new Duma. In January 1994, LDPR lawmaker Georgy Lukava opened the first session at age 68. This year, 90-year-old Resin ceded the right to open the meeting to his United Russia colleague, 79-year-old Yuri Petrov.
Petrov is actually only fourth by age: older than the United Russia member are his party colleague Valentina Tereshkova, 89, and KPRF member Gennady Zyuganov, 82. During his remarks, Petrov asked each of his older colleagues in turn, “Shall we open the meeting?” All three agreed, after which Petrov thanked them “for the trust placed in him,” the Russian business daily Kommersant wrote.
The youngest lawmaker in the new Duma is Georgy Arapov, the former head of New People’s regional branch in Irkutsk region, who turned 27 in September.
Arapov has set the lower end of the age range for elected lawmakers over the past five years: he was also the youngest lawmaker in the previous Duma, when the New People member was only 22.
The record for this metric, however, belongs to 21-year-old Vasily Vlasov, elected to the seventh session of parliament from the LDPR in 2016. Before his election, he worked as an aide to Vladimir Zhirinovsky and headed his secretariat. In March 2021, when Vlasov was 25, he became first deputy head of the LDPR faction. In November 2023, a year and a half after Zhirinovsky’s death, Vlasov lost his parliamentary mandate over absences from meetings.
More about Vasily Vlasov
In August 2017, Yuri Dud asked Zhirinovsky about Vlasov’s path to the Duma on the party’s ticket: “What did he do to become a lawmaker at 21?” The LDPR leader pointed to the legally permitted age for election, 21, and explained: “He knows better what young people his age want.”
Vlasov’s rise within the party caused discontent among its members. According to the Russian business outlet RBC, Zhirinovsky’s son, State Duma Deputy Speaker Igor Lebedev, opposed the appointment. On the independent Russian broadcaster TV Rain, Zhirinovsky denied any conflict with his son and explained his choice of Vlasov simply: “It benefits us [that] he’s good at his job.”
Vlasov now works at the Russian University of Sport in Moscow, where he oversees youth policy.
More than three-quarters of pension-age lawmakers were elected from United Russia
Almost a quarter of the new Duma’s lawmakers — 106 of 450 — are already old enough to retire. A large share of them belong to United Russia.
The KPRF has 16 pension-age lawmakers out of 37 in the faction, A Just Russia has five out of 17, the LDPR has two out of 24, and Rodina has one. New People has none.
A total of 109 United Russia lawmakers are starting their work at 60 or older, compared with 35 in the other parties combined.
Despite the increase in the retirement age, United Russia now has more pension-age lawmakers in the new Duma than before: 81, up from 75. The other factions now have fewer: 25, down from 36 in the previous session.
Over the past three sessions, the share of seats held by lawmakers age 60 and older has grown from 26.9% to 32%. The number of lawmakers in that age group was 121 in 2016, 126 in 2021, and is 144 now.
The number of pension-age lawmakers in the Duma as a whole has fallen. Ten years ago, almost one in three lawmakers fell into this group. Now, about one in four do. The decline, however, is directly tied to the increase in the retirement age — under the pre-reform rules, more than a third of the Duma would now fall into this group.
This last change is particularly telling. Compared with the start of the previous session, the number of lawmakers age 60 and older across the whole Duma has grown by 18. All of that increase came from United Russia, which gained 23 lawmakers over 60. In the other parties, the number is actually five lower.
In 2016, only 19 lawmakers had already turned 70. By 2021, there were 33, and in the current session there are 49, or one in 10. Of these, 34 are United Russia members, 11 were elected from the KPRF, two from A Just Russia, one from the LDPR, and one ran as an independent candidate.
Despite their age, many remain politically active, supporting Putin and the war in Ukraine.
For example, 82-year-old KPRF leader Gennady Zyuganov and his party colleague, 78-year-old Vladimir Kashin, are involved in organizing supplies for the Russian military. In August 2026, the KPRF announced that the two had helped send another convoy to the combat zone. According to the party, along with food and medicine for soldiers, the communists sent drones, thermal imaging devices, camouflage netting, SUVs, and motorcycles.
A Just Russia leader Sergei Mironov is now 73. In January 2023, he received a sledgehammer bearing the insignia of the Russian mercenary group Wagner as a gift from Yevgeny Prigozhin. Wagner mercenaries used a sledgehammer to kill their own comrade at the front, former convict Yevgeny Nuzhin. Even after Prigozhin’s march on Moscow and his death in a plane crash, Mironov said he would keep the gift “in a place of honor” as “a sign of fellowship.”
However, since late August 2026, Mironov has stopped attending party events in person. He said he is being treated for an injury sustained during a trip to Altai. His fellow party members stood in for him during the pre-election debates. Nevertheless, on September 28, Mironov was unanimously reelected as faction leader. He joined the meeting via video link and said he would continue working remotely for now.
The Kremlin openly uses the standing of other experienced lawmakers for its own purposes. For example, in March 2020, Valentina Tereshkova proposed a constitutional amendment allowing Putin to run for president again. She was 83 at the time and is starting the new Duma at 89.
A source in the State Duma told Meduza that Tereshkova’s remarks had been written in the Kremlin. Kommersant wrote that the amendment had been drafted in advance, with Tereshkova’s name added by hand. A source who spoke to Kommersant, close to Russia’s Presidential Administration, said Tereshkova was close to State Duma speaker Vyacheslav Volodin.
After Tereshkova’s remarks, Volodin called on all factions to defend her from criticism: “The attacks being made on Tereshkova today are attacks on our country.”
Hi, I’m Yulia.
I’m an editor at Meduza, and for almost five years now, I haven’t been sleeping well for one reason: I’m worried about my colleagues in Russia.
I’m often woken up by messages from our freelance reporters inside the country. They sometimes work late at night or early in the morning, and they message me at all hours. I never silence my phone at night in case of an emergency. Every notification jolts me awake. Half-asleep, my first thought is always the same: they’re texting me because the police have come to search their home. In Russia, you can go to prison for working with Meduza. Sometimes I have nightmares about my reporters being interrogated by the FSB. Some of those nightmares have come true.
Meduza’s reporters risk their freedom to tell the world what’s happening inside Russia. They believe their work can help make a better future possible, and they refuse to leave. Please donate so they can keep reporting.
New People remains the youngest party. But it’s aging too
The youngest faction, as in the previous session, is New People. Founded in 2020, this was the party’s second electoral cycle, but it, too, has aged in the meantime: the average age of a faction lawmaker was 39.9 in 2021 and is 42 in the current session.
At the same time, the party’s makeup in parliament has changed. The nine lawmakers elected to the Duma for the first time are noticeably younger than their more experienced colleagues: the newcomers average 39.7, compared with 43.8 for the others.
The oldest faction in the new Duma is the KPRF, whose lawmakers average 61.5 years old. The faction has aged by 11.3 years since the first session, though there have been periods in the KPRF’s history when it got younger — after the 2021 election, for example, the average age of the communists fell, though it remained higher than in 1994, when it was 50.2.
Right now, 37 communists have been elected to the Duma. Eleven of them have already turned 70, and another eight have turned 60.
There is only one communist lawmaker under 40: 38-year-old Alexander Ivachev of the Sverdlovsk region. He heads the region’s party branch and previously served as deputy speaker of the regional legislative assembly. Ivachev is known, among other things, for his statements against the Yeltsin Center and his fight to preserve a bas-relief of Stalin on the Officers’ House building in Yekaterinburg, calling the arguments of those who wanted it removed “the sick fantasies of ‘victims of repression.’”
The LDPR faction has aged by 8.2 years over the past 10 years, the largest increase among the four parties represented in the last three sessions. This trend only emerged in recent years — the LDPR used to be one of the youngest parties. In 2000, lawmakers elected from the Zhirinovsky Bloc began their work with an average age of about 40.
A Just Russia lawmakers have gotten an average of 10 years older over five sessions: the figure was 49 in 2007 and is now 59.1.
United Russia’s average age, 54.1, is lower than that of the KPRF and A Just Russia. Within the party, the share of members age 60 and older rose from 26% at the start of the previous session to 31% in the current one.
Some lawmakers have aged along with the Duma. Three of them have voted on bills for almost 33 years in a row.
More than half the lawmakers in the current Duma — 269 of 450 — also served in the previous session, and 143 took part in all three of the last sessions.
A total of 172 people received a Duma mandate for the first time in 2026. About one in eight of them, 21 lawmakers, have already reached retirement age, roughly the same share as five years ago. The average age of newcomers has not changed since the start of the previous session, either: it is about 48.
Overall, lawmakers entering the Duma for the first time are younger than their experienced colleagues, but the incoming generation that has already made it into parliament is not getting any younger from one election to the next.
Not all newcomers, though, help make the Duma younger. For example, former minister and current adviser to the head of Bashkortostan Gennady Bukayev ran for the State Duma for the first time this year. He had turned 79 by the start of the new Duma’s work.
And some of those who received their first mandate already at retirement age have since spent five or 10 years in parliament. United Russia lawmaker Galina Danchikova came to the Duma in 2016, at 62, and is now starting her third session at 72. Her fellow party member Nikolai Doluda became a lawmaker for the first time in 2021, at 69, and had turned 74 by the start of his second session.
Three lawmakers in the current Duma were part of the starting lineup in all nine sessions, including the very first: KPRF member Gennady Zyuganov, his party colleague Nikolai Kharitonov, and A Just Russia member Anatoly Greshnevikov. In 1994, they were 49, 45, and 37, respectively. Now they are 82, 77, and 70.
The Duma’s age makeup does not closely reflect Russia’s population. The most noticeable gap is the shortage of lawmakers under 40: more than a third of Russia’s adult population is under 40, but in the new Duma, only one in nine seats went to a lawmaker that age. Nationwide, there are three times as many people ages 18 to 40 as there are lawmakers in that age group: 35.1% versus 11.3%.
Lawmakers ages 40 to 64 hold more than two-thirds of the seats, even though they make up less than half of the country’s adult population. The share of people 65 and older is nearly the same in parliament and among the population overall, about one in five.
In the new State Duma, 11% of lawmakers are under 40. In Germany’s Bundestag, after the 2025 election, the figure was 28%, and in France’s National Assembly, after the 2024 election, it was 25%. The U.S. House of Representatives, however, had even fewer young lawmakers than Russia at the start of 2025 — only about 8%.
By the end of the ninth session, the average age of State Duma lawmakers is projected to reach 59.3.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Naval expansion propels India to world’s No. 2 arms importer – Russian think tank
articles.body:
Naval expansion propels India to world’s No. 2 arms importer – Russian think tank
India was the world’s second-largest arms importer in 2025, partly aided by a historically large naval buildout, according to a Russian think tank that tracks weapons purchases and military expenditures.
The South Asian nuclear power has been rapidly building up its armed forces following a brief clash with neighbor Pakistan last year, triggered by a terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir.
India’s identified military imports were worth $6.97 billion, or 5.83% of the global total, and the country is projected to retain the position through 2029, the Moscow-based Center for Analysis of World Arms Trade (CAWAT) said.
Poland came in first with $11.91 billion, while Australia was narrowly behind India at $6.96 billion.
Among the major Indian deliveries cited by CAWAT was the Russian-built frigate Tamal, which joined the Indian Navy in July 2025. Two more Project 11356 frigates are being built at India’s Goa Shipyard with assistance from Russian state arms exporter Rosoboronexport. 
India also commissioned the Vaghsheer, the sixth and final Kalvari-class submarine built by state-owned Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders under license from France’s Naval Group. The six-submarine program was valued at $3.6 billion, according to CAWAT.
The Indian Navy is undergoing its largest expansion in history, with plans to induct or commission 18 warships this year. 
New Delhi imported $25.44 billion worth of arms in the 2022-2025 period, placing it third behind Saudi Arabia and Qatar in CAWAT’s four-year rankings. Its annual imports rose from $3.87 billion in 2024 to $6.97 billion last year. 
The think tank projects India’s arms imports at $45.65 billion over 2026-2029, keeping the country in the second position. Poland is expected to remain at the top with $55.32 billion worth of imports, followed by Germany at $36.48 billion. The forecast is based on existing contracts, officially announced procurement plans, and expected tenders as of December 2025. 
Poland’s rise has been particularly sharp. Its arms imports climbed from $2.17 billion in 2022 to $11.91 billion in 2025, driven by major purchases including US-made Abrams tanks and South Korean K2 tanks.
CAWAT projects global arms imports at almost $633 billion over the 2026-2029 period, up 52.5% from in the preceding four years. The center expects Europe to take a larger share of global demand during the period.
The ranking covers identified commercial arms deliveries and does not include weapons supplied free of charge, including Western military aid to Ukraine.
CAWAT’s methodology differs from that of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), which measures the volume of major weapons transfers using a trend-indicator value rather than their sale price. SIPRI says its figures should not be directly compared with the financial value of arms transfers.

articles.title: NATO attempts to cool tensions with Russia ahead of key nuclear exercise
articles.body:
Crew members of aircraft carrier USS Harry S. Truman are pictured during a NATO vigilance activity in the Mediterranean on May 23, 2022. | Andreas Solaro/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — NATO is seeking to reassure Russia that an upcoming nuclear drill in Italy is nothing to fear, with tensions high between the alliance and Moscow.
NATO announced Thursday that 17 allies will participate in the annual Steadfast Noon exercise from Oct. 13-23. But this year, the exercise follows a tense exchange of letters between Moscow and NATO after allies conducted exercises near Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave in August.
“We have been doing this every year and … this is also a clear message to nations like Russia that there is no need to worry,” said Nassima Barrows, NATO’s nuclear policy director. “This is predictable and there is no reason to miscalculate.”
Advertisement
“Its purpose is really essentially to train our allied forces so that we are ready and prepared, and we ensure the safety and security of our nuclear capability,” she told reporters.
Following the previous NATO exercises, Moscow sent a letter to the alliance threatening to hit allied territory and mentioning the use of its nuclear arsenal — a move that NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte publicly rebuked last week.
Tensions are rising as European countries accuse Russia of sabotage and growing so-called hybrid attacks across the continent.
“Our intention is to really keep things calm,” said a senior NATO official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. Russian officials “keep ratcheting up this mood of tension and we are going to keep trying to calm the mood.”
U.S. Col. David Bull, chief of NATO’s nuclear operations, said the exercise has garnered “similar” participation to previous years and involves everything from a “simulated alert to [a] live flight exercise” — but “no live nuclear weapons.”
It will also feature dual-capable aircraft and ground troops to support the exercise and train on loading, fueling, and maintaining planes, a senior NATO military official added.
Russia’s embassy to Belgium didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Lithuania puts up to 100 soldiers on Kaliningrad border as officials brace for possible Russian mobilization
articles.body:
Lithuania plans to deploy up to 100 soldiers to support border guards along its frontier with Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said on 7 October.
Lithuanian Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas has described the deployment as a preventive measure linked to possible Russian mobilization and a recent incident on the Latvia-Belarus border, where masked, armed escorts tried to push a group of migrants into Latvia. Katelynas said Lithuania could face people trying to avoid mobilization and seeking asylum.
Kaunas said he had granted permission to use Lithuanian soldiers to strengthen border protection for the next several weeks.
“The order starts being implemented immediately,” he wrote on Facebook.
Russia denies a new mobilization
The Kremlin denies a new mobilization is coming. In early September, Russian President Vladimir Putin called reports of one "complete nonsense" and "an information attack on Russia." Ukraine's military and foreign intelligence services say Russia's General Staff has prepared a scenario to mobilize 600,000 people over 2026 and 2027. On 28 September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that "in effect, the Russians have already begun additional mobilization."
Frontier-station patrols for a couple of weeks, possibly longer
On 8 October, the Lithuanian army said soldiers were being brought in to help the State Border Guard Service from that day. A company-sized unit was planned for the assignment, initially for two weeks, with the option to extend. Soldiers will patrol with border guards in frontier-station areas, while mobile patrols, mobile observation posts, and military police crews may be added as needed. The army described the deployment as preventive and a normal form of interagency cooperation.
Kaunas had told LRT TV the soldiers would stay until 16 October. On the morning of 8 October, he said the deployment "was supposed to start" overnight and that he would check with the army. On 8 October, the Lithuanian army said soldiers were being brought in to help the State Border Guard Service from that day. Kaunas also said that “on the Kaliningrad side” there were no physical barriers, unlike the border with Belarus.
Lithuania says its border guards are stretched
On 8 October, Katelynas said the border guard service’s capacity was insufficient, with shifts growing while officer numbers were not increasing. He said the threat level had not changed. In a Facebook post the previous day, he said the situation at Lithuania’s border was calm and there was no reason to panic. He said Russia was planning mobilization after the elections and that Lithuania may face people trying to avoid it and seeking asylum.
Lithuania's State Border Guard Service had turned back 1,693 people trying to cross illegally from Belarus this year and about 26,300 since the migration crisis began, as reported by ELTA on 8 October. Katelynas said 43 migrants tried to enter southern Lithuania last week and were turned back.

articles.title: Counter-Drone Task Force Taps Directed Energy Systems for December Shoot-Off
articles.body:
The Pentagon’s counter-drone task force recently selected four directed energy weapons it will test in a December shoot-off to identify lasers and microwave systems that could defend U.S. military installations from future aerial attacks.
The three laser weapons and one microwave system are the first to be selected for the Joint Interagency Task Force 401’s counter-unmanned aircraft systems directed energy pilot program, according to a Pentagon announcement. The pilot is a congressional requirement in the 2026 National Defense Authorization Act.
“High-energy lasers and high-powered microwave systems are tools that can be effectively used in a layered drone defense,” Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, director of JIATF 401, said in the announcement. “This pilot program will test these capabilities in an operational environment so we can understand how best to integrate and sustain them to defend the homeland.”
The four weapon systems selected to participate in the shoot-off at Dugway Proving Ground, Utah are:
- AeroVironment’s Palletized High-Energy Laser system
- Epirus’ Leonidas High-Powered Microwave system
- Kord Technologies’ Firefly High-Energy Laser system
- Boeing’s Compact Laser Weapon system
In May, JIATF 401 selected Grand Forks Air Force Base, N.D. and Whiteman Air Force Base, Mo.—along with Fort Huachuca, Ariz.; Fort Bliss, Texas; and Naval Base Kitsap, Wash.—to “support rigorous testing and operational assessments across diverse environments” for the pilot effort. U.S. Northern Command and the Federal Aviation Administration are also involved in the pilot, the announcement states.
The announcement of the four systems selected for the shoot-off comes seven months after an incident involving the firing of a military counter-drone laser on the southwest border that prompted the FAA to shut down all flight traffic over El Paso. The Pentagon and the FAA then quickly completed a “data-informed Safety Risk Assessment” of a high-energy laser counter-drone system which found that the counter-drone technology does “not pose undue risk to passenger aircraft.”
Epirus’ Leonidas system is the only high-powered microwave selected for the shoot-off so far. The Army awarded a $43.5 million contract to Epirus in July 2025, which included the delivery of two Integrated Fires Protection Capability High-Power Microwave, or IFPC-HPM Generation II systems, which rely on “weaponized electromagnetic interference” to down drones.
AeroVironment’s Palletized High-Energy Laser system features the firm’s LOCUST X3, a 30-kilowatt system the Army selected in September with a production contract valued at roughly $465 million.
Boeing’s Compact Laser Weapon is available in 2-kilowatt and 5-kilowatt versions. The 5-kilowatt system plugged into the Army’s Forward Area Air Defense Command and Control network to defeat Group 3 drones weighing up to 1,320 pounds during the September 2024 Red Sands Integrated Experimentation Center in Saudi Arabia, according to Boeing.
Kord’s Firefly High-Energy Laser is a palletized, mobile system that features scalable power from 5-kilowatts up to 30-kilowatts. It relies on advanced AI detection and tracking algorithms to “detect, track, intercept and defeat incoming drones at standoff ranges,” according to Kord, a subsidiary of KBR.
JIATF 401 plans to evaluate additional directed energy technologies that could be selected to participate in the shoot-off event, according to the announcement.
“Directed energy gives commanders another option within a layered defense, complementing existing counter-UAS capabilities with a scalable, safe, and effective way to respond to drone threats,” Ross said. “This pilot program will give us vital information in a real-world environment so we can employ these systems to protect the homeland.”
The Air Force is looking to up its counter-drone capabilities to defend bases, a mission it refers to as “point defense.” The service’s primary weapon system for doing so is the Small Unmanned Air Defense Systems, or SUADS. The system is capable of identifying and tracking enemy missiles or drones of multiple sizes, and downing incoming drones with an electronic warfare weapon, but officials have declined to identify what that system is. It can also interface with commercial counter-drone systems and other air defense systems, depending on the needs of a commander.
It’s unclear how much the service has spent or plans to spend on new counter-drone tech. The Air Force requested more than $1.5 billion for SUADS in the fiscal 2027 budget, most of it for missile defense components, according to budget documents. Additional counter-drone systems are being acquired with the assistance of JIATF 401, but those are not listed in the budget request and both Air Force and JIATF 401 officials have declined to provide funding details.
The Air Force Research Laboratory has experimented with high-powered microwave systems to down drones—in 2023, AFRL used the Tactical High-power Operational Responder, or THOR, to disable a drone swarm.

articles.title: France Develops IRIFI Strike Drone With Range Of 2,000 km — Morocco to Be First Customer
articles.body:
French defense company Harmattan AI has unveiled the new long-range IRIFI strike drone, with Morocco set to be its first customer.
Harmattan AI has provided details on the new drone’s specifications.
The IRIFI UAV is designed to deliver high-precision strikes at ranges of up to 2,000 kilometers. The drones will be launched from mobile container-based launchers, allowing for rapid deployment and use in large numbers.
The drone is equipped with an autonomous navigation system that does not rely on GNSS satellite signals, as well as an optical guidance system for the final phase of flight. According to the developer, this ensures resistance to electronic warfare and strike accuracy down to one meter.
Before launch, the operator identifies the target and route, after which the drone autonomously carries out the mission without constant communication with the ground control station.
Harmattan AI positions the IRIFI as a relatively inexpensive means of delivering massive, high-precision strikes. The company has not yet disclosed the warhead’s weight, the drone’s speed, dimensions, or cost.
According to the developers’ plan, a single operator will be able to manage the deployment of dozens of such drones. Artificial intelligence will be used to plan strikes by analyzing satellite imagery. However, the decision to engage targets will remain with a human operator.
The French publication Le Desk reports that on October 7, during the Marrakech Air Show, representatives of the Moroccan Defense Ministry and Harmattan AI signed a letter of intent regarding the procurement, joint development, and production of the IRIFI within the kingdom.
As part of the collaboration, production facilities for the new UAVs are to be established in Morocco. In particular, critical technological components are planned to be developed and manufactured directly in the country with the involvement of local specialists.
At the same time, the signed document is currently a letter of intent, not a final supply contract. The number of drones planned for procurement, the cost of the program, and the timeline for the start of serial production have not been disclosed.
The new program builds on the strategic partnership established in June 2026 between Harmattan AI and the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces. The initial agreements called for the establishment of local production of autonomous defense systems, a research and development center for artificial intelligence, and collaboration with educational institutions.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that in October 2025, Ukraine’s Skyeton and France’s Harmattan AI announced a partnership to integrate artificial intelligence technologies into Raybird drones.
In February 2026, it was also reported that Harmattan AI planned to integrate its compact Sahara synthetic aperture radars into Ukrainian drones. These radars enable reconnaissance even in cloudy and foggy conditions.

articles.title: Ukraine’s FM links Russian plague scare to history of cover-ups, from anthrax to Chornobyl and COVID-19
articles.body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Russia's handling of a suspected pneumonic plague case fit what he described as Moscow's history of concealing information about dangerous incidents, citing the 1979 anthrax outbreak, the Chornobyl disaster, and the COVID-19 pandemic, according to his post on X on 8 October.
A 28-year-old worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, Daria Shipilova, died at Shelekhov District Hospital on 2 October. The hospital was placed under quarantine, and nearly 200 people who had contact with her were put under medical observation.
Sybiha has called on Russia to disclose all the facts surrounding the case, provide transparent epidemiological data, and cooperate with international mechanisms.
"Russia has a long record of concealing the truth: the 1979 anthrax leak in Sverdlovsk, the 1986 Chornobyl disaster, and the true scale of COVID-19 in 2020–2022," he said.
Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is usually found in small mammals and their fleas. Bubonic plague, the most common form, is caused by the bite of an infected flea. Pneumonic plague is the most virulent form: left untreated, it can be fatal within 18 to 24 hours of onset, though common antibiotics can cure it if given early.
But each time, the consequences were devastating.
Sybiha warns of the risks of secrecy
Sybiha added that there is compelling evidence that Russia has used chemical weapons in Ukraine and has threatened to use nuclear weapons in its genocidal war. His remarks came amid rumors that the plague could have originated in a biological laboratory developing weapons.
"The world must not wait for another catastrophe before asking questions," he said.
Russia must disclose all the circumstances surrounding the case, provide transparent epidemiological data, and cooperate with international mechanisms because “when dangerous pathogens are involved, secrecy is a threat to everyone,” Sybiha added.
WHO seeks more information from Russia
The World Health Organization (WHO) says it still lacks the data it needs for a full risk assessment, while Russia has told the organization that no cases of plague have recently been reported in Irkutsk Oblast.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus says that the organization has asked Russia for "further information on the laboratory tests conducted on the individual who died and the contacts," more details on what prompted the public health measures, and the health status of the contacts. The organization also seeks verification of media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause.
Based on "unofficial information," the public health risk to the general population appears to be low, WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier says, according to Forbes.
US officials say they know little about what is happening in Russia
On 6 October, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said information з приводу вирогідної хвороби from Russia was "still quite limited."
The next day at the White House, a reporter asked US President Donald Trump whether the plague in Russia was a bioweapon, according to CNN.
"Well, we don't think so. We're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so," he said.
The reporter also asked whether Trump was “getting the same vibe right now from Russia that you got from China at the start of COVID.”
"Well, China didn't say much, and Russia's not saying much either, but they do say they have it very much under control," Trump answered.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Drones Hunt Down Russian Osa Air Defense System—and Strike It Twice, Video
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Drones Hunt Down Russian Osa Air Defense System—and Strike It Twice, Video
Ukrainian drone operators struck a Russian Osa short-range air defense system twice on the Donbas front, according to footage released by the Signum Battalion of the 59th Assault Brigade of Unmanned Systems on October 8.
The video shows Ukrainian drones engaging the Russian surface-to-air missile system during a broader series of strikes against military equipment and logistics.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Signum operators highlighted the irony themselves, playing on the system’s name—Osa means “Wasp.”
“We ‘stung’ the Osa twice,” the battalion said.
The same footage shows Signum operators targeting Russian logistics across the Donbas, including pickup trucks, UAZ vans, cargo trucks, semitrailers, and other vehicles used to move troops, ammunition, and equipment.
The battalion said its crews routinely work against the routes Russian forces depend on to keep frontline units supplied, with the Osa becoming one of the more valuable targets caught during the latest operation.
The 9K33 Osa is a Soviet-designed mobile short-range air defense system developed beginning in 1960 and introduced into service in 1971. At the time, it was notable for combining its target-acquisition radar, tracking radar, and missiles on a single amphibious vehicle, allowing the system to operate without separate radar vehicles.
Built on the six-wheeled BAZ-5937 chassis, the Osa was designed to accompany ground forces and protect them from low-flying aircraft and other aerial threats. Its radar can detect targets at distances of roughly 30 kilometers, while later variants can engage targets at ranges of around 10 kilometers.
The system underwent several upgrades during its service life, including the Osa-AKM introduced in 1980, which brought improved tracking and enclosed missile canisters.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S2 air defense system using FP-2 strike drones, with footage showing the system burning before its ammunition detonated and tore the vehicle apart.

articles.title: Iran war could force Israel to postpone election, IDF chief tells US officials
articles.body:
IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir has told senior U.S. government and military officials that a renewed military escalation with Iran could force Israel to postpone its general election, currently scheduled for October 27, according to a source familiar with the discussions.
Zamir raised serious concerns about the security and political consequences of another direct confrontation with Tehran, warning that a major outbreak of fighting so close to the vote could make holding the election on schedule impossible. Israel’s security chiefs have already described the weeks leading up to Oct. 27 as a particularly sensitive period and held a joint assessment this week focused on ensuring the election can be held safely.
The warning comes as U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that Washington would not attack Iran “at any time prior to the midterm elections” on November 3. Trump said talks with Tehran were “productive,” while insisting that the pressure campaign and blockade against Iran would remain in force.
Despite Trump’s declaration, the IDF remains on heightened alert. The Israeli Air Force and Military Intelligence Directorate are maintaining readiness for a possible escalation with Iran, which the military continues to regard as its primary strategic theater. Any Israeli involvement in another major confrontation with Tehran would be coordinated with Washington.
The IDF and U.S. military have remained in close coordination since the end of the latest round of fighting with Iran. Israeli military intelligence is meanwhile building an extensive new target bank inside Iran, covering ballistic missiles, launch and production infrastructure and sites connected to Tehran’s nuclear program. The IDF declined to comment on Zamir’s reported remarks.
The warning fits a broader pattern of heightened preparations ahead of the election. Zamir recently canceled a planned trip to the United States, where he had been due to meet the commander of U.S. Central Command and the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, saying the security situation made it inappropriate for him to leave Israel.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also warned during a visit to Tel Nof Air Base last week that there were “signs” Israel’s enemies could attempt an attack ahead of the election. “Don’t mess with us, not now and not ever,” he said. “Our long arm will reach you anywhere and at any time.”

articles.title: Trump envoys, European officials to discuss ‘new ideas’ for Ukraine peace in Miami
articles.body:
Trump envoys, European officials to discuss ‘new ideas’ for Ukraine peace in Miami
US President Donald Trump’s envoys will meet Ukrainian negotiators and European officials in Miami on Friday to discuss new proposals to end Russia’s war in Ukraine, two US sources told AFP. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will present ideas developed during recent talks with both sides, one source said Thursday.
President Donald Trump's envoys will meet Ukrainian and European officials in Miami on Friday to discuss "new ideas" and seek a unified proposal to end the war with Russia, two US sources told AFP.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the talks after a day in which a Russian strike on buses killed 30 people in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, one of the deadliest attacks in weeks.
"The Ukrainian negotiating team is due to meet Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the US tomorrow," Zelensky said Thursday. "The meeting is expected to last two days. We are also counting on a European team to join our negotiating group."
Zelensky said his chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, as well as Ukraine's top officials: Rustem Umerov, Sergiy Kyslytsya and David Arakhamia will take part in the talks in Florida.
Read moreBlack sea and black ops: How exposed is Europe to Ukraine war spillover?
The US-led peace efforts to end the Ukraine war have been largely stalled, with Washington focused on its conflict with Iran despite Kyiv saying Russia has ramped up aerial attacks.
But US officials said they were making a fresh effort in an enlarged format, following visits to Moscow and Kyiv by last month by Witkoff, Trump's business friend-turned-roving envoy, and the president's son-in-law Kushner.
"They will discuss new ideas and proposals that American negotiators began developing with the Russians and Ukrainians during their recent visit to the region," one of the US sources familiar with the talks told AFP.
"The American negotiators also invited national security advisors from the United Kingdom, France, and Germany, as well as officials from NATO and the European Union."
US officials said the envoys would discuss "security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war prosperity plan, and other aspects of the conflict."
Read moreMore than 30 killed in Russian strike on buses in Ukraine's Kramatorsk as Kyiv targets data centre
They added that the Europeans had expressed "frustrations" to Washington about energy costs -- which Trump has blamed on Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel refineries, rather than his Iran war.
"They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop," the US source said.
"So, the United States is trying to mediate with the sides with the goal of creating a unified proposal."
Zelensky said last week that the United States wanted to revive peace efforts by trying to broker a new round of talks with Ukraine and Russia and hold it by the end of October.
The Kremlin said last month that three-way talks on ending the war could take place in October.
Previous rounds of talks have failed to yield tangible progress towards peace, with Moscow unwilling to drop its maximalist conditions to end the fighting.
Trump said earlier this week that he had a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin, although it was expected to focus on the reported death of a researcher at a Russian plague lab.
In a sign that Ukraine was under discussion, Witkoff was seen by AFP reporters traveling with Trump on Air Force One on Wednesday on a campaign trip to Texas for the US midterm elections.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
