articles.title: Polish SIM cards found inside Russian drones in Poland, raising new questions over 2025 incursion
articles.body:
Polish SIM cards were found inside some of the Russian drones that entered Polish airspace during a mass incursion in September 2025, Polish outlet RMF24 reported, citing findings from a Polish prosecution investigation.
SIM cards can allow drones to connect to local cellular networks for functions such as communications, data transmission, telemetry, or navigation-related services. However, investigators have not said what the Polish SIM cards found in the Russian drones were used for. The details remain classified.
The SIM cards were discovered in some of the Russian Gerbera drones recovered after the incursion, RMF24 reported.
Investigators have not disclosed whether the SIM cards were stolen or obtained illegally.
The investigation into the September 9–10, 2025 incursion was ultimately closed after prosecutors failed to identify those responsible for violating Polish airspace.
More than 30 drones entered Poland
The incursion took place overnight on September 9–10, 2025, during a large Russian missile and drone attack on Ukraine. More than 30 Russian Gerbera drones entered Polish airspace from the east and came down at 27 locations across the country, according to RMF24.
Polish forces intercepted and shot down multiple drones, with the Territorial Defense Forces deployed to search for wreckage and other objects that came down on Polish territory. Poland also maintained contact with NATO command throughout the operation.
The incident prompted Poland to close four airports – Warsaw Chopin, Warsaw-Modlin, Rzeszów-Jasionka and Lublin – because of the military activity.
Polish officials described the airspace violations as unprecedented and a serious threat to national security. The incident marked the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine that Polish forces had used weapons against Russian aerial objects that entered the country's airspace.
The mass incursion subsequently became the subject of a criminal investigation into the violation of Polish airspace and the threat to public safety.
Investigation closed without identifying perpetrators
After months of investigation, Polish prosecutors closed the case because they were unable to identify the perpetrators, according to Lublin District Prosecutor’s Office spokesman Marcin Kozak, as cited by RMF24.
Most of the case files, including the justification for the decision, are classified.
Last September, Poland downed four of 19 Russian drones. This September, drone reached NATO’s missile shield in Redzikowo, and troops guarding it called 112
Prosecutors cleared Poland's military response
Investigators also examined whether the Polish military had responded properly to the drone incursion.
According to RMF24, prosecutors concluded that the military acted in accordance with procedures. Polish troops had the right to use force and shoot down hostile objects, and prosecutors found no irregularities in their response.
The investigation was therefore closed both over the failure to identify the perpetrators and over the assessment of the Polish military's actions.

articles.title: EU supportive of extending UNIFIL Lebanon mandate, says Kallas
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
EU supportive of extending UNIFIL Lebanon mandate, says Kallas
Visiting EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told AFP on Thursday that the bloc favoured avoiding a security vacuum and extending a UN peacekeeping mandate in south Lebanon, where Israel invaded while fighting Hezbollah.
The EU's top diplomat also said that the bloc would soon be launching a training mission for the Lebanese army, calling it "a major upgrade in the security relationship" with the Mediterranean country.
Lebanon's cash-strapped, under-resourced military faces enormous challenges, including in completing its deployment to south Lebanon under a US-sponsored framework agreement reached between Israel and Lebanon in June.
"Our member states have been saying that there can't be any security vacuum in southern Lebanon, so everybody is worried about the UNIFIL mandate ending," she said in an interview during a visit to Lebanon where she met senior officials.
"It would be most welcomed if this mandate is extended, so that is the position of the member states," she added.
The United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, which now counts some 7,500 personnel from nearly 50 countries, has been in place since 1978, although its presence has not prevented repeated outbreaks of conflict.
Under US pressure, the UN Security Council voted last year to end UNIFIL's mandate on 31 December 2026.
'Dangerous'
But in March, Lebanese militant group Hezbollah drew the country into the broader Middle East war by attacking Israel, which responded with massive airstrikes and a ground invasion that Lebanon says have killed more than 4,300 people.
Israel now maintains troops in a self-declared "security zone" running around 10 kilometres (six miles) inside Lebanon along the border.
Violence has decreased since a ceasefire following a US-Iran understanding in June, and the US-sponsored Lebanon-Israel framework agreed later that month.
The framework deal involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon's south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in test areas known as "pilot zones", but the process has largely stalled.
Kallas said that under the deal, "there should be somebody who is verifying whether the parties are keeping to their agreements".
"So, as long as you don't have any kind of international force yet ready to do that... it's dangerous when one mission like UNIFIL ends and the other one has not started yet," she said.
Lebanese officials have repeatedly called for the mandate to be extended.
President Joseph Aoun's office said that he told Kallas that Lebanon is "counting on the support of the European Union to find an alternative formula" for after the UNIFIL mandate ends.
France and Italy, major contributors to UNIFIL, have previously said they are willing to set up a multinational coalition to succeed the force.
EU training mission
Kallas also said a planned EU training and advisory mission would soon be established, emphasising that it would not replace the peacekeepers.
On Monday, "we sit down with the EU foreign ministers to give this final push... to launch this mission", she said.
She expressed hope that the civilian-military mission, which will not only focus on south Lebanon, "would be ready already by the end of this year".
"The focus is on supporting the Lebanese Armed Forces, and supporting the Lebanese Internal Security Forces, in order to keep control of the country and security," she said.
"That means training, that means also working on the capabilities," she added.
"Lebanese sovereignty and territorial integrity is very important. So, it has to be the Lebanese government that is providing services and keeping control of the country," she added.
At a joint press conference with Lebanese Foreign Minister Youssef Raggi, Kallas emphasised that "Lebanon must have full control of its whole territory. That also means moving towards disarmament of Hezbollah".
The EU is a major source of assistance to Lebanon with Kallas noting that in September, the bloc announced 505 million euros ($615 million) in financial assistance until 2027, completing a one billion euro package announced in 2024.
Lebanon is also the third-largest beneficiary of its European Peace Facility fund, she added.
(AFP)

articles.title: Russia steps up sabotage campaign against Danish companies supplying Ukraine, intelligence service says
articles.body:
Russia has begun organizing sabotage operations against Danish companies that supply goods to Ukraine, Reuters reports, citing Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET) senior analyst Josephine Christensen.
Speaking Oct. 7 at a domestic security conference in Copenhagen, Christensen said:
"What we saw in the spring was a lot of planning, but very little carried out; what we saw in early summer is that they started to carry out a lot more," the official said.
The shift marks a significant escalation in Moscow’s hybrid warfare campaign, Christensen said, explaining that Russian authorities had concluded that their earlier tactic of targeting a broad range of sites “did not have the effect of deterring the Western (military alliance) NATO from supporting Ukraine.” Moscow is now “trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line…that means weapons production,” she said.
According to PET, Russian operatives recruit people through Telegram and social media, first assigning them simple tasks such as gathering information and taking photographs before progressing to involve them in sabotage. The recruits can be random individuals, including homeless people and people with drug addictions.
“It could be anyone just looking for quick money. If the first person isn't successful, they'll throw another one at the problem until they succeed.”
Politico previously reported that the European Union is discussing possible responses to a hypothetical large-scale hybrid attack by Russia. Those talks intensified after a drone equipped with a detonator was found in early August near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport in Germany. Poland has also reported arson attacks and other acts of sabotage that the authorities suspect may be linked to Russia, as has Slovakia.
PET chief Emil Gresholm had previously said that Russian intelligence services were recruiting Danish citizens to carry out acts of sabotage against local defense companies involved in military aid to Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia Steps Up Sabotage Attacks on Danish Defense Firms, Intelligence Says
articles.body:
Russia has begun sabotage operations against Danish companies supplying military equipment to Ukraine after concluding that broader efforts to disrupt Western support for Kyiv had failed, Josefine Christensen, a lead analyst at Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET), said Wednesday.
Christensen made the remarks at a homeland security conference in Copenhagen, describing the shift as a significant escalation in Moscow’s hybrid warfare campaign.

Denmark’s defense intelligence service said last month that Russia was likely to intensify hybrid attacks against Western countries in the coming months, following Germany’s accusation that Moscow was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.
In September 2025, ahead of Denmark hosting an EU summit, drones disrupted air traffic at six Danish airports, including Copenhagen, the Nordic region’s busiest. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the incident a hybrid attack against Denmark.

articles.title: Meet the German spymaster turned treason suspect
articles.body:
The former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service built a lucrative second career trading on his security expertise. Now prosecutors accuse him of profiting from secrets belonging to the state.
The former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service built a lucrative second career trading on his security expertise. Now prosecutors accuse him of profiting from secrets belonging to the state.
By ANTOANETA ROUSSI
Photo-Illustration by Natália Delgado/POLITICO
August Hanning spent seven years at the top of Germany’s foreign intelligence service, the BND, with access to some of the country’s most closely guarded secrets. Then came a second act: private consulting, corporate intelligence and business stretching across Europe, into Russia and Asia.
Now, the 80-year-old former spymaster is himself at the center of an espionage investigation, after German federal prosecutors arrested him Tuesday on suspicion of treasonous espionage, attempted treason and other espionage offenses. They allege he obtained a stream of secret intelligence from his former chief of staff and used the material to benefit his private consulting business.
“It’s catastrophic for Germany and for Western intelligence services. Everyone is in shock. The scale of it is enormous, especially at a moment like this,” said one EU intelligence official, who — like others in this report — was granted anonymity to discuss a clandestine arena. “And given that investigators stumbled across this while working on an entirely separate case, we’re likely to learn much more.”
Advertisement
For the BND, the case comes at an uncomfortable moment. Just last week, German parliamentarians began debating a new law proposed by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government to grant the agency sweeping new authority, as part of an effort to return Berlin’s foreign intelligence service to the top ranks of global espionage. The timing is equally awkward for European intelligence more broadly. With Russian hybrid attacks continuously targeting Europe, governments across the bloc are rewriting decades-old security laws to give their spy agencies greater powers and be taken more seriously.
Prosecutors say Hanning’s former chief of staff, identified under German privacy rules as Manfred D., supplied him with roughly 2,000 BND documents between 2010 and June 2022. Many contained classified information intended exclusively for internal intelligence work, including material used to brief senior German officials.
In comments to German newspaper WELT, a lawyer representing Hanning said some of the allegations against the ex-spymaster were true but that he did not harm Germany.
“He was in possession of confidential documents. Incorrect, however, is the accusation that he had passed on information contained therein to the detriment of the Federal Republic of Germany — let alone [for] payment. Further investigations will show that,” he said.
In one case, prosecutors suspect Hanning used classified material to prepare an analysis for an employee of foreign intelligence service. They also allege he maintained a relationship with a representative of another foreign intelligence service for several years, passing along political information that was partly based on material obtained from Manfred D.
Prosecutors have not publicly identified either foreign service but German media has named Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan. Azerbaijan has denied any connection.
Advertisement
“In intelligence services, everything is logged — who accesses which documents and when. If an analyst working on right-wing extremism suddenly started looking at intelligence on China, that would raise red flags. But the position of chief of staff has access to virtually everything, so it wouldn’t look suspicious because of the seniority of the position,” said a second EU intelligence official.
Chiefs of staff often stay on when directors change, unless they don’t get along with the incoming boss, the official added.
“Every intelligence service will now be looking at what information it shared with the BND and assessing what damage may have been done,” he said.
Revolving door
Hanning led the BND from 1998 to 2005, before serving as state secretary at Germany’s interior ministry until 2009. Once out of government, he wasted little time entering the private sector.
In July 2010, Hanning and his wife established Hanning Consult. It was in the spring of that same year that Manfred D. agreed to provide him with intelligence from inside the BND in exchange for payment, according to the prosecutor’s statement. Hanning then used that information in his private consulting activities, they added.
Roderich Kiesewetter, a Christian Democrat lawmaker on the Foreign Affairs Committee in the German parliament, said that within Germany there is a “very widespread network” of people who use the contacts and knowledge acquired while they were in service to influence Berlin’s policy on behalf of foreign governments like Russia and China.
Advertisement
“It’s not only sad, it’s damaging the reputation of Germany,” Kiesewetter told POLITICO. “You could also say if you want to talk to Russia, take former members of the government or former members of the secret services.”
Hanning also became involved with Samuel Danilowitsch, a German businessman, who led the Swiss corporate intelligence consultancy, Pluteos. There, Hanning eventually became chairman and the two were listed as attending a 2019 Moscow gathering focused on Europe-Russia relations, attended by Russian political and business figures, where the annexation of Crimea was brought up as a “necessity” rather than a choice. Pluteos did not respond to a request for comment.
From around 2014, Hanning joined British consultancy G3 as a senior adviser, according to archived web pages seen by POLITICO. He later oversaw its work involving Russia and the former Soviet republics, according to German media outlet Correctiv. G3 did not respond to a request for comment.
In 2019, Hanning was invited as a “guest of honor” to a gathering organized by Russia’s Security Council of officials and experts from Arctic Council countries. It was chaired by former secretary of the Security Council of Russia, Nikolai Patrushev, one of the most powerful figures in President Vladimir Putin’s security orbit. As part of the cultural program, the group visited the remote Valaam Island monastery where Hanning was pictured next to Patrushev.
Delegates from Arctic Council countries visited the Valaam Island monastery on Oct. 2, 2019. August Hanning stands on the far right of the front row, next to senior Russian security official Nikolai Patrushev. | Valaam monastery
Hanning has also publicly ventured into some of the more politically explosive questions surrounding Russia’s war on Ukraine.
In 2024, he told WELT TV that he considered it “very likely” that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy knew about the 2022 operation that destroyed the Nord Stream pipelines. Days later, Hanning went further, suggesting an agreement between senior Ukrainian and Polish figures was behind the attack. Germany has since charged a Ukrainian national it identified only as Serhii K., with his trial due to begin in Hamburg in October.
Advertisement
None of those business relationships, contacts or statements establishes a connection to the espionage case now facing Hanning, though they paint a picture of the influence he continued to amass after leaving the German government. Prosecutors have not accused him of spying for Russia.
The steakhouse heiress
Investigators got onto Hanning’s trail starting with an extraordinary custody dispute involving Christina Block, an heiress to a German steakhouse empire.
Block is accused by the Hamburg Public Prosecutor’s Office of orchestrating the abduction of her two youngest children from their father in Denmark. Prosecutors in that case say Block and two men commissioned an Israeli security team to seize her children, then aged 10 and 13, from their father, Stephan Hensel.
According to the indictment, masked men beat Hensel and took the children across the Danish-German border, to southern Germany. The children were reunited with their father in Denmark four days later, under a court order. Block denies knowing about the abduction.
In September 2025, Hamburg investigators searched Hanning’s home and business premises in connection with the Block case, according to local media. Prosecutors suspected Hanning and a retired police officer had accepted a contract worth more than €100,000 to intercept the children on their way to school in November 2022. The plan ultimately failed as their father noticed suspicious figures and alerted Danish police.
German broadcaster Taggeschau reported that the investigators, in the search of Hanning’s premises, discovered around 2,000 digital BND documents that ultimately triggered scrutiny of his handling of sensitive government information. Federal prosecutors took over the resulting investigation in May 2026.
Advertisement
Manfred D. had been Hanning’s chief of staff at the intelligence service and subsequently served several of Hanning’s successors, remaining in a senior position until March this year.
Both men are now in custody.
“He’s reflecting the Germany between 1998 and 2011, so he has not the feeling of having done something evil,” said Kiesewetter. “He was just mirroring [the] state policy of the center-right Christian Democratic and conservative political alliance.”

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russian glide bomb strikes in Kramatorsk kill at least 33
articles.body:
Key developments on Oct. 8:
- At least 33 dead after Russian glide bomb strikes Kramatorsk buses
- Russian drone barrage on Kyiv kills 4, injures 19, disrupts electricity, water supplies
- Polish SIM cards found in Russian drones downed in Poland
- US, Russia confirm Trump's latest Ukraine peace push is falling apart
- Ukraine strikes Russia's Omsk oil refinery in Siberia, General Staff confirms
- UK ramps up sanctions against Russian shadow fleet, crypto industry, big oil
A Russian glide bomb strike on two minibuses in Kramatorsk killed 33 people on the morning of Oct. 8, Ukraine's emergency service (DSNS) said.
Twenty-two more people were injured in the Russian attack, Donetsk regional governor Vadym Filashkin said. Fire broke out in at least two busses following the Russian strikes, according to DSNS.
"Russia comes to the Ukrainian land with death. She hits our cities, kills our people and multiplies her crimes every day," Filashkin said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that doctors were still fighting for the lives of some of the injured people and warned that the number of dead may still increase. Two dead people could not yet be identified due to the severity of their injuries, he added.
"This strike will not go without our response. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this," Zelensky said.
The Kramatorsk and Sloviansk military administrations ordered the stop of all public transport.
"The Russians are targeting civilians. For them, a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one hit can kill as many people as possible," Filashkin said.
Across Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast, four more people had been killed and six injured by Russian attacks as of the morning of Oct. 8, prior to the Kramatorsk strike, according to the governor.
In total, Russian forces shelled settlements in the Donetsk region 31 times over the last day, and 256 people, including 32 children, were evacuated from the front line, according to the Donetsk governor.
read also
Russian drone barrage on Kyiv kills 4, injures 19, disrupts electricity, water supplies
Russian drone strikes on Oct. 8 have killed four people and injured at least 19 in Kyiv, the city's authorities said.
A Russian drone struck a four-story commercial building in Solomyanskyi district, killing two and injuring two, and leading to a fire, while the wreckage of another fell on the Holosiivskyi district, Klitschko said.
Prior to that strike, Klitschko said that Russian attacks on the capital this morning had killed one person and injured 11 others.
A fourth person died of their injuries in hospital, the Kyiv city military administration (KMDA) said in the afternoon.
Klitschko raised the number of injured to 19, 13 of which were hospitalized, in an update on 07:21 p.m. local time.
At 10:00 a.m. local time, Ukraine’s biggest private energy firm DTEK announced emergency energy shutdowns in Brovary, Buchanskyi, Vyshgorod, and Boryspil districts of the oblast.
Shortly after, KMDA announced that the right bank of Kyiv may experience interruptions in water supply, as the power decrease in the electricity grid also meant a decrease in pressure of the water supply network. This applied especially to the Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomyanskyi and Shevchenkivskyi districts.
The drop in voltage from external power supply centers also temporarily halted Kyiv Metro train services and escalator operations, the KMDA said.
DSNS also said that a fire broke out at a logistics facility in the Buchanskyi district in Kyiv Oblast following a Russian drone strike.
In Sviatopetrivske in Buchanskyi district, a school-kindergarten and a nearby playground in a residential complex were damaged in the attack, Kyiv Oblast Governor Tymur Tkachenko said. In another settlement in the district, a woman was injured and hospitalized, he added.
Overnight, Russian drone strikes on Kyiv had already killed four people and injured 21 across four districts, KMDA said.
read also
Polish SIM cards found in Russian drones downed in Poland
Polish military prosecutors found Polish SIM cards in some of the Russian drones downed during a Russian mass drone incursion into the country on the night of Sept. 9 to Sept. 10, 2025, RMF24 reported on Oct. 8.
Polish authorities didn't disclose whether three Polish SIM cards had been stolen or obtained illegaly, according to RMF24. The investigation was discontinued after it did not lead to the identification of the specific people responsible for the Russian incursion.
"The investigation was discontinued because the perpetrator of the crime of violating Polish airspace and thus posing a threat to public safety was not identified," Marcin Kozak, spokesman of the District Prosecutor’s Office in Lublin, said.
On Sept. 9, 2025, more than 30 Gerbera-type drones breached Polish airspace, some of which were shot down by the Polish military, RMF24 reported.
read also
US, Russia confirm Trump's latest Ukraine peace push is falling apart
Ending Russia's war against Ukraine through negotiations is currently unattainable, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Greek media outlet Kathimerini on Oct. 8, casting further doubt on President Donald Trump's latest push to broker peace.
The comments confirm earlier Kyiv Independent reporting that Washington's latest effort to advance negotiations faces growing uncertainty.
At this point, there appears to be no prospect of a negotiated settlement, Rubio said. He added that the goal remains out of reach because Russia insists on gaining full control over Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast without fighting, a demand Kyiv has rejected.
The latest rounds of peace negotiations have also stalled over Moscow's territorial demands.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv surrender the partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine. Moscow is effectively seeking territory that Russian forces have failed to capture militarily.
Ukraine has instead called for a ceasefire along the current front line.
The diplomatic effort now faces another obstacle: Moscow has given little indication that it intends to take part in further talks. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said on Oct. 7 that there were currently no plans for U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine.
"There are currently no plans to hold talks in this format," Ryabkov told reporters.
The latest effort began in early September, when Trump's envoys traveled to Kyiv and Moscow seeking progress before the U.S. midterm elections. The trips produced one tangible outcome: an agreement in principle to hold a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.
A month later, however, even the trilateral meeting remains uncertain.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Oct. 8 that Ukrainian negotiators will meet with Trump's envoys in the U.S. later this week to discuss the prospects for peace talks with Russia.
read also
Ukraine strikes Russia's Omsk oil refinery in Siberia, General Staff confirms
Ukraine's General Staff confirmed that its forces struck Russia's Omsk oil refinery in Russia's Omsk Oblast on Oct. 8.
"The destruction of such facilities is the exercise by Ukraine of its inalienable right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military-economic potential of the Russian Federation," the General Staff said.
Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point had previously reported an attack on the refinery, saying that the refinery was hit with its own long-range FP-1 attack drones.
Videos and images from local residents, shared by Ukrainian monitoring channels, show explosions, fire, and smoke rising from the area surrounding the oil refinery.
Omsk Oblast Governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed that there was a drone attack on the region. Ukrainian authorities have not yet confirm a strike on the refinery.
Omsk is located in southwestern Siberia, north of the Kazakh border. The city of more than 1 million people is some 2,500 kilometers (about 1,550 miles) east of Ukraine controlled territory.
The Omsk oil refinery is owned by Russia's state-owned energy giant Gazprom. It's the country's largest refinery by refining capacity, processing more than 21 million metric tons of crude oil per year.
The plant produces a wide range of fuels, lubricants, and petrochemical products and is involved in supplying the Russian military, Ukraine's General Staff said after Ukraine struck the refinery on July 6. According to the military, the facility has a refining depth of about 99%, one of the highest rates in Russia.
Earlier, an overnight Ukrainian strike on the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery in Russia's Bashkortostan region caused a large blaze at the plant, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed on Oct. 8.
read also
UK ramps up sanctions against Russian shadow fleet, crypto industry, big oil
The U.K. published 38 new sanctions listings on Oct. 8, targeting ships helping Russia evade existing sanctions and a range of companies in Moscow's military-industrial complex, energy, and cryptocurrency sectors.
"The message is simple: if you help Russia fund or equip this war, you will face the consequences," reads a U.K. government press release.
Among the businesses in the new sanctions listings are three cryptocurrency exchanges and two payment platforms.
Xeltox Enterprises, one of those listed entities has "been involved in obtaining a benefit from or supporting the government of Russia by carrying on business in a sector of strategic significance (...) the financial services sector," reads the U.K. government's sanctions listing.
Russia has increasingly sought to use cryptocurrency, which is hard to track, to circumvent global sanctions, and the new U.K. sanctions target the "A7" network, which is at the heart of Moscow's attempts to evade financial sanctions.
That has prompted the U.K., the U.S., the EU, and Ukraine to target crypto schemes in recent sanctions packages.
Also featuring on the listings are two further oil companies: Zarubezhneft and INK Capital.
"The U.K. was the first country in the G7 to sanction the top four Russian oil companies," reads the press statement.
The U.K. has also added 12 ships to its list of sanctioned vessels accused of being part of Russia's shadow fleet — dilapidated vessels suspected of helping Moscow evade price caps and bans on its trade in oil and gas.
That takes the number of ships sanctioned by the U.K. to 645 and the total number of Russia sanctions to 3,537.

articles.title: Trump envoys pitching ‘new ideas’ to settle Ukraine conflict – media
articles.body:
Trump envoys pitching ‘new ideas’ to settle Ukraine conflict – media
US President Donald Trump’s top negotiators are preparing to pitch “new ideas and proposals” aimed at breaking the deadlock in the Ukraine conflict, with talks involving representatives of Kiev and its European backers scheduled to begin in Miami on Friday, according to Reuters and Axios.
Special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner are expected to hold a two-day working session with the Ukrainian delegation in an effort to develop a unified proposal that could later be presented to Moscow.
The pair could then travel to the Russian capital later this month for another round of talks with President Vladimir Putin, Axios reported, citing a source familiar with the discussions.
According to Reuters, the ideas were developed during and after Witkoff and Kushner’s diplomatic tour of Moscow and Kiev in early September. The pair have since remained in contact with both Russian and Ukrainian officials while working on an updated peace initiative.
One proposal reportedly under consideration is a partial ceasefire covering attacks on energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping. The talks are also expected to address possible security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-conflict economic plan and other elements of a potential settlement.
Witkoff and Kushner met Trump on Thursday to present the latest proposals and receive his input ahead of the Miami talks, according to Axios. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Deputy National Security Adviser Mike Needham also attended the meeting.
Kiev's European backers ‘nervous’ about winter
Kiev will reportedly be represented by Vladimir Zelensky’s chief of staff, Kirill Budanov, intelligence chief Rustem Umerov, diplomatic adviser Sergey Kislitsa and top lawmaker David Arakhamia.
National security advisers from Britain, France and Germany, as well as representatives of NATO and the EU, have also reportedly been invited.
A US source told AFP that European governments have privately complained about soaring energy prices and other economic costs stemming from the conflict, adding that there is growing concern about another winter of hostilities.
“They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop,” the source said.
Trump has also repeatedly pressed Zelensky to stop “hurting the world” and halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, arguing that the attacks are worsening a global diesel shortage and driving up fuel costs in the US.
Kremlin agrees with Rubio on ‘stalemate’
The new diplomatic push comes as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the conflict as a “dangerous stalemate,” warning that further escalation could spill beyond Ukraine and trigger a broader confrontation.
“This war needs to end in a negotiated settlement. The sooner, the better,” Rubio told reporters in Lisbon on Thursday, while cautioning that Washington would not invest indefinitely in “pointless processes” that produce no progress.
The Kremlin said it shared Rubio’s assessment of the current diplomatic impasse, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying he “agreed” that no clear prospect of a negotiated settlement was currently visible.
He nevertheless reiterated Moscow’s position that Russia remains open to negotiations, while accusing Kiev of showing no willingness to accept reality and pursue a long-term settlement.
Despite the lack of progress on Ukraine, contacts between Washington and Moscow have continued on other tracks, Peskov added, noting that the two countries are discussing “a whole range” of potentially mutually beneficial economic projects, including possible cooperation in the energy sector.

articles.title: Iran and Oman agree on 'safe routes' in Hormuz
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran announces agreement with Oman over 'safe routes' in Strait of Hormuz
Iran has set out its conditions for ending the war on all fronts and establishing security in the region and the Strait of Hormuz clearly and decisively, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said late Wednesday night, adding that a response to US proposals would be delivered through mediation channels.
Baghaei further said in remarks reported by Iran's ISNA news agency that Iran and Oman had reached an agreement regarding the geographical coordinates for safe navigation routes in the Strait of Hormuz and mechanisms to announce them to relevant international authorities.
US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, on Wednesday evening US time that his envoy Steve Witkoff was currently working to reach an agreement with Iran and was making progress.
"Making a deal is not the option I want, but they are actually ready to give us anything so that we stop, and they certainly will never get nuclear peace," Trump said at an election rally in Texas in support of the state's Republican candidate for the US Senate.
In September, Iran prepared a ceasefire proposal that included reopening the Strait of Hormuz within seven days in exchange for lifting the US naval blockade, ending sanctions on oil exports and resuming nuclear negotiations.
But, Trump rejected the proposal and repeating threatened to return to all-out war.
Baghaei's latest remarks come amid US reports about preparations by the US military to launch widespread strikes on Iran, according to reports in the US media.
US officials had told Axios that the Pentagon had instructed US Central Command several days ago to complete preparations to resume the war on Iran.
The Atlantic newspaper also reported, citing two sources in the US administration, that US President Donald Trump was considering a plan to strike Iran before the midterm elections scheduled for 3 November.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

articles.title: Slovakia sends military attaché back to Russia for first time in 4 years
articles.body:
Slovakia sends military attaché back to Russia for first time in 4 years
Slovakia and Russia are resuming the exchange of military attachés for the first time since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine – a decision that has drawn criticism from the Slovak opposition.
Source: European Pravda with reference to Slovak news outlet Aktuality
Details: During his visit to Moscow in May, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico promised Russian leader Vladimir Putin during their talks that military and diplomatic relations between the two countries would be restored. As part of these arrangements, the countries are resuming the exchange of military attachés after a four-year hiatus.
Fico's government has sent two military officers to Moscow and Bratislava is awaiting the arrival of a Russian attaché.
The last Russian military attaché to serve in Slovakia left the country four years ago. Sergei Solomasov, who held the post, was expelled by the government of Eduard Heger along with other Russian diplomats after Russia invaded Ukraine. Solomasov was also implicated in an espionage case: he bribed Bohuš Garbár, a contributor to the Hlavné správy website, to disseminate disinformation on his instructions.
According to the latest information, Russia's new military attaché in Bratislava could be 46-year-old Maksim Verezhan. The naval officer previously served at the Russian embassy in Rome and has spent the past few years in Moscow.
Slovakia has appointed its military representatives in Moscow. Brigadier General Slavomír Staviarsky will serve as military attaché and Colonel Ivo Gahír will be his deputy.
Tomáš Valášek, an MP from the Progressive Slovakia party, criticised the government's decision to resume military and diplomatic engagement with Russia. He argued that exchanging military attachés would primarily benefit Russia, as the Slovak representative is unlikely to gain access to important information in Moscow.
Valášek also said the Russian military attaché could have an opportunity to take part in disinformation and influence operations in Slovakia, fuel social tensions and sway public opinion towards Russia.
The opposition politician also suggested that the move to restore military relations may have come from Moscow, with the Slovak government simply accepting the proposal.
Background:
- Slovakia's Foreign Ministry, meanwhile, justified the return of military attachés by saying that the government is seeking to establish pragmatic relations with Russia.
- Slovak Defence Minister Robert Kaliňák recently said that Bratislava does not regard Russia as a threat.
- Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has said he does not want Slovakia to become involved in a military conflict "because of some Article 5".
- It was also reported that Slovakia's opposition is demanding explanations from the government and Fico over reports in the German media linking an attempted attack on a Ukrainian drone manufacturer in Prešov to Russian military intelligence.

articles.title: Air defense downs 126 of 142 Russian UAVs – Air Force
articles.body:
Overnight into October 8, Russian occupation forces attacked Ukraine with 142 strike UAVs, including Shahed drones, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reports.
"According to preliminary data, as of 09:30, air defense shot down/suppressed 126 enemy Shahed, Gerbera, and other types of UAVs," the General Staff's Telegram channel statement reads.

articles.title: Ukraine targets Russian industrial hub in Siberia
articles.body:
Ukraine targets Russian industrial hub in Siberia
Ukrainian drones have targeted a major industrial hub in the Siberian city of Omsk, as Kiev carried out another UAV raid inside Russia.
Omsk Region Governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed the attack on Thursday, saying Russian air defenses had intercepted most of the incoming UAVs.
“One drone reached the northern industrial hub. Emergency services are working at the scene,” he wrote on Telegram, without providing details regarding any casualties or damage.
The northern industrial hub is home to several major petrochemical facilities, including the Omsk Oil Refinery, Russia’s largest. The area was previously targeted by Ukrainian drones in July, when several UAVs reached the site.
Operated by Gazprom Neft, the refinery has an annual processing capacity of more than 20 million tons of crude oil and is located approximately 2,500km from the Russian-Ukrainian border.
Kiev has ramped up its long-range UAV attacks on energy facilities and civilian targets inside Russia amid continued setbacks on the battlefield in recent months. On Wednesday, a child was killed and four other civilians were wounded in a strike on Belgorod Region, according to local authorities.
Russian Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik said that Ukrainian attacks took the lives of 29 civilians, including two children, and wounded another 206 between September 28 and October 4.
Moscow has repeatedly described Ukrainian attacks on civilian targets as acts of terrorism. The Russian Defense Ministry has vowed to intensify strikes on Ukraine’s military and military-industrial facilities and related infrastructure in response to Vladimir Zelensky’s threats to expand attacks on oil refineries.
The ministry has since reported large-scale strikes on Ukrainian facilities involved in producing and storing long-range weapons, including sites linked to the domestically developed FP-5 Flamingo missile.

articles.title: Saudi nursery hit by debris as Houthis target Riyadh airport
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi nursery hit by debris as Houthis target Riyadh airport
The Saudi civil defence agency said a kindergarten and a medical complex in Riyadh were damaged by debris from a missile interception on Thursday, as Yemen's Houthis announced attacks targeting the capital's airport.
Two witnesses said that a plane at the airport belonging to national flag carrier Saudia had cracks and holes in its fuselage. A source briefed on the matter said three planes suffered damage.
Saudi Arabia leads a pro-government coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen's civil war. The Iran-backed group has repeatedly targeted Riyadh since the conflict roared back to life in July, vowing to hit critical infrastructure and disrupt Saudi airspace.
The scale and frequency of the attacks on the Saudi capital have been unprecedented in the eight months of wider war in the Middle East.
The Houthis announced three attacks on Thursday against Riyadh airport. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group also launched missiles at an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
Recent attacks have also targeted oil infrastructure in the world's largest crude exporter.
The Houthis on Thursday warned workers to evacuate Saudi Arabia's oil facilities, having days before hit a major refinery south of the capital.
Earlier in the day, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted two missiles fired towards Riyadh.
The kingdom's civil defence agency said "interception debris" had damaged a kindergarten and a medical complex in the city. It did not say if there were casualties or provide details of the damage.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of civilian targets being hit are relatively rare. There have been few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.
Shelter in place
After resuming their fight against Yemen's internationally recognised government following a four-year lull, the Houthis last month seized all of the country's Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive.
The group, whose heartlands are among the Zaidi Shia Muslims in the northwest, had already controlled the capital Sanaa and most of Yemen's major population centres since the start of the war in 2014. Riyadh's military coalition intervened in 2015 to support the government.
Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces have struggled to roll back the Houthis' advance, despite an ambitious counter-offensive aimed at recapturing territory, including the area around a crucial sea route for global energy flows.
In Riyadh, diplomats were instructed to shelter at their respective embassies, some of them told AFP, after explosions echoed around the city on Thursday morning.
There were no text alerts warning residents, as there had been in the past.
An interior ministry campaign has repeatedly warned residents against sharing unauthorised information, images or footage of missiles, drones and their impacts, warning that violators of legal consequences.
Several residents told AFP that international schools were taking precautions, with at least one facility sending children into a basement for safety.
"My daughter called me," one parent told AFP on condition of anonymity, saying she was "completely distraught".
Two people working in Riyadh's business hub, the King Abdullah Financial District, told AFP that some companies were evacuating staff from the area.
'Heightened vigilance'
Numerous flights at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were delayed or cancelled, according to information posted for passengers.
The airport did not immediately acknowledge disruption, pointing only in a short statement to the "necessity" of contacting airlines before travelling.
The United States urged its citizens in Saudi Arabia to "exercise heightened vigilance" following the attacks at the airport, which US government employees now need "special authorisation" to use.
Previous attacks killed a Sudanese national at Riyadh airport, as well as an Egyptian and an Algerian national at Abha airport, civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday.
In Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, civilians are paying the price for the renewed fighting, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.
A humanitarian crisis caused by the war has left most of the nation's population dependent on aid.
After declaring its counter-offensive, Yemen's government claimed to have pushed Houthi fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea coast and the port city of Mocha.
But the Houthis insist they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides have not reported any major changes on the ground.
The rival claims have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
The Houthis recently seized areas south of Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, cutting it off from the government's temporary capital in Aden and sparking shortages and soaring prices for food and energy.
(AFP)

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Yandex data center in Russia, sparking fire
articles.body:
Update. Yandex confirmed that Ukrainian drones struck its data center in Sasovo. The strike sparked a fire that damaged part of the infrastructure. No one was injured, and the data center has been completely shut down; some Yandex services may be unavailable to users.
A fire broke out at the Sasta machine-tool plant in Sasovo, Ryazan region, which houses one of Yandex’s data centers, the independent Telegram channel Astra reported. Journalists reached that conclusion after analyzing photos and videos from eyewitnesses.
Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channels Exilenova+ and Supernova+ claimed the fire started after a Ukrainian strike. Russia’s Defense Ministry listed the Ryazan region among the areas where air defenses shot down Ukrainian drones overnight on October 8. Local authorities have not reported on the aftermath of the attack.
Yandex said “an incident occurred at the Sasovo data center that affected part of the infrastructure.” The company added: “The situation at the site is now under control, and no one was injured. The team is addressing the aftermath of the incident and restoring the affected services.”
After the attack, several Russian websites became unavailable, the independent Russian broadcaster TV Rain reported. They included the auto-posting platform Postmypost and the Ryazan region edition of Komsomolskaya Pravda, a pro-Kremlin Russian tabloid.
Yandex’s data center in Sasovo opened in 2014 on part of the former premises of the Sasta plant, a maker of pipe-threading machines. The plant supplies products to Russian machine-building enterprises and exports some abroad.
In September, the Russian military carried out several strikes on Ukrainian data centers. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed these centers “process and transmit intelligence data for the Ukrainian armed forces” and also threatened Ukraine with a “digital detox.”

articles.title: Armored assaults aren’t dead. Robots got the credit, but it was Ukrainian infantry in armored trucks that reversed a year of Russian gains near Lyman
articles.body:
- Defying the trend toward footborne infantry assaults, the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps deployed armored vehicles for Operation Vivaldi
- The operation was a reminder that vehicles are still useful despite the ever-present danger from drones
- But vehicles need a lot of support to give them a fighting chance
Armored vehicles aren't dead in Ukraine—they just need a lot of help. That's one of the biggest lessons from the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps' Operation Vivaldi, its recent successful counteroffensive just north of the town of Lyman in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast.
18 months building its salient toward Sloviansk; Ukraine took much of it back in three. By 30 September, three of four planned phases in, the operation had returned 176 sq km to Ukrainian control, taken 250 Russian prisoners, and cost Russia more than 5,000 killed and wounded, Ukraine's presidential officeRussi; the figures have not been independently verifieda spent 18 months building its salient toward Sloviansk; Ukraine took much of it back in three. By 30 September, three of four planned phases in, the operation had returned 176 sq km to Ukrainian control, taken 250 Russian prisoners, and cost Russia more than 5,000 killed and wounded, Ukraine's presidential office said. It also foiled a Russian plan to break into the rear of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk urban area, the office said.
Defying critics who insisted vehicles couldn't possibly survive in the drone-patrolled gray zone, the 3rd Army Corps repeatedly deployed mechanized forces as it counterattacked across a roughly 100 sq km salient the Russian 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies had extended toward Sloviansk, one of the last two big free cities in Donetsk Oblast.
Maneuvering for months under a veil of secrecy, the 3rd Army Corps found and exploited gaps along the flanks of the 20th and 25th CAAs, ultimately breaking into the Russian armies' rears and forcing them to pull back across the Zherebets River in order to avoid encirclement.
Armored vehicles were key to the Ukrainian effort. They sped assault troops into battle, dropped them off under fire, and then supported them as they clashed with the Russians. "Maneuver warfare isn't going anywhere," stated Ryan O'Leary, a US Army veteran who once commanded volunteers in Ukraine.
Ukraine is now sending its tanks into battle with drone escorts: they can drive into a Russian kill zone and come back alive
3rd Army Corps commanders knew they were taking a risk deploying armored vehicles in a Russian-controlled salient patrolled by first-person-view drones from Russia's elite Rubicon Center drone unit. But they clearly believed that, with adequate support, the vehicles could accomplish their missions—and survive.
They were right. A dramatic video shot by 3rd Army Corps troopers depicts the troopers disembarking from their armored trucks and rushing into the fight while small arms fire clatters all around them.
Given the intensity of the Russian fire, a mechanized assault "was the only real way to push positions in an effective manner to keep losses low as well as gain and hold momentum and aggression," O'Leary wrote. Walking into battle under the cover of trees might help the infantry avoid the attention of overhead drones, but it takes too long to sustain an aggressive assault, and it can be difficult to mass enough footborne infantry to overcome stiff enemy defenses.
"This is something that hasn't changed even with the advent of drone warfare coming of age," O'Leary added. "Suppression tactics and such have changed and now there is more than just indirect fires and counterassaults that you must be able to suppress and plan for."
But the concept of the infantry-carrying armored vehicle "isn't going anywhere," O'Leary stressed. "Especially when it takes a drone tens of minutes to get to target area, acquire target and hit the target. Right now, the front is extremely susceptible to maneuvering forces on assaults if it is planned right and executed properly."
The 3rd Army Corps' Operation Vivaldi is an excellent example of an operation that was planned right and executed properly—in ways that helped the corps' mechanized forces fight and survive.
Trending Now
Careful preparation
The corps explained that it deployed footborne scouts to find the best paths for follow-on vehicular assaults—and subsequent medical evacuations. Scouts "conducted recon of the front lines, ensured the breakthrough of equipment and led adjacent units along secret paths while evacuating the wounded," the 3rd Army Corps stated.
Before the armored vehicles rolled into action along the pre-scouted paths, the 3rd Army Corps deployed robotic engineering vehicles to clear Russian mines. After that, the corps sent in old BTR-60 wheeled armored vehicles modified for remote control and packed with anti-tank mines. These "robotic kamikaze complexes ... were used to demolish the enemy's strongest fortifications," the corps said.
Only after the assault routes were scouted and cleared of mines and Russian strongpoints did the manned vehicles and their precious infantry cargo roll out. We don't know how many losses the 3rd Army Corps' mechanized infantry suffered on the attack, but we do know they ultimately prevailed—when the battered Russian 20th and 25th CAAs retreated.
In Ukraine’s Vivaldi offensive, nobody rides in the BTR-60s. Bulgaria’s old troop carriers go into Russian bunkers packed with mines
"Recent Ukrainian operations demonstrate that maneuver is not dead," stressed Mick Ryan, a retired Australian army general. "Despite the difficulty in ground operations maneuver observed in eastern Ukraine over the past few years, offensive operations are still possible in modern war. But they need the intellectual effort to develop new techniques to make them viable and repeatable at scale."
In addition to the reconnaissance and robots-first engineering and suppression tactics the 3rd Army Corps employed, Ryan recommended commanders deploy more drone-grounding electronic warfare and use AI tools to help plan attacks.
But ages-old human elements are still essential, Ryan wrote. "Developing viable methods for offensive tactical and operational maneuver in the 21st century also demands the inclusion of older ideas about the employment of mass, logistic support and casualty evacuation [and the] maintenance of morale and leader's provision of purpose to their people."
Even when the assault route is clear, it's understandably terrifying to ride in an armored vehicle across drone-patrolled terrain. But a good leader can motivate their troops to try.

- Ukraine keeps finding ways to replace its MiG-29s. It’s running out of MiG-29s to find

articles.title: How Hezbollah's 'Gaza support front' reshaped Lebanon 3 years on
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Hezbollah and the 'Gaza support front': cost of ongoing Israeli war on Lebanon, three years on
The third anniversary of Hezbollah launching what it describes as "the support front for Gaza" falls on 8 October 2023. Its repercussions continue for Lebanon, amid ongoing Israeli attacks and an expanded occupation over more than 60 villages and towns.
Today, many in Lebanon remain afraid of a third round after the September 2024 and March 2026 Israeli offensives.
On the third anniversary, Hezbollah issued a statement, saying: "The enemy has failed to eliminate Hamas, the resistance factions or the people of Gaza, and has failed to achieve peace, or even a temporary truce and stability. The situation remains open to developments whose repercussions will extend beyond the Gaza Strip to the future of the entire region, the Palestinian cause, and international security and peace."
"Hezbollah in Lebanon, which believes in the justness of the Palestinian cause and does not hesitate to support its resisting and oppressed people, renews its strong condemnation of the blatant Zionist genocide that exposes the false values of the international community and holds the US administration and Western countries that remain silent about condemning Zionist crimes responsible, whether those involving genocide or crimes against humanity," it further said.
"We stand firmly with all these resistance factions so that they remain steadfast and united around their vision and position against the enemy's project, its supporters and those complicit with it. We also warn the region's rulers that remaining silent, accommodating and flattering the enemy and its allies will only lead to the undermining of their authority, weakening them and enabling the enemy to determine the future of their countries and peoples," it added.
Victims of the two support wars
Hezbollah's 'Gaza support front' began on 8 October 2023 and was initially confined to south Lebanon. But the geographical scope, consequences, human losses, and economic cost gradually expanded, particularly after September 2024.
More than 8,900 people have been killed and more than 30,000 injured by Israel since 8 October 2023, while the forced displacement of thousands of families continues, whether because their homes were damaged, their villages were occupied or destroyed, or some were destroyed by more than 90%.
Additionally, financial losses are estimated at more than $27 billion, mostly in the south, as well as damage in the Bekaa and Baalbek-Hermel in eastern Lebanon, Beirut, the southern suburbs of Beirut, and other areas to varying degrees.
The war also brought radical changes.
First for Hezbollah, with the loss of its first- and second-tier leaders, most notably its Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah on 27 September 2024 and his successor Hashem Safieddine on 3 October 2024.
It was also subjected to one of the largest cybersecurity operations, with the explosions of "pagers" and "walkie-talkies" on 17 and 18 September 2024.
The Islamic group found its military capabilities significant declined, while it also lost key supply lines, most notably the Syrian route, after the fall of the Assad regime on 8 December 2024, and its external support, particularly Iranian support, decreased.
Moreover, Israel is targeting Hezbollah's financing networks, foremost among them the Al-Qard Al-Hassan Association.
Hezbollah's political position was also impacted with a decline in its influence in state centres and institutions with the beginning of the new era under President Joseph Aoun on 9 January 2025, which came with broad US support, sovereignty-focused slogans and historic decisions.
The most important of these decisions was the cabinet's approval of a measure to restrict weapons in Lebanon and its tasking of the Lebanese army with drawing up a plan to implement this, in August 2025, with progress recorded in implementation south of the Litani River.
This came before Hezbollah's security and military activities were banned on 2 March, after it supported Iran by launching six missiles from Lebanon at Israel, following the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, along with other decisions that also affected the Iranian side.
The choice of launching "support fronts", for Gaza and Iran, also affected Hezbollah's alliances, particularly through the "disengagement" between it and the Free Patriotic Movement headed by MP Gebran Bassil, as well as its relationship with the Amal Movement headed by Nabih Berri, amid differences and varying views that emerged in approaching the issue.
Hezbollah and Amal have continued to seek through ongoing meetings to maintain coordination and cooperation, amid some tensions in southern areas associated with both sides.
This followed media reports about attempts by Hezbollah to establish positions and launch platforms in some towns politically associated with the Amal Movement.
Another major shift is that Lebanon and Israel began direct negotiations for the first time on 14 April 2026, resulting in the signing of a framework agreement in Washington on 26 June, and subsequently encouraged political and media discourse calling for normalisation and peace with Israel, marking a major breaking of taboos.
This was particularly evident with Lebanese channels conducting interviews with Israelis and showing blatant bias towards Israeli narratives, eventually leading to direct cooperation between a Lebanese platform and an Israeli one.
Addressing the cost of the ongoing war for Lebanon, Nasser Yassin, director of the Beirut branch of the Arab Centre for Research and Policy Studies, told The New Arab that estimates indicate that the cost since 8 October until today has exceeded $27 billion.
These losses are divided between direct losses related to the destruction and damage to homes, residences, buildings and infrastructure, as well as losses related to the agricultural, commercial and economic sectors, among others.
Yassin noted that most losses are concentrated in the south, alongside damage also recorded in the southern suburbs of Beirut and the Bekaa in eastern Lebanon.
He pointed out that the number of homes destroyed or requiring complete demolition in this war had reached about 132,000, more than those recorded during the July and August 2006 war, when the number of destroyed homes reached around 12,000.
He also said there are currently about 65 occupied villages and towns in the south where destruction and land levelling are taking place continuously.
Yassin was environment minister in the government of former Prime Minister Najib Mikati, during which indirect negotiations with Israel led to a ceasefire agreement on 27 November 2024.
However, Israel violated it thousands of times while insisting on remaining at five southern positions.
The expanded offensive then resumed on 2 March, increasing Israeli control over southern villages and sites.
Yassin noted the 27 November 2024 agreement was based on Resolution 1701, which brought an end to the Israeli offensive against Lebanon in summer 2006.
Under the agreement, Lebanon affirmed its commitment to the deployment of the Lebanese army and the state's exercise of sovereignty through its own forces in the south, particularly south of the Litani River, while Israel was to withdraw from positions it occupied at the time.
"Today, the situation is different. There is a security zone, Israeli occupation and control over about 65 villages, and an area that Israel has completely eradicated and destroyed. Therefore, the discussion is now taking place in a different context," he said.
As for whether the negotiations could produce the anticipated solution, Yassin acknowledged it is unclear whether the negotiations currently underway will lead to an outcome.
However, Lebanon has no option other than negotiations to achieve a withdrawal, whether directly, indirectly or through Arab or international mediators.
Yassin said the negotiating performance should be better and should primarily place Israel's withdrawal at the top of any framework, since Israel is occupying another country's land, namely Lebanon, thereby violating international law.
Therefore, he added, the withdrawal should not be linked to measures and issues as happened in the framework agreement, even though these are important.
Domestic repercussions
Regarding the domestic repercussions, particularly for Hezbollah, political writer Khaldoun Al Sharif told The New Arab that "[the support front] led to major Israeli breaches that affected Hezbollah, beginning with the pager and walkie-talkie operations and the assassination of Nasrallah and ending with the occupation of a large area of the south."
Al Sharif noted that "the assassination of Nasrallah, the symbolic leader of Hezbollah, along with the assassination of leaders in the Radwan Force, the party's elite force, and military officials, fundamentally changed the equation. This included the leadership, capabilities, military capacity and material resources."
At the popular level, Al Sharif does not believe the support for the war changed much.
There had been no national, international or governmental support for the party's constituency, which led to its continued attachment to the party.
He also noted that it is impossible to assess changes at this level or among the opposing Shia constituency because the usual measure is parliamentary elections, which were postponed because of the war.
According to Al Sharif, the war inevitably affected domestic alliances because political forces in Lebanon only agree on specific interests, rather than principles or values.
"The Amal Movement remains committed to its alliance with the party because the fall of the duo, in one way or another, would lead to the Shiite community being left alone. Therefore, the issue of Shiite unity remains fundamental for both of them regardless of the repercussions," he said.
Al Sharif also said the decisions taken by the government in August 2025 and March 2026 have not been implemented to date, adding that what matters is implementation.
However, he noted there is no doubt that these decisions were taken after the balance of power changed, particularly following the assassination of Nasrallah.
Al Sharif argued that there is a division between two camps in Lebanon, with only a small percentage of people in the middle: "the Iranian camp," which has been left alone, and the US camp and its allies.
He said that before the situation in the Gulf and Iran becomes clear, it is difficult to determine where Lebanon will go.
"If Iran is crushed, we will face a new equation. If it is not crushed, the equation will be different. Therefore, today we are in a state of 'status quo', particularly since the latest round of negotiations held in Rome last August. Whether we like it or not, Lebanon has become tied to the existing regional equations and the international equations that will impose new balances of power in this region," he remarked.
Hezbollah alliances in decline
Mahend Al Hajj Ali, a researcher at the Malcolm Kerr-Carnegie Middle East Centre, told The New Arab that the war weakened and destabilised the political alliances Hezbollah had built since 2005.
Presently, there is a threat emerging against the alliance it also established with the Amal Movement.
This is one of the repercussions at the political level, in addition to its relationship with Christian, Sunni and Druze forces that had been allied with it but are no longer as they were and have become distributed among a group of regional powers that are not allied with the party.
Al Hajj Ali said that at the social and demographic level, the repercussions have been enormous for the community that supports Hezbollah, namely Lebanese Shias, who, as a result of the war, have been subjected to ethnic cleansing that displaced them from their homeland across a large part of Jabal Amel in southern Lebanon.
Currently, the other part north of the Litani River is also exposed to ethnic cleansing, and in his view it has begun and could continue if a third war breaks out, which is very possible.
Al Hajj Ali also highlighted the changes that have taken place at the regional level, including the change in the situation in Syria and the collapse of the Syrian regime, which had repercussions for Lebanon and Hezbollah.
He also pointed to the establishment of a new era and a new government in Lebanon, following a line opposed to that of Hezbollah and based on the principle that weapons come first.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

articles.title: BBC: Eritrea Secretly Deploys Troops to Ethiopia’s Tigray Region
articles.body:
Eritrean troops have crossed the Ethiopian border and advanced deeper into the Tigray region, where fighting is ongoing between government forces and rebel groups.
The British broadcaster BBC reported this on October 7, citing local residents.
According to eyewitnesses, Eritrean troops were moving from the border town of Zalambessa through Adigrat toward Edaga Hamus, located between Adigrat and Tigray’s administrative capital, Mekelle.
One resident of Adigrat said he saw a convoy of approximately 40 trucks carrying soldiers traveling south. Another eyewitness reported seeing 20–30 large trucks with Eritrean license plates heading toward Edaga Hamus.
According to other accounts, the convoys also included vehicles equipped with heavy weapons, including anti-aircraft guns. Some Eritrean troops were traveling on foot. One BBC source estimated that the convoy seen by his relatives consisted of around 60 trucks.
Local residents also report the deployment of Eritrean units in mountainous areas near Edaga Hamus. According to them, drone strikes targeting military positions have taken place near the town.
Meanwhile, the BBC emphasizes that it has been unable to independently verify reports of Eritrean troop movements. Journalists were also unable to verify the authenticity of videos of military convoys circulating on social media.
A new phase of fighting in Tigray began on September 23 following several months of growing tensions between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).
On October 4, government forces and allied formations regained control of Mekelle after TPLF units withdrew. The rebels said they were temporarily relocating their regional administration.
The day before, on October 1, Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with Ethiopia following the closure of the Ethiopian embassy in Asmara and the expulsion of Eritrean diplomats. Addis Ababa accuses its neighbor of supporting the rebels, although Eritrean authorities have previously denied the allegations.
Ethiopian government representative Abraham Belay accused Eritrea of directly participating in the fighting in an interview with Fana Television. According to him, the Eritrean army suffered casualties and captured personnel, and Ethiopia is preparing a response to its intervention.
From 2020 to 2022, Eritrea, by contrast, fought alongside the Ethiopian federal government against the Tigray People’s Liberation Front. The two-year conflict claimed hundreds of thousands of lives and ended with the signing of the Pretoria Peace Agreement in November 2022.
Since then, relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have deteriorated sharply. One of the main reasons has been the Ethiopian leadership’s demand for access to the Red Sea, particularly through Eritrea’s Port of Assab. Eritrea views such statements as a threat to its sovereignty.
Militarnyi previously reported that on September 21, seven Ethiopian armed groups announced the formation of a unified alliance against the government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. The alliance includes the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, the Oromo Liberation Army, and the Fano militia operating in the Amhara region. The alliance said its goal was to overthrow the current government and establish a transitional administration.
Militarnyi also reported that in August 2026, Tigray People’s Liberation Front rebels used NWF10 FPV drones, manufactured by the Turkish company North Weapon, against the Ethiopian army.

articles.title: NATO is trying to reduce tensions with Russia ahead of large-scale nuclear exercises in Europe
articles.body:
NATO is trying to reduce tensions with Russia ahead of large-scale nuclear exercises in Europe
Kyiv • UNN
The Steadfast Noon exercises will take place from October 13 to 23 with the participation of 17 NATO countries. The Alliance assures that operational nuclear weapons will not be used.
NATO is preparing for its annual Steadfast Noon nuclear exercises, which will take place in Italy from October 13 to 23 with the participation of 17 Alliance countries. At the same time, Brussels is trying to reduce tensions in relations with moscow and assuring that the maneuvers do not pose a threat to russia, Politico reports, writes UNN.
Details
NATO Director of Nuclear Policy Nassima Barrow emphasized that the exercises are held every year, and their main goal is to test the readiness of allied forces and the security of the Alliance's nuclear capabilities.
We do this every year, and it is also a clear signal to countries such as russia that there is no need to worry. It is predictable, and there is no reason for misinterpretation
NATO spoke about moscow's nuclear threats
Tensions between the Alliance and russia intensified following NATO exercises near the Kaliningrad Region in August. According to Politico, moscow sent the Alliance a letter threatening strikes against allied territory, including with the use of nuclear weapons. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte publicly condemned the threats.
The US is sending Marines to the Baltic Sea to support a NATO mission02.10.26, 07:31 • 8762 views
A senior NATO official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that the Alliance seeks to maintain calm despite the actions of the Russian side, which continues to increase tensions.
During Steadfast Noon, the military will practice various scenarios – from simulating a combat alert to aircraft flights. Dual-capable aircraft and ground personnel will take part in the maneuvers, training to service, refuel, and prepare aircraft to carry out missions.
NATO separately emphasized that live nuclear weapons will not be used during the exercises.

articles.title: Budanov Heads to US With Ukrainian Negotiating Team for ‘Important Meetings,’ European Leaders Set to Join
articles.body:
Head of the Presidential Office Kyrylo Budanov announced that he is on his way to the US with Ukraine’s negotiating team, where several important meetings are planned.
“We cannot discuss everything, but we must remain wise and united and support our own military,” Budanov said in a statement on Thursday, Oct. 8. “Peace is not achieved through loud statements – it requires hard work together,” he continued.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
European team to join the talks
Earlier on Thursday, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that Ukraine’s negotiating team is scheduled to meet with senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Oct. 9-10.
According to Ukrainska Pravda, alongside Budanov, National Security and Defense Council Secretary Rustem Umerov, Servant of the People faction leader Davyd Arakhamia and First Deputy Foreign Minister Serhii Kyslytsia will also be present.
“Two days of meetings are expected, and we are counting on a European team joining both our negotiating group and the American negotiating group,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky announced separately on Thursday that he discussed the upcoming talks with European Council President António Costa.
A trilateral format with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had also been discussed and agreed upon, Zelensky said, without providing a specific date.
The two leaders also went over the timeline for opening new clusters in Ukraine’s EU accession talks, a winter energy package and additional financial aid, ahead of the European Council summit in Brussels on Oct. 15-16.
Zelensky Visits Pryluky With UK’s Miliband, Thanks EU for €1.2B Tranche for Drones
Diplomatic momentum began early September
The diplomatic visit comes as Kyiv works on maintaining the diplomatic momentum that began in early September, when Witkoff and Kushner traveled to Moscow, where they met Russian President Vladimir Putin and senior Russian officials. A day later, on Sept. 6, the two envoys visited Kyiv for the first time since taking office.
While all three sides described the talks as substantive, Russia has continued to launch large-scale attacks across Ukraine, striking civilian infrastructure and killing civilians almost daily.
Zelensky met with US President Donald Trump in New York in late September on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), where he laid out Kyiv’s positions on a potential energy ceasefire, trilateral talks involving Putin, domestic production of Patriot missiles and Russia’s growing threats to Europe.
Moscow, for its part, has so far rejected every ceasefire proposal put forward by both Ukraine and the EU. During the same summit, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, who represented Russia in place of Putin, said Moscow would not halt its aggression on Ukraine even during negotiations.
The Kremlin has also continued to insist on full control of Ukraine’s Donbas region as a condition for peace, a demand Kyiv has categorically rejected, arguing that it should not have to give up its sovereign territory in exchange for a possible settlement.
Meanwhile, efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table have so far made little progress.
The Russian leader last met Trump at a summit in Anchorage, Alaska in August 2025. He has since been invited to the G20 summit in the US held December, but the Kremlin has said it is too early to discuss the trip, and reports suggest Putin may skip it altogether.
