articles.title: Shadow Tanker Hit by Ukrainian Drones Threatens Spill Off Russia's Black Sea Coast
articles.body:
Authorities in the Russian Black Sea resort region of Sochi said that a massive oil tanker set afire and left adrift by Ukrainian drones is no threat to local bathers and waters, and that beaches closed to protect bathers and wetlands are now open to the public, local media reported on Thursday.
Sochi Mayor Andrey Proshunin said in a Wednesday statement that his office was closely monitoring offshore sea quality, telling voters the situation was under control and that citizen safety was his highest priority.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“At present the open fire on the tanker has been liquidated and rescue vessels are observing. Pollution of water with the oil cargo [carried in the tanker] has not been recorded. The tanker is drifting with the current along the shoreline,” Proshunin said.
“Local environmental watch agencies are checking pollutant levels in water, air and the ground across the greater Sochi region, and as a safe measure all beaches will be closed to swimming until those checks are complete,” he continued.
Proshunin told voters to remain calm.
“I ask all to remain calm, to observe current rules and restrictions, and to trust only reliable sources of information. The situation is under constant monitoring by the city operational staff,” he added.
Russia’s national environmental watch agency Rospotrebnadzor, in a Wednesday announcement published by the Kremlin-sponsored news agency TASS, took the same position but didn’t mention the drones.
Poland Ends Russian Drone Probe After Failing to Identify Perpetrator
“There is no pollution to the Black Sea as a result of the fire aboard the tanker near Sochi. Agencies are monitoring the shore belt and waters of the Black Sea,” the agency said.
Dmitry Plishkin, head of the Sirius region containing Sochi and adjacent towns and villages, said in a Thursday statement that all local waters and beaches had received a clean bill of health for environmental safety and are now open.
Plishkin’s statement made no reference to the damaged 107,000-ton tanker which, according to Sochi-based news platforms, was in international waters drifting slowly northeast in light seas.
The Liberia-flagged Aframax Rio, a 246-meter (807-feet) long and 107,113-ton deadweight vessel built in 2004, is sanctioned by Ukraine as a shadow tanker Russia uses to evade Western oil export sanctions. The Aframax was southbound when it was hit and set fiercely afire in an early Tuesday evening drone attack.
The blaze under clear skies some 15 nautical miles (30 km) off the shore of Sochi – the heart of the “Russia Riviera” Black Sea resort region – was observed by thousands of local residents and tourists.
Video of the burning ship showed flames engulfing the entire top deck, with the fiercest fires concentrated around the middle of the tanker. The US Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), run by NASA, showed fires burning near the tanker for more than 24 hours before being extinguished.
                                                                                                                                                                         The Liberia-flagged Afromax Rio burns following a Ukrainian drone strike offshore from the Russian resort port of Sochi on Oct. 6, 2026. The vessel, sanctioned by Ukraine as a shadow tanker, was reportedly fully loaded and left drifting. (Photo via sochiradar / Telegram)                             
Imagery of the fire and its expansion recorded live from shore on Wednesday showed the blaze most concentrated in the central portion of the ship’s upper deck, an area often targeted by Ukrainian airborne drones attacking tankers in the past. Ukrainian sea drone attacks in past strikes on tankers have focused on engine rooms and propellers near the stern.
The Russian local news platform Sochi Radar reported that the Aframax Rio was fully loaded and that so much oil had spilled into the water and caught fire that firefighters were prevented from moving to extinguish the blaze quickly.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, in his Wednesday evening broadcast, said the Ukrainian military had attacked and badly damaged a tanker in the Black Sea, but he did not name the vessel, nor did he specify the type of drones used in the attack.
Local Russian news platforms identified the Ukrainian military as having operated the drones that attacked the tanker.
The US-based shipping information platform Marine Executive, in a Thursday article, said that the fire started in the center of the ship in the cargo tank area and then spread aft down the starboard side. Later that evening, the report said burning oil that had escaped from the tanker’s holds was visible on the water, beneath a towering column of smoke.
According to the world civilian vessel tracking group MarineTraffic, the last time the Aframax Rio turned on its transponder was Oct. 5 off the coast of Georgia, and since then its location has not been visible to satellite tracking. Its registered owner is Rio Enterprises SA, a Marshall Islands company.
The Greek news platform Protothema, in its Wednesday article, reported the tanker “is linked to Andreas Hadjiyiannis’ Hellenic Tankers.” As of Thursday, no major ship tracking platform showed the ship’s location.
Marine tracking platforms showed past port destinations for the vessel included Sapsun, Turkey and Sika, India.
According to Kyiv, both countries help Russia evade sanctions by receiving shadow tankers loaded with Russian crude, which is then refined into legitimate product not subject to sanctions.
The Black Sea shipping tracker Blackseanews.net showed the vessel’s operator as Hellenic Tankers Co LTD, an Athens-headquartered business, and its last officially recorded voyage as from Russia’s Novorossiysk port to Saudi Arabia’s Rabigh port in May 2026.
On Sept. 22, Robert “Magyar” Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (USF), claimed his strike forces had attacked and disabled 300 Russian “shadow-fleet” tankers since July 6, with 134 strikes in the Sea of Azov and 166 in the Black Sea.
The most environmentally damaging Russian shadow fleet tanker sunk in those waters was the Vologaneft-212, which went down in a December 2024 storm near the resort port of Anapa with more than 4,000 tons of heavy fuel oil aboard.
Leaking product souked hundreds of kilometers of resort beaches and sensitive wetlands on the Russian Black Sea coast and in Russia-occupied Crimea. The most intense period of the Black Sea storm season is from late October through March.
A press release from the ship’s declared operator, a Singapore-based company called Executive Ships Management, said all 23 crew members were safe ashore after the drone strike. The company said it was investigating the ship’s current status, including any potential threat it might pose to navigation, waters or the shoreline in the area.

articles.title: Trump rules out new Iran attack before US midterm elections
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump rules out new Iran attack before US midterm elections
President Donald Trump on Thursday ruled out attacking Iran before the US midterm elections on 3 November, saying Washington was holding "productive discussions" with Tehran.
Trump's post on his Truth Social platform followed a surge in oil prices on Thursday driven by media reports suggesting potential new US strikes prior to those elections.
"I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect...we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," he wrote.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," he added, without providing additional details.
The Atlantic magazine reported on Wednesday that the White House had asked the Pentagon to develop options to strike Iranian targets that could be used before the midterms. The New York Times published a similar report on Thursday, saying the plans were being developed despite Trump's "ambivalence".
The rise in crude oil prices has also been fueled by persistent tensions in the Strait of Hormuz - a strategic chokepoint for the global oil trade - as well as hostilities between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
In a recent sign of those tensions, an oil tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar reported being struck "by multiple projectiles," causing an unspecified number of casualties, the UKMTO maritime agency said Wednesday.
Polls suggest that US voters are strongly dissatisfied over rising fuel prices, linked to the conflict launched by the United States and Israel against Iran in February.
The US leader has repeatedly insisted in recent weeks that the United States has effectively won the Iran war, despite ongoing unrest and a recent security threat that forced the withdrawal of American bombers from a base in England.
But Trump's claims that prices will fall as soon as the Iran war is over have so far fallen on deaf ears with voters.
The midterm elections will shape the final two years of Trump's presidential term as his Republican Party risks losing its current grip on Congress.
Although Trump is not on the ballot, he is heavily involved in the campaign, holding numerous rallies in an attempt to limit the damage or even turn the political tide.
Trump has warned he faces a possible third impeachment if Democrats retake the House of Representatives, and the White House is preparing for a slew of investigations into corruption and abuse of power.
The US president also on Thursday sought to calm a furor over his comments at a rally earlier this week that Iran could "take out" the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego.
Trump, 80, blamed the "fake and artificial news" for misinterpreting the remarks, which Democrats pounced on.
"In actuality, what I was talking about was that a temporary increase in the price of Gasoline is a small price to pay for Iran not having a Nuclear Weapon and, if you want to see a big price, can you imagine what it would be like if they bombed San Diego and/or Los Angeles?" Trump said on Truth Social.
(AFP)

articles.title: Ukrainian strikes blast Russian frigates at Novorossiysk
articles.body:
A single Ukrainian drone attack on Novorossiysk has significantly degraded the land-attack cruise missile capability of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, accounting for forty per cent of its Kalibr-capable surface ships, according to a Defence Intelligence update published by the UK Ministry of Defence.
In its update on Thursday, Defence Intelligence said: “Ukraine has launched two large scale uncrewed aerial system (UAS) attacks against the Russian Novorossiysk Naval Facility and Commercial Port within the last two months. The 08-09 September 2026 attack led to successful strikes against a GRIGOROVICH class frigate and a SVIYAZHSK light-frigate.”
It went on: “Both vessels have likely sustained sufficient damage to prevent them taking part in KALIBR Land-attack Cruise Missile (LACM) firings into Ukraine, likely for the short-medium term. This single attack has significantly degraded the LACM strike capabilities of the Black Sea Fleet, representing 40% of the KALIBR-capable surface fleet.”
Two ships out of action amounting to two fifths of the capability says as much about the size of the remaining fleet as it does about the damage. Russia has been firing Kalibr missiles at Ukrainian cities and infrastructure from Black Sea platforms since the opening days of the full-scale invasion, and the surface ships able to carry them have never been numerous.
The Admiral Grigorovich class are Project 11356R frigates, the newest conventional surface combatants the Black Sea Fleet has, each able to carry Kalibr in a vertical launch system. Defence Intelligence describes the second vessel as a Sviyazhsk light-frigate, a smaller Kalibr-armed surface combatant.
Ukrainian strikes drove Russian warships out of Sevastopol over the course of 2023 and 2024, and the Krasnodar Krai port became the main operating base for what remained. Pushing the fleet east was supposed to put it beyond easy reach.
Defence Intelligence uses a probability yardstick in which “likely” sits between 55 and 75 per cent, so the assessment that both ships cannot take part in Kalibr firings is a confident judgement without being a certainty. The phrase short to medium term carries no fixed definition, though repairs to a vertical launch system and the surrounding structure on a frigate are not quick work, particularly in a yard under periodic attack.
UK Defence Intelligence publishes its guidance on the use of probabilistic language at this link.

articles.title: Kyiv police neutralize 2 unexploded ballistic missiles after enemy attack
articles.body:
Explosive ordnance disposal technicians of the Kyiv police have neutralized two unexploded ballistic missiles used by Russia in the attack on the capital on October 7, the Kyiv police report.
"The warheads of two Iskander-M missiles, weighing about half a ton each, fell near residential buildings in the Shevchenkivsky and Darnytsky districts," the capital's police department said in a statement on its Telegram channel on Thursday.
According to the report, police officers neutralized the hazardous components of the warheads and prepared them for safe transport.
"Subsequently, using specialized equipment and in cooperation with State Emergency Service sappers, the missile fragments were transported to a temporary detonation site for subsequent destruction," the capital's police specified.
Law enforcement reminds citizens that upon discovering missile fragments, drones, or other suspicious objects, one must not approach or touch them. "Move to a safe distance and report the finding by calling 101 or 102," the police explained.

articles.title: Pentagon says execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
articles.body:
Pete Hegseth has said the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, will be a public event when the sentence is carried out later this year. A defense department official later confirmed the execution will be livestreamed.
In an interview with Real America’s Voice, the Pentagon secretary said the firing squad will carry out the sentence at Fort Hood, Texas, at 1pm on Thursday, 3 December. This would be the first US military execution in more than 60 years.
“It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said.
Hasan opened fire at a medical processing center on the Texas base on 5 November 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013, and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. He exhausted his appeals last year, which cleared the way for Donald Trump to approve the sentence this week on a recommendation from Hegseth.
Investigators had found that Hasan had exchanged 18 emails with Anwar al-Awlaki, a radical cleric who was subsequently killed in a US drone strike, in the months before the attack. At his court martial, Hasan said he had acted to stop American soldiers from deploying to Afghanistan to kill fellow Muslims, before his own impending deployment. A review led by William Webster, a former FBI director, concluded that the bureau should have investigated his correspondence more thoroughly.
In the interview, Hegseth said Barack Obama had called the attack “workplace violence”. The Pentagon initially treated the shooting as a workplace-violence incident rather than a terrorist attack, a classification that affected the victims’ eligibility for Purple Hearts and other combat-related benefits.
But there is no record of Obama himself using the phrase. At a memorial days after the attack, he instead described the victims as Americans who had been unable to escape “the horror of war”, while calling the shooting a tragedy and saying the killer would face justice.
The last known case of a military firing squad in the US was in November 1945, but the Trump administration has sought to bring it back in Trump’s second term to expedite capital punishment cases. Five US states allow for firing squads: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah.
Abroad, Amnesty International’s most recent annual review lists Afghanistan, China, North Korea, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Taiwan, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen among the countries that still use firing squads.
Asked whether Hasan had made a final request or reached out to Trump, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”

articles.title: Russia kills 30 in strike on two passenger buses in Kramatorsk
articles.body:
Russian forces struck the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk on the morning of 8 October, hitting two route buses carrying residents and killing dozens of civilians. The Donetsk Oblast prosecutor's office opened a war-crimes investigation.
Russia has turned everyday movement in frontline Donetsk Oblast into a lethal risk, striking city buses, ambulances, and cars in places its army has not been able to capture.
A route bus run turned deadly
The attack came at around 10:00, catching two route buses in the impact zone. The prosecutor's office said the attackers likely used a UMPB D-30SN. HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence, describes it as a guided glide bomb that can fly up to 100 km when released from an altitude of 12–15 km and carries a warhead equal to a FAB-250 aerial bomb.
The toll rose through the day, from 12 dead in the first reports to 30 killed and 20 wounded by 14:55, Donetsk Oblast head Vadym Filashkin said. Across Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed 33 people that day, including the 30 in Kramatorsk and three in nearby Bilenke, the State Emergency Service said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strike would not go unanswered.
Buses pulled off the roads
Filashkin ordered the Kramatorsk and Sloviansk city military administrations to suspend public transport, citing the sharp deterioration in security. Buses had become an attractive target for Russian forces, he said, and the authorities could not risk the lives of passengers and drivers. He also urged everyone still in Donetsk Oblast to leave for safer parts of Ukraine. Kramatorsk is a frequent target of Russian attacks. Russia had not commented on the strike as of publication.
The city has been under daily fire. On 5 October, Russian FPV drones hit ambulances and an apartment block in Kramatorsk, killing a woman and wounding four, the prosecutor's office reported. Over the previous day, Russian forces shelled Donetsk Oblast settlements 31 times and 256 people left the front line, Filashkin said.

articles.title: Iran taking concrete steps to resolve conflict with US – Putin
articles.body:
Iran taking concrete steps to resolve conflict with US – Putin
Tehran is striving to find a diplomatic solution to the war imposed on it by the US, Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday at a meeting with his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian.
The Russian president noted that Tehran had recently put forward a proposal aimed at resolving the conflict peacefully, adding that Moscow is willing to play a constructive role in the process.
“Iran is making real efforts to end the conflict, which broke out in the region through no fault of its own, through no fault of Iran,” Putin said.
Putin also hailed the deepening cooperation between Russia and Iran, especially in trade and humanitarian affairs, during bilateral talks in Turkmenistan, where he is set to take part in a leaders’ summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) and a Caspian Sea environmental summit.
Moscow has repeatedly condemned the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran and called for a diplomatic solution. During his visit to Tehran in July, former Russian president and current deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council Dmitry Medvedev said that “there was no serious reason for the American attack” as Tehran “posed no threat” to Washington.
In late September, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi announced that Tehran had submitted a peace plan to the US. Under the roadmap, the Islamic Republic signaled its readiness to restore navigation through the Strait of Hormuz – a strategically important waterway for crude oil exports from the Middle East.
In exchange, Iran, which imposed a blockade on the crucial oil shipping route after the start of the conflict, expects the US to lift its own blockade of the Islamic Republic, ease restrictions on its oil exports, and release some of its frozen assets. Tehran is also seeking an end to hostilities on all fronts, including Israel’s military operation in Lebanon.
Addressing the UN General Assembly in New York last month, President Pezeshkian reiterated that his country was prepared for “dialogue and diplomacy” but would not negotiate under threats.
While there have been media reports of indirect negotiations between the two countries in recent weeks, President Trump has rejected the Iranian proposal outright. He told reporters that Tehran wants to “make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make.” The US president has also suggested that Washington is not ruling out resuming strikes on Iran in the coming weeks.

articles.title: ‘Not great, not terrible’: Why nobody trusts Russia to tell the truth about plague
articles.body:
A security worker looks out from the door of an infectious diseases hospital in the town of Shelekhov, where an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East had died, on Oct. 7, 2026. | Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP via Getty Images
As whispers circulate of plague in faraway Siberia, it’s worth remembering that Russian obfuscation is so ingrained that it’s become a meme.
In HBO’s dramatized 2019 series about the nuclear disaster at Chernobyl, a Russian atomic scientist scoffs at a radiation reading that suggests a major calamity is taking place.
“Not great, not terrible,” says the fictionalized version of Anatoly Dyatlov, the real-life deputy chief engineer at Chernobyl in April 1986, as he looks at a dosimeter noting 3.6 roentgen per hour, just below a critical radiation level.
Advertisement
Except that reading was not accurate. Not even close. The nuclear reactor had already exploded and unleashed catastrophic levels of radiation that would go on to cause thousands of cancer-related deaths in the worst nuclear power plant disaster in history.
While dramatized, the scene is emblematic of a long-standing Soviet and Russian desire to downplay critical incidents — and even cover them up. That pattern has flared this week, with senior world health officials, the European Union and U.S. President Donald Trump demanding that Moscow be more transparent about a suspected outbreak of plague in far eastern Russia.
In dark comedic twist in the face of the potential plague, Dyatlov’s dismissive remark is now ubiquitous. Not great, not terrible.
Into the unknown
The death of a 28-year-old employee at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East last week triggered unease across the globe due to her laboratory work — and a local Russian official linking her death to a case of plague.
Russia was quick to clamp down. Rospotrebnadzor, the country’s national public health agency, said that the employee died from “pneumonia of unknown etiology” and that no microorganisms associated with her work were identified in the patient sample.
Still, Russian health authorities placed nearly 200 people under supervision and local media reported that several hospitals were placed under quarantine. Rospotrebnadzor said Thursday these measures were taken due to “the patient's professional activities.”
Advertisement
The World Health Organization, which leads global response to international health threats, got in touch with Russian health authorities on Oct. 3. It requested more information using one of the tools laid out in the International Health Regulations, which Russia is signed up to. Under the IHR, countries have 24 hours to respond to the WHO — though Russia sent its response on Oct. 6.
Russian authorities said that “no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk” and “no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts.”
World Health Organization epidemic and pandemic management head Maria Van Kerkhove, who said "we still don't know exactly how this person died, at a press briefing in Geneva on Oct. 7, 2026. | Fabrice Coffrini/AFP via Getty Images
As of Thursday, Russian health authorities maintain that there is no “epidemic risk” in the region. Rospotrebnadzor said that it had concluded health inspections and found “no emergency situations involving pathogenic microorganisms.” It had also completed monitoring of 90% of the contacts, without identifying any infections, the agency added. Simultaneously, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov slammed media reports about the case as false and said Russia has been communicating with global health authorities.
Yet the WHO insists there’s still much left unknown about the events inside Russia.
“We don’t know exactly how this person died,” said Maria Van Kerkhove, director of epidemic and pandemic management, during a press briefing Wednesday. “We know that she had pneumonia. We know it was a fatal case. We understand that some laboratory tests have been done. They haven’t found the causative agent. This is why we need more information.”
The WHO said it requested further details on what laboratory tests were conducted, which pathogens were evaluated, which further analyses are being done to determine the patient’s cause of death — if not plague — along with more details on any potential lab incident and the 200 contacts.
Advertisement
Until those questions are answered, it’s impossible for the WHO to conduct a risk assessment.
“We don't yet have the full picture of this event, and we are not able to conduct a full risk assessment,” said Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the organization’s director-general. “Timely, complete, and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”
Omertà in Russian
It might be that the cause of death of the 28-year-old lab worker is not, in fact, plague.
But Russia’s incomplete, late and hazy communication about the case is fomenting fears and uncertainty from Geneva to Brussels to Washington. It would also not be the first time the Kremlin has downplayed or attempted to cover up public health threats.
That goes beyond the Soviet-era Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant disaster, in what is now northern Ukraine, where the Kremlin was slow to take action and effectively denied the cause of the incident.
In 1979, according to an investigation by U.S. scientists, the Soviet Union covered up a deadly anthrax outbreak in the city of Sverdlovsk, now Yekaterinburg, which killed at least 66 people. Officials said the victims had fallen ill from eating contaminated meat, when in reality they had been exposed to anthrax because of an accident at a secret biological weapons lab.
Advertisement
Russia was also accused of covering up a mysterious 1988 alopecia outbreak in Chernivtsi region, in which more than 175 children lost their hair. Soviet authorities said the children suffered from thallium food poisoning, but later studies raised questions about that, with some suggesting the cause was hydrazine, or acid rain.
Over the years, the Kremlin has also dismissed, downplayed and underreported HIV cases, even while in the middle of a deadly epidemic. And, more recently, during the Covid-19 pandemic, Russia was accused of downplaying coronavirus deaths, particularly at the beginning.
An image taken from a helicopter in April 1986 shows a general view of the destroyed fourth power block of Chernobyl's nuclear plant a few days after the catastrophe, which was downplayed at the time by Soviet authorities. | Vladimir Repik/AFP via Getty Images
The tradition extends beyond public health. The 1999 apartment block bombings, the 2000 sinking of the Kursk submarine and the 2014 downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 by Kremlin-backed separatists all raised questions over Russia's public messaging and commitment to transparency.
Talks with Putin
The EU and the U.S. are monitoring the Irkutsk situation closely, with both seemingly growing impatient with Russia’s communication.
“The whole world is waiting for the information from Russia,” said European Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova on Thursday.
“Russia should make information about the plague available as soon as possible,” she told reporters. “We need information from Russia. It’s linked to the Russian membership in the WHO Europe, sharing timely, precise, exact information so that the experts can assess the situation, because [it] can have cross-border implications.”
Advertisement
The European Commission’s directorate-general for health and food safety is planning to send a technical letter to Russia asking for more information, a Commission spokesperson confirmed.
In the meantime, Russia’s “patchy” communication is dangerous, said a Commission official, granted anonymity to speak candidly on the matter.
“This fuels speculation into all directions. It also renders preventive [and] precautionary action difficult, if not even meaningless,” the official said. These types of events happen all the time, but there is usually an exchange with the WHO and health authorities, the person added. “The lack of precise [and] reliable info is logically reducing adequate good preparedness.”
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday urged Russia to share more information, adding that it would be “irresponsible” to speculate until then. The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that the U.S. sent a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting more information about the woman’s death and reminding the Kremlin that it has obligations under international law to share information about disease outbreaks in a timely manner.
U.S. President Donald Trump even said Tuesday he had a "call scheduled" with Russian President Vladimir Putin "very soon" to discuss the situation.
But, by Thursday, the two leaders were yet to talk, with Trump noting that Russia was “not saying much.”

articles.title: MEP blasts ‘Euro-Gestapo’ for lecturing Russia on democracy (VIDEO)
articles.body:
MEP blasts ‘Euro-Gestapo’ for lecturing Russia on democracy (VIDEO)
Brussels is steering Europe toward totalitarianism and a “Euro-Gestapo” while lecturing Russia on democracy, Slovak MEP Lubos Blaha has warned.
Blaha made the remarks during a European Parliament debate on Tuesday, responding to EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who denounced Russia’s recent parliamentary elections as undemocratic.
The politician questioned why Brussels was focusing on Russia while cracking down on dissent within the bloc.
He cited arrests of pro-Palestinian protesters in Germany and the imprisonment of Estonian opposition figures, who he claimed were jailed for opposing war with Russia.
“Are you going to set up the Euro-Gestapo here, Mrs. Kallas, and lock up everyone who wants peace?” he asked.
"Will you set up a Euro-Gestapo here, Ms Kallas, and lock up all of us who want peace?" Slovak MEP Blaha calls out warmongers von der Leyen and Kallas. "You criticize the Russians for holding elections, but you do not mind that Zelensky has been governing for a third year without any elections, without a mandate. You hypocrites."
— Chay Bowes (@BowesChay) October 7, 2026
The Slovak lawmaker also questioned why Brussels was debating Russia’s elections while Europe faced mounting unrest.
“You may not have noticed, but Spain is in the streets, France is in the streets, and you are here dealing with Russian elections. You must be joking,” he said.
Blaha went on to accuse Brussels of double standards over Ukraine’s suspended presidential elections.
“You blame the Russians for having elections, but you don’t mind that [Ukraine’s Vladimir] Zelensky has been governing for three years without any elections, without a mandate,” he said. “You are hypocrites!”
Zelensky’s presidential term expired in May 2024, but elections have remained suspended under martial law.
Blaha also cited the annulment of Romania’s 2024 presidential election, claiming the vote was canceled because “the wrong candidate won.” Romania’s Constitutional Court scrapped the result over alleged irregularities and accusations of Russian interference after EU- and NATO-skeptic Calin Georgescu won the first round. Pro-EU candidate Nicusor Dan won the rerun in May 2025.
The MEP argued that Russia had held elections despite the ongoing conflict and daily Ukrainian missile and drone attacks on its territory.
The September poll saw the ruling United Russia party win nearly 58% of the party-list vote.
Blaha also defended Russian President Vladimir Putin, contrasting his popularity with that of Western European leaders.
“You have nothing to criticize Putin for, Mrs. Kallas,” he declared. “Unlike you and your Merzes and Macrons, he has the support of his own population.”
Recent polls have put German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s approval rating at a record low of 10% in October, while French President Emmanuel Macron’s support fell to 17% in September. Neither Kallas nor European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was directly elected to her current position by voters, having assumed office through the EU’s institutional appointment process.
Blaha belongs to Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico’s Smer-SD party, which opposes EU sanctions on Russia and has criticized Western military assistance to Ukraine.

articles.title: NATO says 'Steadfast Noon' in Italy is a nuclear exercise
articles.body:
NATO on Thursday said its upcoming
'Steadfast Noon' exercise in Italy was a nuclear exercise,
obviously not featuring live weapons.
                                    
The exercise starting in Italy October 13 will be a "nuclear"
exercise, explained NATO's head of nuclear policy, Nassima
Barrows, during a meeting with media outlets, including ANSA.
                                    
While no live nuclear weapons are used in the exercise, training
to the high standards required for a mission of this type
remains crucial.
                                    
"It is therefore essential to ensure both discipline and the
ability to collaborate on collective defense—of which the
nuclear mission is a vital component," stated Colonel David
Bull, the Alliance's Head of Nuclear Operations.
                                    
photo: NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte

articles.title: Zelenskyy and UK foreign secretary visit site of Russian missile strike in Pryluky
articles.body:
Zelenskyy and UK foreign secretary visit site of Russian missile strike in Pryluky
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ed Miliband, the Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs of the United Kingdom, have visited Pryluky in Chernihiv Oblast, where a Russian missile struck an apartment block on 7 October.
Source: European Pravda, citing Ukrinform
Details: Zelenskyy thanked the UK secretary, who arrived in Kyiv on an official visit, adding that Miliband was invited to visit Pryluky to "see for himself what is really happening, what daily strikes look like and how our people endure this struggle".
He called on partners, including the United Kingdom, to step up assistance to Ukraine, particularly with air defence systems.
Zelenskyy also emphasised the need to strengthen the negotiation process.
Quote: "In addition to the air defence factor, which is in short supply because our country is large and incoming strikes happen everywhere, we would certainly like to draw attention to the negotiation track, because, in our view, the United States of America should raise the pressure through sanctions and other steps – both financial assistance and specific air defence support for Ukraine. And through such steps... force Putin to sit down at the negotiating table."
According to the latest data, 22 people were killed, including five children, as a result of the Russian missile strike on Pryluky on 7 October.
Background:
- Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna condemned another massive Russian attack on Ukraine, urging partners to increase pressure on Moscow.
- Zelenskyy announced meetings between Ukrainian negotiators and the American side on 9 and 10 October.
	
Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: “They were smiling as they shot at us”: The Insider speaks with Israelis whose lives were turned upside down on October 7, 2023
articles.body:
On October 7, Israel marked the third anniversary of the Hamas terrorist attack of 2023. The Insider spoke to three people whose lives were changed forever that day: a survivor of the attack from Kibbutz Be’eri, a Hamas hostage who spent two years in captivity, and a soldier who was among the first to enter Gaza as part of an armored brigade.
- 1.Pyotr Stolba, resident of Kibbutz Be’eri: “Cars and houses were burning, the whole street was littered with bodies”
- 2.Former hostage Maksim Kharkin: “They were killing people and smiling”
- 3.Vitaly Cheberdin, Israeli soldier with the 188th Armored Brigade: “The army had never done anything like this in Gaza”
Pyotr Stolba, resident of Kibbutz Be’eri: “Cars and houses were burning, the whole street was littered with bodies”
On October 7, 2023, several thousand Hamas militants broke into Israel from the Gaza Strip. They initially headed for the Be’eri and Nahal Oz kibbutzim along the border with the Strip. For the first seven hours of the attack — before the army arrived — Be’eri was defended by just 26 people. A total of 101 residents, including 10 children aged from several months to 17 years, were killed. Another 32 residents were taken hostage by the terrorists.
Three years after “Black Saturday,” just one burned-out house remains in Kibbutz Be’eri — a reminder of the tragedy. Its roof has collapsed and its walls are riddled with bullet holes. The house stands on an empty lot surrounded by a large metal fence. Just one year ago, there were more destroyed houses here, but they have since been demolished. Local residents are divided over what to do with the last one – preserve it as a memorial to the attack or remove it so that it does not remind their own children of the horror they experienced.
Pyotr Stolba has lived in Be’eri for 34 years. He immigrated to Israel from Moscow in 1996 with his wife and settled in the kibbutz almost immediately:
“There were two families living in this house: the Kipnises and the Alons. The Alon family was later rescued alive by the Israeli army, while the Kipnis couple – husband and wife – were killed by the terrorists inside the house, which they then set on fire.
At 6:30 a.m. on October 7, Qassam rockets began falling here. Of course, we went into the safe room. I was at home with my wife, my older son, my pregnant daughter-in-law, and my 10-month-old grandson.
We were told not to leave the safe rooms because there were terrorists in the kibbutz. We thought there were just a few of them. No one could have imagined that 400 terrorists would enter Be’eri.
They smashed through the glass balcony door. They shot at the glass and it shattered. They opened the door and came inside. The dog met them and started barking, and they immediately shot it.
They tried to break into our safe room, pulling at the door handle. My son and I held the door from inside. They knocked and spoke to us in English: "Come out, we won’t hurt you." But my older son had served in the territories [in the West Bank], in combat units. He said, 'Dad, we don’t talk to Arabs. Stay quiet.'
We stayed there for 19 hours, until the army rescued us.
The electricity went out half an hour after the terrorists stormed into the kibbutz. While our phones still had battery power, everyone was passing along information. The Losev family from Zaporizhzhia lived near that transformer station. They were close friends of ours. Marina was burned alive in the house. She was identified only by her teeth. Igor was found shot dead near the fence.
Marina was burned alive in the house and identified only by her teeth, while Igor was found shot dead near the fence
The terrorists were drinking on my balcony and shooting at the road. They used heavy machine guns to shoot anyone who drove past or tried to escape. They shot at chandeliers and the TV. A tree burning next to the house heated the roof tiles until they glowed and began to fall. My wife said, 'Listen, the house is collapsing!' I said, 'All we can do is pray. There’s nothing else we can do.'
When the army arrived, we went outside – everything around us was burning. Cars and houses were on fire; bodies lay in the street. The dead were everywhere: terrorists, Israelis. Children, women, and men lay on the sidewalks and in the roads.
We were taken from there to a hotel by the Dead Sea. That’s where we learned who had been killed and how. One of my friends said, 'I don’t know where my wife is, where my daughter is.' It turned out they had been killed.
I returned to Be’eri four months after the attack to get the local printing press running again. My wife and I now live in temporary housing and are preparing to move into a new home. A new military base has been built next to us. I think that will give us some protection in case of a sudden attack.
We never doubted that we wanted to return, because this is our home. But some families do not want to come back because of the trauma. Maybe with time it will somehow fade, but it’s impossible to ever completely forget that day."
Former hostage Maksim Kharkin: “They were killing people and smiling”
On October 7, Maksim Kharkin went with friends to the Supernova music festival, which was attacked by Hamas. Maksim was held hostage for two years:
“I had never been to Supernova before. It was a huge, very well-organized event, with all the necessary permits. There was police and internal security. We went there to enjoy ourselves and listen to music.
But at 6:27, a massive rocket attack began. That’s when I realized the war had started. The road was cut off, and the terrorists were already advancing. I ran into a field. At some point, a friend called me: ‘Max, where are you?’ I said I’d managed to get about 100 meters away. He asked, 'Max, come back and help me. I don’t know what to do.'
The shelling could already be heard from all sides. But they weren’t shooting directly at us yet – there had been no direct contact.
I heard my friend’s wife screaming into the phone: 'Max, help me, save me.' So I went back.
We decided to lie down in a ditch. The shelling was coming from all sides – from both sides of the road and from the direction of the party itself. The terrorists were advancing from two sides, calmly spraying everything with gunfire: rat-a-tat-tat-tat.
At some point, they reached us – and that was it. My friend managed to fire a shot. He had his service weapon, and he took one of them down, but he was immediately shot in the back.
They first shot at my head, but the bullet whistled over it. By then, I had basically given up hope.
I saw them killing everyone who was there. They were smiling – killing people and smiling. They let their victims scream out their pain, plead and cry. Then they shot them with a smile.
There was a young guy running around with a camera. I called him the “wedding photographer.” He walked around filming everything, enjoying himself.
You see how many of them there are — thirty here, another hundred there. And they’re in no hurry. Everything is fine, everything is great, it’s a celebration.
They tied my hands, pulled a stocking over my head, and took me to the Gaza Strip with another hostage. Every second could have been my last.
I decided I was already a dead man. They brought me to Gaza with my hands and feet tied and pushed me to the floor. I fell to my knees first, then they shoved me again and I fell face-first onto the floor. When I first fell to my knees, I realized that from that moment on, every second I was alive, every breath I took, was a gift.
“When I first fell to my knees, I realized that from that moment on, every second I was alive, every breath I took, was a gift.”
We were held in ordinary homes in the Gaza Strip. Apart from Hamas fighters, the only people we had contact with were the heads of the households. Their sons, boys around 15 to 17, carried machine guns and could casually transport grenades and ammunition in UNICEF bags.
If one of us did something wrong – for example, if they saw someone talking to another hostage, even whispering or communicating with their fingers – you could get a beating for that.
The house where I was held came under fire, and the upper floor was destroyed. After that, I was moved to an underground tunnel. I spent another year and four months there. Some tunnels are designed for people to live in. They can have tile, floors, and entire rooms — basically apartments. Ours was nothing like that. It was a transport tunnel. There were just concrete beams, about 20 centimeters wide and a little over a meter high. Then came a concrete arch of the same thickness, another beam, and another beam on the floor. That was it. The entire tunnel was built that way.
How did we use the toilet? I dug a hole, and that’s where I went.
At one point, there were six of us. We came down with every illness imaginable, including COVID. We never left the tunnel. Your condition gets to the point where you stand up and immediately start swaying. You can’t walk properly; you’re constantly staggering.
There was no light. The only light was a small LED bulb, if there was one. Sometimes there wasn’t. If they called you from one room to another and you didn’t have a flashlight, it was pitch-black. You couldn’t see anything, absolutely nothing.
We were fed infrequently, and it got worse as time went on. Especially during the last five months, we could easily go 27 to 30 hours without eating. Lunch was a tablespoon of some kind of sauce and half a pita. I weighed just 50 kilograms when I came out. When I entered the tunnel, I weighed 90 kilograms.
Hamas guards had a separate room for themselves in the tunnel. There was a core group that stayed there permanently, while others rotated in and out. They had a room like ours, only larger — with a satellite TV, a kitchen and food.
We’d get the shit beaten out of us, then they’d interrogate us, then we’d get the shit beaten out of us again. 'Who are you? Where are you from? What’s your mother’s name? Your father’s? What did you do in the army? Where did you come from? Why did you come here?' We had to make up some kind of half-true story.
Hamas fighters hardly ever spoke to the hostages. From time to time, they would tell us something demoralizing or offer food or other concessions in exchange for converting to Islam. Eventually, I converted to Islam, which let me wheedle a radio out of them — supposedly to listen to prayers recorded on a memory card. They had deliberately broken off the antenna, but the base was still there, along with a manual tuning dial.
I studied a little physics at the Suvorov military school. I understood that as long as electricity was running through the cables in the tunnel, you couldn’t pick up anything. But when the power was off, a cable could work as an antenna. Everyone told me, 'You’re crazy. What waves? What radio? You’re making this up.' We put it under the cable – and suddenly we had a signal!
There was no electricity in the wires from 5:30 p.m. until 9:30 a.m. That was when we listened to all sorts of things – stations from neighboring countries: Egypt, Syria, Lebanon. We quickly picked up the Israeli military station Galei Tsahal. That’s where we got our news and learned what was really happening.
I think I managed to pick up Vesti Moskvy once, or at least hear Russian being spoken. That was hugely important because I hadn’t spoken Russian with anyone for two years.
At the moment we were released, at 7:30 a.m., they lined us up and said that nothing was over yet. If anything went wrong, they would either kill us on the spot or, at best, send us back into the tunnel. From the start, I told myself I wouldn’t believe we were free until the door of the Red Cross armored Land Cruiser closed behind me.
When it did, I exhaled for the first time. But you’re still there, and they’re still all around you."
Vitaly Cheberdin, Israeli soldier with the 188th Armored Brigade: “The army had never done anything like this in Gaza”
In late October 2023, after three weeks of bombardment, the IDF launched a ground operation in the Gaza Strip. The stated goals of the operation were to destroy Hamas’s military and governing capabilities, return the hostages, and prevent further attacks on Israel.
During the operation in Gaza, tens of thousands of people were killed, and around 85% of buildings in the Strip were damaged or destroyed. The figures were cited by Nikolay Mladenov, the UN High Representative for the "Board of Peace," who is respected by both Israelis and Palestinians.
Israeli soldier Vitaly Cheberdin entered Gaza in December 2023 with the 188th Armored Brigade. According to him, the troops had initially been preparing for possible fighting in Lebanon, so the deployment south came as a surprise:
“The army had never done anything like this in Gaza. Before that, they had only entered small areas. It’s densely populated there, which makes fighting, especially with tanks, extremely difficult.
On the first day, we had to advance about 10 kilometers in our tanks and bring in several battalions so the security services could begin operating there. When we entered Gaza, I saw the sky glowing pink from the explosions. Hamas fighters started firing back. Something came flying in our direction.
We just kept moving forward, firing as we went – they shot at us, we shot back. I saw houses, movie theaters, cars, things exploding. It was like something out of a movie.
One of my unit’s main tasks was to search for Hamas weapons depots and tunnels. We mostly went to Hamas fighters’ homes looking for weapons. If we found anything – a weapons cache or other infrastructure – we blew it up on the spot.
There were also addresses where hostages were believed to be held. That was a priority for everyone, but honestly, we didn’t expect to find anyone. Whenever there was a small operation involving hostages, we dropped everything and focused entirely on it.
We didn’t want to kill anyone, but it happened. Once, we started entering a house, reacted to movement, and shot a woman. Everything was filled with smoke; the house was already on fire. There was also a dead girl inside, though it wasn’t clear what had killed her – a tank or infantry fire. Three girls were still alive, around 14 or 15 years old, along with an adult woman and two men. We took them all outside.
We gave the women food right away. The men were initially in their underwear. Obviously, that’s all they could wear when they came out. We then brought them blankets, and after some time handed them all over to the Red Cross. We fed the civilians and shared our food with them.
A man started coming out from somewhere. He was shot in the head. I don’t know by whom. He immediately fell backward, his brains blown out. His family came out behind him; they were spared.
“A man started coming out from somewhere, was shot in the head, and his family came out behind him – they were spared”
Civilians suffered mainly because Hamas put them in harm’s way. Hamas fighters don’t look like they do on TV, either. Most walk around in flip-flops and shorts, carrying a grenade launcher or a Kalashnikov. They often hide among civilians — it's guerrilla warfare.
Once, our unit spent the night in a girls’ school. I went into the teachers’ room and started looking at photographs from school parades – pictures of them supposedly destroying something resembling Israel, trampling on it, pretending to slit its throat. They’re steeped in hatred.
I still have a girl’s album that I took from one of the apartments. She draws beautifully, she has talent, but the pictures — she drew the Islamic Jihad symbol, terrorists, Yasser Arafat.
I’ll never forget this image: you’re standing in a building on high ground, with the whole city spread out below, and it’s burning — burning intensely. And you realize you’re part of all this, that you’re the reason for it.
COVID was going around there for a while. I felt sick, but I got through it relatively easily. My gunner, though, just collapsed. He was in the tank as we were attacking and advancing, lying unconscious in the back with a temperature close to 40°C. He couldn’t take part in anything and just rode along with us. We pressured the officer, and they took him back to Israel that same evening. He ended up in the hospital.
In total, I spent four months in Gaza. The first time, I came out more or less okay. But the second time, I had a completely dead look in my eyes. I didn’t feel like doing anything.
You drive into Israel and there’s so much light. We were like frightened idiots. A friend told me that when he got home, he walked into the room, went up to his mother, and asked, 'Can I turn on the light?'
The first day I got home, I couldn’t sleep because it was so quiet. The birds are singing here, while over there you had mortars pounding."

articles.title: High explosive payloads keep a human in the loop
articles.body:
Where a person sits in the decision depends on what the system is carrying, and anything with a high explosive payload will keep a human in the loop, a panel on autonomous mass heard at the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Freddie Bradshaw, head of business development at the Estonian company Ark Robotics, said the use case has to come before the autonomy question, because the answer changes completely between a one-way strike vehicle and a resupply run.
He said: “We’re certainly seeing that it’s very important to have human in the loop when it comes to a one-way strike effector, for instance. If you’ve got a system that has a payload of high explosive, the chances are we aren’t going to allow AI to be controlling that, and we need to have some sort of human in the loop.”
Further back from the front the balance shifts, and that is where he sees autonomy earning its place, taking the cognitive burden off a commander and handing it to the system so that one person can manage a fleet.
Antony Quinn, the Europe director of Havoc, argued that the vocabulary needs tightening before the debate can go anywhere, since human in the loop and human on the loop get used interchangeably and mean different things. Adding waypoints and watching a vessel follow them round makes the operator the bottleneck, which defeats the point of mass in the first place.
Three things have to be right in his account before any of it works, the first is the human interface, which should use simple accessible language and let an operator give intent and supervise instead of constantly intervening or monitoring camera feeds. The second is trust, earned by designing, testing and assuring the system the way trust is extended to an officer commanding a tactical unit. The third is policy and doctrine, which he does not think needs reinventing.
He said: “There is a point at which the system, whatever it is, is trusted to the person or computer you have trained, with its boundaries and actions on, and doctrine already supports this. So yes, humans are critically important in or on the loop, but a lot of it is not that unfamiliar, actually.”
Mr Bradshaw made a related point about interfaces, saying his company works to ensure its own plugs into a number of command and control systems so it can be operated through NATO compliant architectures, and that it has to be easy enough to use that scaling is possible at all.
From the user’s side, Oleksii Krymeniuk, the chief unmanned systems officer of the 2nd Corps of Ukraine’s National Guard, gave the position a name. “I’m not a huge believer in full autonomy. I’m more a believer in something that could assist our guys in the staffs and on the ground and help them make faster and more efficient decisions,” he said.
What he wants next is one operator running many drones, which he was careful to distinguish from swarming. The arithmetic is what makes it matter, since a mission needing dozens of aircraft currently needs dozens of operators, and bringing that ratio down multiplies what a unit of fixed size can achieve. Mr Bradshaw agreed that ground autonomy has not arrived yet, saying there is still a way to go in the uncrewed ground vehicle domain.
Mike Wilmot, head of UK land at Helsing, came at it from the opposite direction, arguing that there are tasks where an automated process deserves more confidence than a person does, with air defence engagement the obvious case. He drew an ethical conclusion from that.
He said: “There isn’t just a financial expense of sending an F-35 across the forward line of enemy troops. There is also a potential human expense, and if we have that safety confidence in a platform to be able to deliver its task, then there does become an ethical consideration of why send a human pilot or a collection of human pilots when you could first send autonomous platforms.”
None of the four speakers argued for removing the person altogether, and the disagreement between them was about where the line falls, not whether there should be one. Mr Quinn’s closing advice to anybody buying this technology was that the decision making does not need to change as much as people fear, and that a degree of the caution around it is unjustified.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force shows Morocco the F-35A it reportedly wants
articles.body:
- U.S. Air Force F-35As flew with Moroccan F-16s on the opening day of the Marrakech Airshow, which runs Oct. 7-10.
- Morocco’s first new F-16 Block 72 flew on Oct. 6, and reports say Rabat has discussed buying F-35s, though no sale has been approved.
U.S. Air Force F-35A Lightning II stealth fighters flew alongside Moroccan F-16s on the opening day of the Marrakech Airshow, putting the jet in front of a country that has been reported to be interested in buying it and that already fields a growing list of American weapons.
The airshow runs Oct. 7-10 at a Royal Moroccan Air Force base in Marrakech. Lockheed Martin, which builds both aircraft, posted that Morocco’s F-16s and the U.S. Air Force F-35As took to the skies to open the four-day event. According to the U.S. Department of War, the F-35A flyby is the centerpiece of about 45 U.S. military personnel taking part. The fighters come from the 48th Fighter Wing at RAF Lakenheath in England, the largest U.S. fighter wing in Europe, which flies both F-35As and F-15E Strike Eagles.
The U.S. contingent also includes two aircraft on static display: an HC-130J Combat King II search-and-rescue plane from the Alaska Air National Guard’s 176th Wing at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, and a KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refueling aircraft from the Utah National Guard’s 151st Wing. The Utah National Guard has been paired with Morocco since 2003 under the State Partnership Program, which links U.S. National Guard units with foreign militaries for regular training and exchanges.
“It is an honor to be at Marrakech ahead of the 250th anniversary of the U.S.-Moroccan Alliance,” said U.S. Air Force Brig. Gen. Matthew J. French, Air National Guard assistant to the commander of U.S. Air Forces in Europe and Air Forces Africa. “Hosted by the United States’ oldest Ally, this forum best illustrates our goal of establishing strong and enduring Allied and partner forces for an evolving security environment. It makes us stronger in both our individual and combined capacities.”
Morocco was the first country to recognize U.S. independence, in 1777, and Washington designated it a major non-NATO ally in 2004.
Morocco’s air force is about to receive a major upgrade of its own. On Oct. 6, Lockheed Martin said the first of 25 new F-16 Block 72 fighters built for Morocco had made its maiden flight in Greenville, South Carolina. The U.S. approved that sale, worth an estimated $3.8 billion, in 2019, along with a separate package of about $985 million to upgrade Morocco’s 23 existing F-16s to a similar standard.
Rabat has also been one of the steadier buyers of American ground equipment in Africa, including M1 Abrams tanks, AH-64E Apache attack helicopters and HIMARS rocket launchers. In 2024, the U.S. State Department approved the sale of 612 Javelin anti-tank missiles to Morocco for an estimated $260 million.
Morocco’s interest in the F-35 has surfaced repeatedly. Reports since 2025 have said Rabat was in talks for up to 32 of the stealth fighters. The U.S. government has not announced any approval of an F-35 sale to Morocco, and neither government has confirmed negotiations.
“The Marrakech Air Show is a world-class exhibition of aviation innovation and a powerful testament to the enduring, nearly 250-year friendship between the United States and the Kingdom of Morocco. For decades, our nations have flown side-by-side, from our vital pilot training pipelines to our complex joint operations. The United States remains deeply committed to standing with our Moroccan partners, delivering cutting-edge aerospace capabilities and working hand-in-hand to promote regional peace, stability, and shared prosperity across the African continent,” said Duke Buchan III, the U.S. ambassador to Morocco.

articles.title: Israel's long road to a Gaza without Palestinians
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
With or without 7 October: Israel's Gaza endgame was always ethnic cleansing
In April 2023, six months before the 7 October attacks, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held a meeting with Yoav Gallant, his then defence minister, and Alon Davidi, the mayor of Sderot - an Israeli city built on top of the historic Palestinian village of Huj.
Gallant and Davidi casually joked about flattening Gaza to rebuild Jewish-only settlements on its ruins. “I would also like to build in Beit Hanoun (in Gaza), but I will settle for Sderot,” said Davidi. Gallant replied, “In order to build in Beit Hanoun, you first need to flatten the area there.”
A month earlier, Israel’s Minister of Settlements Orit Strook said explicitly, “I don't know how many years it will take...returning to Gaza will take a lot of sacrifices. Gaza is part of the land of Israel, and we will return to it one day.”
Strook was reiterating what the deputy head of Israel’s Knesset, Limor Son-Har Melech, said the same day. “Our task now is to return to the settlements in Gush Katif and rebuild them,” he said, in reference to Israeli settlements in Gaza that were evacuated in 2005.
Israel’s finance minister and de facto ruler of the occupied Palestinian territory, Bezalel Smotrich, had also promised on the eve of the Netanyahu government’s formation in December 2022 that Israel would “return” to rebuild Jewish settlements in Gaza.
Three years into Israel's war, these statements now sound like prophetic declarations of intent.
Beit Hanoun was levelled to the ground during the war, just as Gallant said. Earlier this year, Limor Son-Har Melech led a group of settlers deep inside Gaza, planting trees to mark the first step towards rebuilding settlements in the enclave. He bragged: “Gaza will be Jewish, because only in this way will we ensure victory.”
Israel Katz, meanwhile, Israel’s new defence minister, has formally announced intentions to start building settlements in Gaza.
That is why Israel's military rabbi Amichai Friedman described the month of October 2023 as “the happiest month of my life”. He added, “We're finally realising who we are. All of this land is ours. The entire land, including Gaza and Lebanon. Gush Katif is tiny compared to what we will get with God’s help to achieve... We will destroy everyone.”
An ambition decades in the making
Seven months before 7 October, Israel’s former defence minister and right-wing politician Moshe Yaalon sounded the alarm that Israel’s “Jewish supremacist” ministers, whose beliefs, he said, reflected “Mein Kampf in reverse”, wanted to provoke “the final war” of “Gog and Magog.”
Yaalon warned that Smotrich and Ben-Gvir would try to provoke Palestinians, through massacres, for instance, to use any Palestinian retaliation as a pretext for the 'final battle'.
As soon as Itamar Ben-Gvir became Israel’s security minister, he rushed, as Yaalon anticipated, to abuse Palestinian prisoners to ignite that war. Some of his first decisions were to ban pita bread for detainees, reduce their shower time to two minutes per day, overcrowd their cells, and let a Palestinian hunger striker, Khader Adnan, die in solitary confinement.
The cruelty meted out to Palestinian detainees is thought to have served as one of the core justifications, and strategic drivers, for Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar to launch the 7 October attacks on Israel.
But even without Hamas’s attack, the concept of ‘transfer’, or ethnic cleansing, has long been embedded in official Israeli policymaking.
“You shall continue to live like dogs, and whoever wishes may leave… It's possible that in five years, there will be 200,000 fewer people, and that's an enormous thing,” said Israel’s then defence minister Moshe Dayan shortly after the 1967 war.
The “live like dogs or leave” dichotomy was reiterated in 2017 by Smotrich in a manifesto Israeli pundits themselves described as “genocidal.” Smotrich gave Palestinians three options: submit to living as inferior subhumans, leave the land, or resist and get killed.
Israel has used this policy in Gaza since the 1948 Nakba. Even before it captured Gaza officially in 1967, the Israeli government sought to push for mass migration from the enclave through intimidation, bribery, periodic massacres, and destruction of vital infrastructure.
After Gaza fell under Israeli occupation, Israel used more force, coercion, destruction, intimidation, and bribery to empty Gaza.
When Israel imposed a blockade on Gaza in 2006, economic warfare and starvation were systematically imposed, punctuated by periodic “high-tech killing sprees” to inflict the maximum destruction possible in order to make the enclave uninhabitable and force its people out.
Before 7 October, about 10% of Gaza’s population (205,000 people) had already emigrated from the Strip since the blockade started. Half of that significant figure were people who left in the five years that preceded Hamas’s attack.
A senior Israeli official even bragged in 2019 that Tel Aviv was “actively pushing Palestinian emigration from Gaza.” The official said Israel was reaching out to Western and Middle Eastern countries to encourage accepting Gazan migrants and even offered to cover the costs of travel.
Israel’s focus on displacing Gaza’s population stems in part from the fact that the overwhelming majority of the Strip’s population are refugees displaced from villages in what is now Israel, leading it to view the population as a persistent potential source of insurgency.
Israel’s then defence minister Moshe Dayan said in 1956, “Why should we blame [Palestinians in Gaza] for their burning hatred for us? For eight years they have been dwelling in Gaza’s refugee camps, as before their eyes we have transformed the land and the villages in which they and their forefathers had dwelled into our own property.”
7 October gave Israel its opening
The 7 October attacks provided a powerful accelerant for Israel’s longstanding displacement of Palestinians in Gaza.
Almost immediately, Netanyahu called on Gazans to leave, while his government ordered the mass evacuation of northern Gaza. The assault also revived an older Israeli conception of the conflict as an unfinished war of national survival, with Netanyahu later explicitly invoking the 1948 War of Independence, or Nakba.
In the first days of Israel’s response, Tel Aviv, with US help, rushed to pressure neighbouring Arab countries to transfer the entire population of Gaza into the Sinai desert under the pretext of “temporary relocation until Hamas is defeated.”
When those countries refused, Israel pushed most of Gaza’s population towards Rafah at the Egyptian border in the hope of pushing them to cross into Sinai on their own. When that failed, Israel invaded Rafah and devastated the city, only to propose sending Palestinians back towards the area again - this time into a so-called “humanitarian city” that Israel’s own former prime minister Ehud Olmert described as a concentration camp.
Even after Israel signed President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan for a ceasefire - which included Hamas’s disarmament, the withdrawal of Israeli troops, and reconstruction - Israel promptly reneged on its commitments and continued to push for building the Rafah ‘humanitarian city’.
The push to empty, and resettle, Gaza
Since the ceasefire began, Israel’s Defence Minister, Israel Katz, has repeatedly emphasised that Tel Aviv’s long-term goal in Gaza remains its total ethnic cleansing.
“There is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration… I think there is no other solution for everyone’s good,” he said in September, despite Hamas agreeing to lay down its arms. Katz added that Israel remains “organised and prepared to get [Gazans] out – by sea, by air, by every way possible.”
Israel’s Security Minister Ben-Gvir presented a concrete plan in September for the ethnic cleansing of 1.86 million Palestinians in Gaza over the next 7 years, called “disengagement 710.”
Through this scheme, Israel would expel 250,000 Gazans in the first year, 1.11 million by the third year, and the entire population by 2034. During the genocide, more than 100,000 Palestinians have already left Gaza.
That is why, even in the “new Rafah” camp, Israel made clear it would not allow any permanent construction with concrete, but rather would only give the caged population temporary and portable shipping containers to live in, making clear those camps are a mere transit towards expulsion.
The Israeli defence minister made clear that all Israel now needs to “finish the job” in Gaza is a pretext. “When it becomes clear that Hamas is not fulfilling its commitment. Then we will get a green light to advance militarily, territorially, and in other areas as well,” he said.
The same applies to the West Bank, where Katz revealed on Tuesday that the Israeli army has been instructed to plan for a scenario of war with the Palestinian Authority (PA). Despite the PA being Israel’s peace partner and security subcontractor, Katz made clear that Israel is ready to replicate its ‘Gaza model’ in the West Bank.
Any war on the PA “would be short and forceful and would include the use of ground and air forces and special means, the elimination and expulsion of senior officials, the destruction of weapons, and the large-scale evacuation of residents and destruction of terror infrastructure inside the cities and in all refugee camps,” Katz said, referencing the Gaza and Lebanon “models”.
Katz’s threat to the PA is not limited to an Israeli retaliation against violent Palestinian attacks on settlers or soldiers. A “war scenario” would also be unleashed if Palestinians organise a popular uprising.
“There will not be an Intifada lasting years, as there was in the past, but rather a short and forceful war with a clear decision and a change in the reality,” he emphasised.
A political consensus on Palestinian subjugation
The upcoming Israeli election is one of the most heated and competitive in the country’s history. But the one thing that unites the Israeli ruling coalition with most opposition parties is the subjugation of Palestinians.
In 2024, the Israeli Knesset saw an unprecedented moment of bipartisanship in rejecting Palestinian statehood and self-determination. In February of that year, 99 Israeli members of Knesset from both the opposition and ruling coalition voted in favour of a resolution rejecting international recognition of Palestinian statehood. Only nine members opposed the resolution, all of whom were from Palestinian parties.
In June, another resolution passed with only the same nine members opposing it. This time, the resolution rejected Palestinian statehood in absolute terms, even if such statehood comes through negotiations and diplomacy.
In this election cycle, Israel’s former prime minister and opposition leader Naftali Bennet is campaigning on calling the Trump plan for Gaza “unworkable” and opposing the plan’s promise of returning the Palestinian Authority to the enclave.
Israel’s former defence minister Avigdor Lieberman is similarly campaigning on dismantling the PA and resuming military operations in Gaza. Israel’s former war minister and likely the next prime minister Gadi Eisenkot attacked the roadmap for decommissioning Hamas’s weapons in return for the Israeli military’s withdrawal and called it a “capitulation” to Trump “without achieving the war’s objectives.”
The 7 October attacks did not create this Israeli mainstream consensus. At most, it provided the cover of war to make it more flagrant and explicit.
Israel’s stated long-term goal in Gaza and the West Bank is the natural culmination of a settler-colonial project that was created on the premise of grabbing the “maximum land with a minimal number of Arabs.”
Palestinians have for decades been pushed by Israel into ever-shrinking confines with two options left to them: submission or departure.
The only substantial debate about this endgame in Israel’s election is about the pace and packaging of that expulsion and subjugation.
Muhammad Shehada is a Palestinian writer and analyst from Gaza and the EU Affairs Manager at Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor
Follow him on Twitter: @muhammadshehad2
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: U.S. Navy moves bunker-busting Tomahawk toward production
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy plans a sole-source contract with Raytheon for low-rate initial production of the JMEWS warhead for the Tomahawk Block Vb.
- The notice moves the warhead from development into production but does not disclose contract value, quantity or delivery schedule.
The U.S. Navy plans to award Raytheon a sole-source contract for low-rate initial production of the Joint Multiple Effects Warhead System, a new warhead that lets the Tomahawk cruise missile strike bunkers and other hardened targets, according to a notice Naval Air Systems Command posted on October 7.
The contract would move the warhead program out of its engineering and manufacturing development phase and into production for the Tomahawk Block Vb variant. The notice did not give a contract value, the number of warheads to be built or a delivery schedule.
The Navy’s Tomahawk program office at Patuxent River, Maryland, said it intends to negotiate only with Raytheon in Tucson, Arizona, the RTX business that has been the sole developer, designer and manufacturer of the Tomahawk since 1994. The Navy said RTX alone holds the current configuration and manufacturing data for the missile and is the only known source able to do the work on schedule without duplicating costs.
The notice is not a request for competing bids. Other companies may submit capability statements by 4 p.m. EDT on October 22, which the Navy said it will consider. The Navy also noted that Tomahawk data is export controlled and not available to foreign sources.
The warhead, known as JMEWS, combines blast-fragmentation and penetration effects in a single two-stage design. It is meant to give the Tomahawk more options against hardened and heavily defended targets such as bunkers, underground facilities and missile sites, as well as against targets spread over a wide area. The Block IV Tomahawk it builds on carries a 1,000-pound-class unitary warhead.
Raytheon won a $90.4 million contract for the warhead’s engineering and manufacturing development phase, the final stage of development before production.
The Block Vb missile is one of two new variants in the Navy’s Block V modernization, which recertifies existing Block IV Tomahawks with upgraded navigation and communications and extends their service life. The Navy received its first Block V missile in March 2021. The other variant, the Block Va Maritime Strike Tomahawk, adds a seeker so the missile can hit moving ships at sea.
The Pentagon’s weapons testing office reported in its fiscal 2023 annual report that the Navy had conducted JMEWS arena tests and planned to complete the warhead’s live-fire test campaign in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, which ended in September. The office has not yet published an assessment of the warhead’s lethality.
In 2022, the Navy’s Tomahawk program manager, Capt. John Red, said the JMEWS variant was expected to reach initial operational capability in 2027.

articles.title: "Putin himself will sit down at the negotiating table": Zelenskyy urged the US to open Starlink for Ukraine
articles.body:
"Putin himself will sit down at the negotiating table": Zelenskyy urged the US to open Starlink for Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy urged the US to open Starlink for Ukraine and strengthen its air defense. He believes that the necessary capabilities already exist.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on the United States to help Ukraine protect its skies and provide the necessary Starlink capabilities. He said this in a comment to Ukrainian media, UNN reports.
Details
Open Starlink for Ukraine. You opened it when responding to Iran, didn’t you? Everything worked there. Israel had full control of the skies over Iran. So, when you need it, does it work?
Zelenskyy also said that China is nearing the creation of an alternative to Starlink, which it is providing to Russia.
I said frankly: give us [what we need], help us protect the skies and dominate there, and then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table
At the same time, the President of Ukraine expressed his conviction that the United States already has the necessary capabilities to provide such assistance.
We remind you
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that today and tomorrow, October 8 and 9, there will be "important negotiations" with partners, from which a "concrete result" is expected regarding the strengthening of Ukraine’s defenses.

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with 142 drones, more than half of them jet-powered — how many were shot down
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with 142 drones, more than half of them jet-powered — how many were shot down
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of October 8, Russia launched 142 drones at Ukraine, including 82 jet-powered Shaheds. Air defense shot down or suppressed 126 UAVs.
Russia attacked Ukraine with 142 drones during the night of October 8. A total of 126 of them were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia launched and from where
