According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 8 (from 18:00 on October 7), the enemy attacked with 142 Shahed-type attack UAVs (82 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones launched from the following directions: Oryol, Kursk, Shatalovo — Russia; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiiske.
How the air defense performed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 09:30, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 126 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types
Hits by enemy air-attack weapons were recorded at 7 locations, as well as the سقوط of downed aircraft (debris) at 4 locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several enemy UAVs in the airspace.

articles.title: 80% of Moldovans say country is unprepared for attack as Russian drones flow into its airspace, but few back NATO membership
articles.body:
More than 80% of Moldovans believe the country is not prepared to withstand external aggression, according to a CBS AXA poll presented ahead of the Moldova Security Forum 2026, NewsMaker reports.
The findings come as Moldova has faced a sharp increase in Russian drone incursions linked to Russia’s war against Ukraine. Moldova recorded 44 airspace-violation incidents in the first nine months of 2026, compared with 17 in all of 2025. Authorities have reported Russian drones crossing Moldovan airspace, while drone and missile debris has also fallen on Moldovan territory.
According to NewsMaker, more than 60% of those surveyed said Moldova is completely unprepared for a possible armed attack, while nearly 24% described its preparedness as weak.
Moldovans see country as unprepared for attack
The survey found that 82% of respondents also do not feel sufficiently informed or prepared to know what to do in a major crisis. According to CBS AXA Deputy Director Vasile Cantarji, respondents tend to trust specialized emergency institutions more than Moldova’s main state institutions.
More than half said they trust Moldova’s General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations, while 35% expressed trust in the church. Trust in the government, parliament, and courts was much lower, at roughly 4–6%.
The findings come as Moldova faces a security environment shaped by Russia’s war against Ukraine, hybrid threats, energy dependence, and disinformation. Moldova’s government has supported Ukraine and strengthened security cooperation with European partners, while repeatedly condemning Russia’s war and its spillover effects.
The repeated drone incursions are now increasingly exposing Moldova to risks from the war next door.
Three Russian missiles and two drones strike Moldovan territory in morning attacks on neighboring Ukraine. Moldova is increasingly exposed to the risks of Russia’s war next door
Most favor neutrality over NATO membership
Despite the widespread perception that Moldova is poorly prepared for external aggression, only about 4% of respondents said joining NATO would be the right way to make the country safer.
Around 45% instead favored maintaining Moldova’s neutrality. At the same time, six in 10 respondents said Moldova needs continued external support to strengthen its security and defense.
Nearly two-thirds considered cooperation with the European Union and Romania important for Moldova’s development.
Moldova’s constitution establishes permanent neutrality, while the country has been deepening security and defense cooperation with European partners.
EU seen as preferred source of emergency assistance
The poll also asked whom Moldova should turn to for help during a major disaster such as an earthquake or flood.
About 33% selected EU countries, followed by Russia at roughly 16% and Romania at 15%. The CIS, NATO, UN, and Ukraine each received support from 4% or fewer respondents.
War in Ukraine is one of several security concerns
Respondents identified a range of threats to Moldova’s security, with internal problems ranking alongside external risks.
Corruption was cited by more than 15% of respondents, while poverty was named by 13.5%. Just over 13.5% identified the war in Ukraine as a security risk. Energy dependence and disinformation were each cited by nearly 10%.
Other concerns included economic instability, crime, and external aggression.
CBS AXA conducted the survey from August 25 to September 9 among 2,009 Moldovans aged 18 and older. The reported margin of error is 2.2%. NewsMaker published the findings on October 7.
Moldova strengthens protection at Ukrainian border
Moldovan authorities are now responding to the Russian drone threat by creating protected areas at border crossings with Ukraine where border guards, officials, and civilians can shelter during potential drone attacks, Interior Minister Daniela Misail-Nikitin said on October 7, according to NewsMaker.
Authorities are also moving Moldovan personnel from joint checkpoints located on Ukrainian territory back to Moldova. The measures follow an incident at the Palanca–Maiaki–Udobne crossing in which a Moldovan border guard was injured by a falling projectile.
Transnistria adds another security challenge
Moldova also faces a longstanding security problem in Transnistria, a breakaway region along the country’s eastern border with Ukraine. The region declared independence from Moldova in 1990 and has remained outside Chisinau’s control since a brief war in 1992.
Transnistria is not internationally recognized as an independent state. Russia maintains a significant troop presence there and has long supported the separatist authorities, making the region a persistent source of tension between Chisinau and Moscow.

articles.title: Gaza 3 years on: The unfinished fight for Palestinian workers
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Gaza 3 years on: The unfinished fight for Palestinian workers
Three years after Israel began its genocide in Gaza, the fate of Palestinian workers detained after 7 October remains unclear, though their odyssey of humiliation, torture, and, on occasion, murder is beyond doubt and is mostly documented by their Israeli tormentors on social media and aired live by the far-right Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Gazans who had crossed the Green Line desperate to earn a living, mostly in blue-collar jobs, were stripped of their permits, rounded up, and held without contact with lawyers or families. Their treatment should push one to wonder what international trade unions did when fellow workers in this part of the world were imprisoned and abused.
Israel closed the crossings and revoked Gazan workers’ permits, turning people previously authorised to work into supposed illegal residents. Thousands were detained in Israel and the occupied West Bank. On 3 November 2023, more than 3,000 were released into Gaza, where bombardment continued. Release offered no guarantee of safety.
Workers described, in testimonies published by Human Rights Watch in January 2024, beatings, electric shocks, humiliation, and deprivation of food and water. The rights watchdog also independently documented mass detention without contact with the outside world.
International allies
Warnings of the ongoing abuse were already coming out earlier. On 11 October 2023, the Palestinian Democracy and Workers’ Rights Centre denounced violence against Gazan workers. On 25 October, it demanded their immediate release and appealed to the international labour movement. The workers’ predicament was already being placed before their supposed international allies.
Their case cuts through the claim that Palestine is somehow outside a union’s remit. These Gazan workers had employers, wages, and families dependent on their earnings. Stripped of work permits, thrown in torture dungeons for weeks, should have triggered a global public outcry among trade unionists and industrial organisers everywhere.
Calling the subsequent response universal silence would be inaccurate. The International Trade Union Confederation’s 2024 Global Rights Index described thousands of workers held in illegal detention, denied basic rights and legal representation. It recorded reports of abuse and degrading conditions, alongside two deaths in custody. The world’s principal union confederation had publicly acknowledged the violations.
Australia’s Union Aid Abroad–APHEDA published Palestinian union allegations of torture deaths in January 2024. In March 2025, the International Labour Network of Solidarity and Struggle endorsed reports from the Arab Workers Union in Nazareth concerning disappeared Gazan workers, torture and deaths in detention. These were clear acts of solidarity, but circulating allegations is only the beginning.
On 27 September 2024, nine global unions filed a complaint with the International Labour Organisation detailing the draconian working conditions of more than 200,000 Palestinian workers in Israel. The nine organisations condemned “widespread wage theft due to the suspension of work permits and the unilateral termination of their contracts.”
Signatories included the ITUC, IndustriALL, Education International, Public Services International, UNI, and the international federations representing transport, construction, food workers and journalists. The OECD’s Trade Union Advisory Committee also joined. Its stated legal focus was wage protection; however, not accountability for torture.
The demands of Palestinian unions
While such a solidarity move is worth applauding, it still exposes a long-running problem of “economism” that has long marred the trade union movement.
What resources went toward locating missing workers, supporting survivors, securing independent investigations and pursuing those responsible? A complaint about stolen wages surely matters enormously to impoverished families. It cannot substitute for a “political” campaign against imprisonment, torture, military occupation and genocide.
Palestinian unions had also identified what their counterparts could do. Their 16 October 2023 appeal asked workers to refuse to manufacture or transport weapons for Israel, challenge complicit companies and pressure governments to stop military trade. This was an action plan for international unions. Were the latter ready to organise around those demands and protect members prepared to act?
The wider response to Gaza shows that stronger positions were possible. The World Federation of Trade Unions was calling for an end to genocide by October 2023. IndustriALL’s executive committee explicitly condemned the continuing genocide in May 2024 and urged affiliates to support boycott, divestment, and sanctions.
Education International’s 2024 congress demanded an end to arms transfers to Israel. These were formal positions of international organisations, not merely statements by dissident branches.
Other unions organised material support. In November 2023, the International Transport Workers’ Federation created a Palestine Solidarity Fund. Public Services International established its Gaza fund in March 2024. By August 2025, European Union federations were demanding sanctions, suspension of the EU–Israel Association Agreement, and an end to economic relations with Israeli settlements.
Influential national unions in several countries also took a firm position in solidarity with the Palestinians, sometimes aligning with their governments’ stated positions and sometimes opposing them.
South Africa’s teachers’ union SADTU explicitly condemned genocide in 2023. Ireland’s ICTU demanded economic sanctions, while Britain’s TUC called for ending arms licenses and suspending the trade agreement. Canada’s CUPE described the assault as genocide and supported Palestinian workers’ rights organising.
In July 2024, seven US unions demanded an immediate halt to military aid: UAW, UE, SEIU, the postal workers’ APWU, flight attendants’ AFA, painters’ IUPAT and National Education Association. Their demand confronted the material support sustaining Israel’s assault, even if a letter alone could not stop it.
Disrupting the deadly occupation machine
Workplace action offered another, certainly more effective, route. A trade union representing workers in 11 major Indian ports refused to handle weapons shipments for Israel. France’s CGT endorsed workers at Fos and Roissy who refused to facilitate arms deliveries. Such examples show where unions’ distinctive power lies: in their capacity to interrupt production and transport.
Italian unions took action to another level by organising a general strike explicitly in solidarity with Gaza. On 22 September 2025, USB and other grassroots unions organised a nationwide stoppage against the genocide, disrupting transport, schools and ports.
Following Israel’s interception of the Global Sumud Flotilla, CGIL and USB called another general strike on 3 October. According to CGIL, the stoppage disrupted major services, and more than two million people rallied across over 100 cities.
Such organising efforts developed across borders. Italy’s USB, Greece’s ENEDEP, the Basque union LAB, Turkey’s Liman-İş and Morocco’s ODT called a joint ports action for 6 February 2026, demanding an end to arms shipments feeding the genocide and a trade embargo on Israel. Their initiative connected solidarity with opposition to militarisation and the erosion of dockworkers’ conditions.
But other union leaders shamefully obstructed solidarity. In October 2023, the AFL-CIO intervened against a ceasefire resolution adopted by Washington state’s Thurston-Lewis-Mason labour council. The federation eventually, under pressure, called for a negotiated ceasefire on 8 February 2024.
Germany’s DGB declared solidarity with Israel after the Hamas attacks. Its position cannot fairly be reduced to unconditional approval of everything Israel subsequently did: a July 2025 resolution demanded an end to attacks on civilians and supported a ceasefire. Yet the same resolution sharply defended Histadrut against criticism within international union bodies.
The Histadrut, for its part, is hardly an ordinary “trade union.” It has been the backbone of the settler colonisation of Palestine from the start, and a major instrument of segregation and discrimination against Arab workers. The international labour movement should isolate, boycott, and deplatform it.
Union members everywhere need to hold their own leaders accountable for these decisions. Those who blocked solidarity or defended Israel’s actions should face a challenge from below, with their record on Gaza brought into branch meetings, congress debates, and leadership elections. Members can demand disclosure of their unions’ ties to Histadrut and organise to sever them.
The fight is far from over. Missing workers must be accounted for, survivors supported, stolen wages recovered, and those responsible for torture and deaths held accountable. These demands belong alongside the struggle to end the occupation and dismantle the structures that leave Palestinian workers dependent on those who dispossess and exploit them.
The strikes and port actions point toward what comes next: sustained organising to stop arms shipments, challenge complicit employers, and defend workers who face retaliation for taking action. Every solidarity resolution needs an organising plan behind it. Palestinian workers deserve a labour movement prepared to use its power, and a rank and file ready to act when its leaders refuse.
Hossam el-Hamalawy is an Egyptian scholar-activist in Germany, focusing on the military, policing, and labour.
Follow Hossam on X: @3arabawy
Have questions or comments? Email us at editorial-english@newarab.com
Opinions expressed in this article remain those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of The New Arab.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia strikes back after deadly Houthi attacks on Riyadh and airports
articles.body:
Explosions heard in Saudi capital Riyadh after Houthis' deadly attacks on airports
Several explosions were reported on Thursday in Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh amid ongoing fighting between the kingdom and Yemen's Houthis. A day earlier, three people were killed and 36 wounded in attacks on Abha and Riyadh’s King Khalid international airports claimed by the Iran-backed rebel group.
Several explosions echoed across the Saudi capital Riyadh on Thursday, AFP journalists heard, during the war between the kingdom and Houthi fighters in Yemen.
The Iran-backed group has claimed repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent days.
On Wednesday, Saudi authorities said that three people were killed in attacks on two of the kingdom's international airports, including in the capital Riyadh, after Yemen's Houthis claimed to have fired on both transport hubs.
Read moreHouthis claim attacks on Riyadh airport as Saudi-led forces strike Yemen
The Iran-backed fighters earlier took responsibility for a flurry of attacks that included firing a ballistic missile at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport as the conflict deepens with Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government.
"On Tuesday and Wednesday... Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport were subjected to attacks targeting their facilities," the kingdom's civil aviation authority said in a statement.
An Egyptian and an Algerian national were killed at Abha airport and a Sudanese national was killed at the airport in Riyadh, the agency said, with 36 people wounded in the attacks.
The Saudi-led military coalition that backs pro-government forces in Yemen said on X that it "destroyed the ballistic missile launch platform" used in the attack on Riyadh.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
In a subsequent statement, the coalition directly blamed Houthi forces and said it would retaliate.
"The brutal attacks by the Terrorist Houthi Militia on civilian and civilian objects in the Kingdom, most recently targeting (the two airports) will not go unpunished," it said on X.
The coalition said as a result it struck and destroyed 82 "legitimate military targets", including Houthi mountain-based ballistic missile facilities, command-and-control centres, communication systems and Houthi gathering sites.
The Yemeni group, which controls most of the country's northwest, is battling for territory against the Saudi-backed forces after the civil war reignited in July and it captured swaths of coastal land.
The fighting has displaced more than 200,000 people within the country, the United Nations said Wednesday.
Yemen's internationally recognised government this week declared a major counter-offensive and claims to have pushed Houthi fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha.
Read moreYemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels seize strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha
But the Iran-backed Houthis say they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
Flight diverted
"Our armed forces have just targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile. The strike was accurate, by God's grace, and led to a disruption of air traffic," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Wednesday on X.
The Saudi-led coalition said the missile was intercepted.
The Houthis also said they targeted a military supply convoy near the airport in Aden, the interim capital for Yemen's government.
The government's Saba news agency reported missiles and drones targeting that airport.
The agency cited transport authorities as saying one of the missiles landed near the runway minutes before the scheduled arrival of a flight from Cairo, which was forced to divert to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia.
Houthi drones and missiles also targeted Saudi Arabia's Abha airport and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, spokesman Saree said, claiming they had "hit their targets accurately".
It is the second time this week Houthis claimed to have attacked Riyadh's main airport.
Read moreYemen's government declares counter-offensive as Houthis cut vital route to besieged city
'Terrified'
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition fighting the Houthis since 2015, and is now trying to roll back the group's latest advance.
The coalition said Monday it was providing air support for the Yemeni government's counter-offensive.
After a four-year ceasefire, Yemen's civil war re-erupted in July. Last month the Houthis seized the entire western coastline along the Red Sea in the country's deadliest fighting in years.
New clashes Wednesday in Yemen's west left at least 62 combatants dead, including 37 Houthis, military sources from both camps told AFP.
Saba also reported the Houthis fired a missile at Taiz, a city held by government forces, wounding five civilians.
Read moreYemen's government declares counter-offensive as Houthis cut vital route to besieged city
"We went out into the street to check on the wounded and saw young civilians who had been hit. The Houthi shell landed in the middle of the street, right in an area crowded with civilians," resident Al-Fateh al-Eisaei told AFP.
Yemen's government has announced a goal of retaking all Houthi territory – home to most of the country's population, and much of it held for more than a decade.
The humanitarian crisis caused by the war has left most of the nation's population dependent on aid.
Mohammed, a 33-year-old charity worker who fled from Mocha to Aden, told AFP on Tuesday that "people there are terrified" of the Houthis.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
Keywords for this article

articles.title: Three Killed as Houthis Target Saudi Airports With Missiles
articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthi rebels claimed Thursday that they had hit Saudi Arabia’s main international airport in Riyadh with a missile, while Saudi authorities said three people were killed and 36 wounded in attacks on two international airports.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on X that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile and disrupted airport operations.
“Our armed forces successfully targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile, which accurately struck its target and disrupted airport operations,” Saree said.
The Houthis said the Riyadh airport strike killed three people and injured several others, and claimed it was the third time this week they had targeted the airport.
Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said attacks on Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport took place on Tuesday and Wednesday, targeting facilities at both airports.
An Egyptian and an Algerian national were killed at Abha airport, while a Sudanese national died at the Riyadh airport, the authority said. A total of 36 people were wounded.
The Saudi-led military coalition supporting pro-government forces in Yemen said on X that it had destroyed the ballistic missile launch platform used in the attack on Riyadh.
The coalition later directly blamed Houthi forces and said it would retaliate.
“The brutal attacks by the Terrorist Houthi Militia on civilian and civilian objects in the Kingdom, most recently targeting (the two airports) will not go unpunished,” the coalition said on X.
The coalition said it had subsequently destroyed 82 “legitimate military targets,” including mountain-based Houthi ballistic missile facilities, command-and-control centers, communication systems and gathering sites.
The conflict in Yemen has increasingly spread beyond the country’s borders since fighting resumed in July.
Saudi Arabia has backed Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which announced a major counteroffensive against the Houthis a day earlier as it seeks to retake additional territory.
The Houthis, who control most of northwestern Yemen, are fighting Saudi-backed forces after the civil war reignited in July, when the group captured large areas of the coastline.
The United Nations said Wednesday that more than 200,000 people have been displaced within Yemen.
This week, the Yemeni government said its forces had driven Houthi fighters from strategic positions along the Red Sea coast and around the port city of Mocha. The Iran-backed Houthis, however, said they were holding their territory, while military sources from both sides contacted by AFP reported no major changes on the ground.
The warring parties’ claims could not be independently verified because the situation is changing rapidly and journalists face difficult access.
The Saudi-led coalition said the missile fired at Riyadh had been intercepted, while the Houthis also claimed to have targeted a military supply convoy near Aden, the interim capital of Yemen’s government.
The government’s Saba news agency reported that missiles and drones had targeted the airport in Aden. Citing transport authorities, it said one missile landed near the runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to arrive, forcing the aircraft to divert to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia.
Saree also said Houthi drones and missiles had targeted Abha airport and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, claiming they had “hit their targets accurately”.
The Houthis also warned passenger airlines against using Saudi airspace.
“We reiterate our call and warning, for the last time, to all international airlines against continuing to operate flights through Saudi airspace,” Saree said.
The Houthis had claimed a second attack on Riyadh’s main airport earlier in the week.
Saudi Arabia has led an international coalition against the Houthis since 2015 and is now supporting the Yemeni government’s effort to reverse the group’s latest advance.
The coalition said Monday that it was providing air support for the government’s counteroffensive.
After a four-year ceasefire, Yemen’s civil war resumed in July. The Houthis seized the entire western coastline along the Red Sea last month in the deadliest fighting the country had seen in years.
New fighting in western Yemen on Wednesday killed at least 62 combatants, including 37 Houthis, according to military sources from both sides who spoke to AFP.
Saba also reported that the Houthis fired a missile at Taiz, a city controlled by government forces, injuring five civilians.
“We went out into the street to check on the wounded and saw young civilians who had been hit. The Houthi shell landed in the middle of the street, right in an area crowded with civilians,” resident Al-Fateh al-Eisaei told AFP.
Yemen’s government has said it aims to retake all territory held by the Houthis, much of which has been under the group’s control for more than a decade and is home to most of the country’s population.
The war has created a humanitarian crisis that has left most of Yemen’s population dependent on aid.
Mohammed, a 33-year-old charity worker who fled Mocha for Aden, told AFP Tuesday that “people there are terrified” of the Houthis.

articles.title: Trump promises not to attack Iran before November’s US midterms
articles.body:
Donald Trump has promised not to attack Iran before November’s US midterm elections, outlining a pause on the protracted war he has struggled to end after almost eight months.
In a Truth Social post on Thursday, the US president said Washington was “having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran”, which he claimed was “in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily”.
The strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passed through before the war, was all but closed after the US and Israel struck Iran in late February.
On Thursday, however, Trump suggested that oil was moving through the strait in record volumes: “22 Million Barrels, last night alone”, he claimed, “with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran”. The figure could not be independently verified.
“We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump wrote. “IRAN WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!”
The US first imposed a blockade on the strait of Hormuz in April after talks in Islamabad collapsed, and reinstated it in July after a short-lived June deal to end the fighting. Fighting flared again in early September, when US forces struck rocket launchers on Iran’s Larak Island and Tehran responded with missiles aimed at American military bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates.
Trump’s public position on the elections has shifted over the past month. On 2 September, as the US exchanged fire with Iran for the first time in weeks, he told reporters he was “not affected by the election”, adding that he was not on the ballot himself but intended to help his party.
A week later, before heading to the Republican “midterm convention” in Dallas, he said he expected the war to end almost as soon as the voting was over, and accused Tehran of holding out in the hope that a change of power in Congress would leave it free to pursue a nuclear weapon. He also conceded that US oil prices were unlikely to fall before polling day.
A Reuters/Ipsos survey from late September found that only about a third of Americans approved of the strikes on Iran, while more than four in five expected the conflict to last for an extended period, and that approval for Trump among Republicans had fallen from 82% to 73% in a week.
Polling averages now show Democrats leading Republicans by roughly nine points on the generic congressional ballot, according to forecaster Nate Silver, the widest margin of this election cycle.
The Wall Street Journal reported in September that JD Vance, the US vice-president, and secretary of state Marco Rubio had privately warned Trump the conflict could extend through the remainder of his presidency.
Trump’s post did not say what the US would do after 3 November.

articles.title: Two 14-year-old boys killed by an explosive device in a field in Sumy Oblast
articles.body:
Two 14-year-old boys were killed when an explosive device detonated in the evening in the Konotop district of Sumy Oblast, according to the statement by Oleh Hryhorov, head of the Sumy Regional Military Administration. The children encountered the dangerous device in a field, suffered severe injuries, and died at the scene, the statement said.
In 2022, Russian forces occupied parts of Sumy Oblast, but Ukraine liberated the region in April. Russia intensified its offensive again in 2025. Today, mines, unexploded ordnance and Russian drones shot down over the region pose a danger, as their warheads can detonate after falling. Overall, 146 children in Ukraine have suffered mine-related injuries, former Interior Minister Ihor Klymenko reported in April. For example, two months ago, an 11-year-old boy and a 15-year-old boy in Sumy Oblast were injured when an explosive device detonated.
Hryhorov expressed his condolences to the parents and relatives of the victims and urged people to remain cautious:
“Please be as careful as possible and remind children: do not approach unknown or suspicious objects, touch them, or try to move them. Take care of yourselves and your loved ones,” Hryhorov said.
Demining efforts continue in Sumy Oblast
On 24 February 2022, Russian forces entered the territory of Sumy Oblast. The first battles in the region took place that same day. In particular, Russian forces attempted to break through to Sumy, but Ukrainian troops repelled the offensive. On 11 April 2022, Ukraine restored control over the entire Sumy region.
As early as 7 June 2022, deminers were working in the Konotop, Sumy, and Okhtyrka districts, according to the Government Portal. That day, they surveyed areas and neutralized explosive devices.
The work of deminers remains deadly dangerous. In September 2024, two pyrotechnicians from Dnipropetrovsk Oblast were hit by a mine while demining Sumy Oblast: one died, while the other was hospitalized. In July 2025, deminer Oleh Petrenko was killed during humanitarian demining operations in Shostka District when a Russian FPV drone detonated, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine reported. Another pyrotechnician was injured, the statement said.
Nevertheless, the work continues despite the danger. In 2025, State Emergency Service deminers in the Sumy Oblast found and neutralized 5,283 explosive devices, the agency said in April. Sumy Oblast ranked sixth among all Ukrainian regions by this figure.
Twenty-two percent of Ukraine’s territory is potentially contaminated with explosive devices — more than 133,000 square kilometers, former Interior Minister Ihor Klymenko reported in April this year. Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, State Emergency Service and National Police deminers have surveyed more than 248,000 hectares of territory and found more than 1 million 112 thousand explosive devices, the statement said.

articles.title: Blackouts return to Kyiv as Russia prepares to freeze civilians over the winter
articles.body:
Power outages have returned to Kyiv after Russian attacks damaged the energy infrastructure supplying the capital, with authorities warning that the situation could worsen as Russia intensifies its campaign against Ukraine’s energy system ahead of winter.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine’s power, heating, and other critical infrastructure to disrupt the systems civilians depend on and create a humanitarian crisis during winter. Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned that this winter will be especially severe, as Russia has expanded its strike capabilities since the summer and Ukraine continues to face shortages of air-defense systems needed to protect its energy infrastructure.
Ukrenergo said on 8 October that emergency outages were being imposed in parts of Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast because of falling voltage in the high-voltage network. Previously announced hourly schedules were suspended, with predictable schedules to resume once the system stabilizes.
In the evening, further disruption came after a Russian attack on an energy facility important to Kyiv. Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said that energy workers were working to restore power.
Kyiv has been under Russian attack throughout the day, with four people killed and 19 injured.
The attack continues into the evening of 8 October, with air raid alerts active across most of the country.
Kyiv loses power, water, and public transport
The damage throughout the day quickly spread beyond electricity.
The Kyiv City Military Administration said power disruptions temporarily halted metro trains and escalators. Part of the capital’s public transport system was also suspended because of the lack of electricity.
Reduced power to water infrastructure caused lower pressure on the right bank of the Dnipro, particularly in the Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomianskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi districts. Some buildings could temporarily lose water, the administration warned.
Russia is hitting the energy system as winter approaches
The outages come as Russia has stepped up attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of the heating season.
Ukrenergo said Russian attacks had caused new power outages in Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. The company said damaged equipment was already limiting the grid’s ability to supply consumers and warned that further Russian strikes could rapidly change the situation.
For 9 October, Ukrenergo announced all-day power restrictions in affected regions, including hourly outages for some consumers. Industrial and business consumers will also face restrictions. The company urged Ukrainians to conserve electricity, particularly during the evening peak from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m.
Ukraine’s energy authorities have been warning about the consequences of repeated Russian attacks for months. In late September, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said attacks on energy facilities had been occurring almost daily since the summer, with the September 29–30 attack marking the first massive combined strike on the energy system since the previous heating season.
The renewed strikes mark the beginning of Russia’s winter campaign against the energy system, with Russian missiles and drones increasingly targeting power-generation and transmission infrastructure in Kyiv and surrounding regions.
Russia has openly threatened another winter of blackouts
The campaign follows years of Russian attacks aimed at disrupting the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainian homes heated and supplied with electricity and water during the winter.
In August, Russia’s Defense Ministry openly taunted Ukrainians over its attacks on energy-related infrastructure, posting images of attack drones with the message that Ukrainians would “get a freeze” in winter.
Russia’s strategy has repeatedly linked attacks on electricity infrastructure to disruptions in heating and water supplies. This makes damage to the power grid particularly consequential as temperatures fall: a strike on an electrical facility can leave not only homes without lights, but also affect water pumps, heating systems, transportation, and other essential services.
The return of blackouts to Kyiv before the heating season is fully underway is an early indication of the pressure Russia’s renewed energy campaign is putting on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure.

articles.title: US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet
The US imposed fresh sanctions on Iran on Thursday, targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels for transporting Iranian crude, oil products and petrochemicals, the Treasury Department said, as Washington stepped up economic pressure on Tehran.
The sanctions are part of the department's "Operation Economic Outcast," which aims to cut Iran's funding for the war with the US, missile construction, cyberattacks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC.
"Today's action represents the most significant blow yet to Iran's remaining illicit maritime infrastructure by neutralizing the vast majority of the shadow fleet," a Treasury official told reporters on a call. "Treasury is cutting off the regime's last major source of illicit revenue and strengthening international pressure to hold Tehran accountable."
The move tightens the squeeze on Iranian oil sales after the US reimposed its blockade of Iranian ports on 14 July following the breakdown of a memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington to end the war.
Iran has only about 20 million barrels of crude oil left on vessels outside the blockade, off Singapore, Malaysia and China, the Treasury official said. The world uses about 100 million barrels of oil per day.
A second Treasury official said Iran has stopped loading and offloading crude oil vessels due to the blockade and sanctions.
President Donald Trump said on social media on Thursday that the US is having "productive discussions" with Iran over the war that began on February 28. Trump said the US will not attack Iran before the midterm elections on November 3.
An analyst said the fact that the US is sanctioning vessels after Iran has delivered virtually all of its oil at sea means the impact will be muted.
"This is economic warfare conducted in the rearview mirror, designed to generate headlines rather than results," said Brett Erickson, a managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors.
Vessels targeted by the US sanctions include the Comoros-flagged Paritosh, the Panama-flagged Bitu and the Bahamas-flagged Gas Lucky.
(Reuters)

articles.title: Callous Kallas: The bitter diplomat dragging the EU down the warpath with Russia
articles.body:
Callous Kallas: The bitter diplomat dragging the EU down the warpath with Russia
Kaja Kallas, the Estonian diplomat and former prime minister currently serving as the vice-president of the European Commission, has shown a deeply confrontational attitude towards Russia and the Russians.
It is perhaps worth pausing here to note that this is particularly personal, given her family history. Her mother, Kristi Kallas, was only six months old when she, together with her mother and grandmother, was deported to Siberia during the Soviet mass deportations of March 1949. She remained there until she was ten, and later studied medicine and worked as a pediatrician.
Her father, Siim Kallas, had a very different experience with the Soviet system. He was a member of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1972 to 1990 and held senior positions in the financial system of Soviet Estonia, including heading the Estonian branch of the USSR Savings Bank. He later became President of the Bank of Estonia, Prime Minister of Estonia and a Vice-President of the European Commission.
These two sides of her family history – one marked by deportation and the other by a successful career within the Soviet system – form a striking background to Kaja Kallas’s present-day political position.
Last month, Kallas described the German people as being blind to the Russian threat because of their resistance to providing further financial support to Ukraine. Now, I suppose Russian people are also considered blind because of the convincing victory of President Vladimir Putin’s party in September’s legislative election. I am definitely not blind.
Kaja Kallas is not alone in her hostility towards Russia. Other senior EU officials, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, have supported substantial financial and military assistance to Ukraine. The EU has committed up to €90 billion in support for Ukraine for 2026 and 2027, including funding for both defense and general budgetary needs.
The question Europeans should be allowed to ask is how these decisions affect their own societies. Public money is limited, and European citizens also need investment in healthcare, education, transport, housing and infrastructure.
Since 2022, Europeans have been paying a heavy price for the transformation of their energy system. The decision to move away from Russian pipeline gas was made in the name of security, and the EU has succeeded in diversifying its supplies. But security has come at a considerable economic cost. The European Commission reports that although wholesale energy prices have fallen substantially from the extraordinary peaks of 2022, industrial gas and electricity prices remain two to four times higher than in the EU’s main trading partners. The Commission warns that this continues to threaten the long-term competitiveness of European industry.
The EU’s energy import bill reached €604 billion in 2022 before falling to €427 billion in 2024. Meanwhile, industrial energy prices remain considerably above their pre-crisis levels. Germany, the industrial heart of Europe, has felt the consequences particularly sharply. German industrial energy consumption fell by 9.1% in 2022 and another 7.8% in 2023, with the German Federal Statistical Office explicitly linking these declines, particularly in energy-intensive industries, to significantly higher energy prices and associated production reductions.
Germany’s broader economic performance tells the same story. Its economy contracted for a second consecutive year in 2024, while manufacturing gross value added fell by 3%. The Federal Statistical Office identified high energy costs, together with stronger international competition and other structural pressures, among the factors weighing on the economy. Manufacturing remained under pressure in 2025, when value added in the sector fell another 1.3%.
Europe faces an uncomfortable question: Is it prepared to accept permanently higher energy costs while production and investment increasingly move towards countries where energy and manufacturing costs are lower? It is one thing to pursue energy security; it is another to allow the foundations of European industry to become the price of achieving it.
The issue of NATO and Ukraine is equally contentious. The argument that NATO expansion towards Ukraine ruined Moscow’s relations with Europe is not just a Kremlin talking point – reputable Western analysts, like Professor Jeffrey Sachs, have repeatedly argued the same point. Even if that analysis remains disputed, it is an argument that deserves to be heard in any serious discussion of the origins and continuation of the war, which continues to have devastating consequences for Ukrainians.
European leaders should be asking what policies can bring the conflict closer to a negotiated settlement rather than simply allowing the confrontation to continue indefinitely.
Perhaps the most revealing part of this story is that the argument is no longer simply between the EU and its critics. It has begun to unfold within Europe itself.
Defense spending in the EU is rising at an extraordinary pace. According to the Council of the EU, member states spent €418 billion on defense in 2025, and expenditure is estimated to reach €454 billion in 2026 – 75.3% higher than in 2021. Defense investment alone is projected to reach almost €163 billion in 2026.
But the question of who decides how this enormous effort should be organized is becoming increasingly contentious. In September, Kaja Kallas withdrew plans for a new high-level advisory group on European defense after several member states objected. Reporting by Defense News and Euractiv identified Germany, France and Italy among the governments pushing back against the initiative. The German position was that NATO remains the primary framework for military capability and defense planning.
The disagreement was not about whether Europe needs defense. It was about who should set priorities, how decisions should be coordinated, and whether another Brussels structure was the right way forward. Even as European governments prepare to spend hundreds of billions more on defense, there is no agreement about the political direction those resources should serve.
The EU, in other words, is having two conversations at once: how much it should spend, and what kind of Europe that spending is meant to create.
Ms. Kallas, Europe needs diplomacy as well as security policy. European citizens need their governments to protect their interests, use public money responsibly and keep open the possibility of a peaceful future.
If the EU continues indefinitely along the present path, the economic and political consequences for European societies will deserve much greater public discussion.
EU citizens have the right to ask difficult questions about how their money is being spent and what kind of Europe they want to build. They may disagree strongly about Russia, Ukraine and NATO, but that does not make their questions illegitimate.
I was born in Ireland and have been affiliated with Russia for thirty years. I have been living here for the last eight years. From that perspective, I believe Europeans should be able to discuss these issues without being dismissed as blind, naïve or sympathetic to one side simply because they question current policies.
Europe has enormous resources and enormous human potential. With wiser choices about priorities, Europeans should be able to expect excellent healthcare, education, transport and infrastructure alongside a responsible security policy.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: Syria denies troops will be sent to Yemen
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Syria denies troops will be sent to Yemen, while expressing support for Saudi Arabia
The Syrian Ministry of Defence has denied that any Syrian forces will take part in fighting Yemen, following reports that Damascus was considering providing military assistance to Saudi Arabia in its war against the Iran-backed Houthi group in Yemen.
A Syrian Defence Ministry source told The New Arab on Wednesday evening that “there is currently no movement of Syrian forces toward Yemen.” 
This was the first statement from the Syrian government following speculation that Damascus might participate in military operations alongside Saudi Arabia.
The source suggested that a discussion on the matter may have taken place between US President Donald Trump and President Ahmad al-Sharaa during the latter’s visit to the United States in September for the UN General Assembly.
The Foreign Media Department at Syria’s Ministry of Information also responded to what it described as “claims that Syria is joining the war in Yemen,” saying that Damascus’s position is “clear.” 
It said that Syria’s support for Saudi Arabia in confronting threats to its security and stability but also added that Syria’s regional policy is “based on stability, peace, and cooperation, not on opening new fronts”.
It stressed that “any military cooperation with partner countries will take place only through official channels and existing bilateral frameworks.”
On Tuesday, Syrian President Ahmed Al-Sharaa visited Saudi Arabia amid intense fighting in Yemen between Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, fuelling speculation about a possible Syrian role in Yemen.
He met with Saudi Crown Prince and de facto leader Mohammed bin Salman and footage broadcast by Syrian media showed Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman accompanying the Syrian president to his aircraft as he departed.
Axios, citing three US officials, reported that Saudi Arabia and Syria were discussing sending Syrian troops to Yemen to participate in the war against the Houthis. The report said the Sharaa was seriously considering the proposal but had not yet made a final decision.
There were also reports that Saudi Arabia wants to reinforce Yemeni government forces, who are internally divided and are considered less well trained than the Houthis.
A source told Axios that Syria could send between 10,000 and 20,000 troops to Yemen. 
There are reports that Saudi Arabia considers Syrian troops better trained and more experienced using Turkish drones than Yemeni government forces.
A Syrian diplomat said that while Damascus strongly supports Saudi Arabia in confronting Houthi attacks, its focus is on domestic priorities, especially recovery from Syria’s brutal 13-year civil war.
“If Saudi Arabia requests any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, it will take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries,” the diplomat said.
Reuters reported that US officials were worried about a sectarian dimension to possible Syrian intervention in Yemen, and that Syria had previously rejected a US request to help fight Hezbollah in Lebanon for this reason.

articles.title: Russian Bombing Forces Tuaregs to Retreat from Kidal, Mali
articles.body:
The Azawad Liberation Front (ALF) announced the forced withdrawal of its forces from the city of Kidal in northern Mali.
The group’s spokesperson, Mohamed Elmaouloud Ramadane, announced the withdrawal in an official statement.
The decision was made following massive airstrikes by the ruling military junta and mercenaries from Russia’s Africa Corps, which destroyed most of the civilian infrastructure.
The Tuareg command stated that leaving the settlement was a temporary measure aimed at preserving its personnel and logistics.
The city of Kidal has been a key political and military center of the Tuareg movement since the start of the 2012 rebellion for Azawad’s independence, when rebels first drove the Malian army out of the city.
In 2013, as part of Operation Serval, French troops and a Chadian contingent entered the city, driving out radical groups and handing control to moderate Tuareg forces.
In May 2014, an attempt by the Malian army to storm Kidal ended in defeat, after which the city remained under the full control of the Tuareg alliance for years.
From 2015 to 2022, the status quo in the city remained largely unchanged: the UN’s MINUSMA mission was deployed there, while de facto control was exercised by local Tuareg forces.
In November 2023, Malian government forces, backed by Wagner Group mercenaries, managed to temporarily seize the city after a prolonged offensive.
The rebels later regained control of Kidal, launching active operations against government forces and defeating a Russian convoy near Tinzaouaten, which shifted the balance of forces in the war.
In July, Mali’s junta forces, together with the Africa Corps, regained control of the city of Anefis in the north of the country.
The city is located approximately 100 km from Kidal and holds significant strategic importance for controlling Mali’s northern regions.

articles.title: Russian missile strike on apartment building in Pryluky, northern Ukraine, kills 22 people, including five children
articles.body:
Russian missile strike on apartment building in Pryluky, northern Ukraine, kills 22 people, including five children
The search and rescue operation has ended at the site of a strike on a five-story apartment building in Pryluky, in Ukraine’s Chernihiv region. A Russian Kh-101 missile partially destroyed the building on the morning of October 7, when many residents were still asleep. The strike killed 22 people, including entire families with children. Five children were killed in all. Another 54 people, including seven children, were injured. “This is the kind of ‘gift’ Putin gave himself for his birthday. Killing children, killing people,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said of the strike. Pryluky declared three days of mourning. Here’s what is known about those killed.
Viktoria Bondarenko’s family
An entire family that lived on the fifth floor, where the Russian missile hit, was killed: 58-year-old Viktoria Bondarenko, her 37-year-old daughter, Kateryna Antypenko, and Kateryna’s 1-year-old son, Sasha. Kateryna’s older daughter, Olya, survived: She was in a room on the other side of the building when the missile struck. Relatives have taken in the girl, whose age was not specified.
Kateryna worked at a tobacco factory to support the family. Viktoria looked after her younger grandson at home. Kateryna’s husband works abroad. After hearing reports of the strike, he set off for home.
Oleksandr Ivanchenko’s family
Those killed in Pryluky included Oleksandr Ivanchenko, a locomotive engineer for Ukrainian Railways; his wife, Yulia, who worked at a local secondary school; and their children, 8-year-old Maksym and 13-year-old Iryna. Ukrainian Railways CEO Oleksandr Pertsovskyi described them as “a family of railway workers spanning generations.”
Daria Maksiuta’s family
The family lived on the fourth floor of the damaged building. Daria, 23, died alongside her 32-year-old husband, Oleksandr, and their 18-month-old son, Kyrylo.
Police officer Oleh Malysh and his mother-in-law, Liudmyla
Oleh Malysh, 47, had returned from the front shortly before the strike. He had fought in the Chernihiv regional police rifle battalion but returned to Pryluky for health reasons. He and his wife, Yulia, also a police officer, lived in the building hit by the missile. On October 6, Yulia’s mother, Liudmyla, and Yulia’s sister, Kateryna, came to visit, along with Kateryna’s 3-year-old daughter, Zlatoslava. Oleh and his mother-in-law were killed. The other family members are in the hospital.
Liudmyla was likely Ukrnafta employee Liudmyla Tsyba, whose death the company reported. She worked as a painter on a corrosion protection crew and had come to visit relatives the day before the strike.
A Ukrnafta employee
Another Ukrnafta employee, Ihor Chub, was killed in the strike on the apartment building in Pryluky. He worked as an assistant driller in Ukrnafta’s well servicing and workover unit. He was 45.

articles.title: Sybiha shares details of talks with UK foreign secretary at Pryluky hospital
articles.body:
Sybiha shares details of talks with UK foreign secretary at Pryluky hospital
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has shared details of his talks with his UK counterpart Ed Miliband, which took place at a hospital in Pryluky, Chernihiv Oblast.
Source: Sybiha on X (Twitter), as reported by Ukrainska Pravda
Details: Sybiha noted that this is Miliband's first official visit to Ukraine as foreign secretary.
Quote from Sybiha: "Alongside President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, we came to Pryluky, where yesterday a Russian missile struck a residential building, killing 22 people, including five children. Ed saw firsthand the devastating consequences of Russia's attacks on Ukrainian civilians. We held our talks at a local hospital."
Details: Sybiha added that he had briefed his UK counterpart on the latest battlefield developments, Russia's intensifying terror, and ongoing diplomatic efforts.
He also said that the talks had covered the steps needed to strengthen Ukraine's position and increase pressure on Moscow to end its aggression.
Quote: "We paid particular attention to immobilised Russian assets and the need to use them fully and make Russia pay for the destruction it has caused. We also discussed tightening sanctions, including against Russia's shadow fleet."
Details: Another important topic was Ukraine's readiness for winter.
Quote: "We discussed additional British assistance to strengthen our energy resilience, protect critical facilities, and keep Ukrainian homes heated and powered."
Details: The officials also addressed Black Sea security, including Russian attacks on civilian vessels and maritime infrastructure that threaten freedom of navigation and global food security.
Quote from Sybiha: "We also launched the second meeting of the Political Pillar of the Ukraine-UK Strategic Partnership Dialogue and agreed to continue expert-level discussions in Kyiv."
Background:
- Earlier, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Miliband, who had arrived in Kyiv on a visit, had been invited to visit Pryluky to see the reality of Russia's daily strikes.
- During his visit to Pryluky, Miliband assured Ukraine that the UK would provide "concrete support".

articles.title: South Korea test-flies its first home-grown hypersonic weapon
articles.body:
South Korea test-flies its first home-grown hypersonic weapon
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung hails the test as a major step in strengthening the country’s conventional defence capabilities
South Korea flight-tested on Thursday its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon, designed to fly at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defence systems, bringing Seoul closer to what it says could be game-changing weapons capabilities.
There was no immediate response from North Korea, which last week tested its own hypersonic missile that landed in the waters near Japan.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung attended the test, saying it was a major step in strengthening the country’s conventional defence capabilities, according to a statement. It did not elaborate where the test took place.
The statement said the weapon separated from its booster rocket at the planned altitude, then descended and manoeuvred both vertically and horizontally before hitting a test target. It said once developed, the weapon would be able to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean peninsula theatre of operations”.

articles.title: Serviceman recruited by Russia while AWOL detained for directing strikes on Ukrainian forces
articles.body:
Serviceman recruited by Russia while AWOL detained for directing strikes on Ukrainian forces
The SBU said this in a statement seen by Ukrinform.
The operation to expose the suspect was carried out with the assistance of the Commander-in-Chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
The Russian agent was a mobilized serviceman from the Poltava region who directed fire at the positions of his assault regiment and adjacent units of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
The investigation established that the Russians were primarily interested in the coordinates of the largest concentrations of Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel and equipment, as well as training grounds where the suspect underwent combat training.
According to SBU cyber specialists, the man was recruited by Russian intelligence services after he was AWOL from his military unit and began looking for easy ways to make money through Telegram channels.
After being recruited, he was instructed to return from his unauthorized absence to his unit and gather intelligence to help direct Russian strikes.
The SBU documented the man transmitting the geolocation of his battalion's temporary deployment site to the Russians before leaving his military unit under the pretext of going to a hospital.
Instead of visiting a medical facility, he went into hiding at his home in Kremenchuk.
SBU officers took advance measures to secure the positions of Ukraine's Defense Forces in the area of enemy intelligence activity and detained the spotter.
During searches, officers found a smartphone that was used to coordinate his actions with his Russian handler. To maintain secrecy, the agent used an anonymous chat and regularly deleted his correspondence.
SBU investigators notified the detainee that he was suspected under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (high treason committed under martial law).
The suspect is being held in custody without the right to bail. He faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property.
